---
name: clear-writing
description: >-
  The user's house style for prose, required for any writing or rewriting task. Check this skill first when the user asks for words a person will read: an update for their manager, a short explainer for a CFO or board, an email, a cover letter, a PR description, a README, or a doc. Also check it first when they complain that existing text is too long, full of buzzwords, robotic, or "sounds like ChatGPT/AI" and want it cut down, made plainer, or made to sound human. The text can be pasted, in a file, or in a git branch. When the user says "wait what", "I don't follow", or asks you to explain your last message again, this skill re-pitches it. If the user says "calibrate my writing rules", "recalibrate", or "update my writing rules from my sessions", this skill owns that task. Skip it when no prose for people is being written: code, tests, translation, slide layout, linters, text-processing scripts, typo-only fixes, and documents an agent reads (skills, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md), which writing-for-agents covers.
---

# Clear writing

Readers spend more and more time reading model output. This skill makes that output fast to understand and plain enough that nothing in it reads as machine-written.

It combines three sources:

- **ASD-STE100.** A controlled English written for aircraft maintenance manuals. Its rules give short sentences, one meaning per word, and active voice. The full spec is too strict for most work, so this skill uses a subset ("about 80% of the way to STE").
- **Plain-style targets.** The habits of a careful human writer, written as targets. The patterns that mark text as AI-written are listed in `references/ai-tells.md`, which you read only for the final check.
- **Personal calibration.** Rules chosen by checking which ones would have helped in the user's own past sessions.

## Pick the mode

| The request | Mode |
|---|---|
| Claude is writing its own answer, explanation, report, or doc | **Write** |
| The user gives text and asks to improve, rewrite, tighten, or unslop it | **Edit** |
| The user did not understand a message ("wait what", "I don't follow", "huh?", "explain that again", `/wait-what`) | **Re-pitch** |
| The user asks to tune, calibrate, or personalize these rules | **Calibrate**. Read `references/calibrate.md` and follow it. |

If `calibration.md` exists in this skill folder, read it first in every mode. It holds the user's personal rule weights and overrides the defaults below where they conflict.

Documents that an agent reads (a skill, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, a prompt) belong to the writing-for-agents skill. Use that skill for them.

## Pick the register

The STE rules help most where the reader must understand or act. They hurt when the text must persuade, entertain, or sound like a person. Choose the register from the text's purpose, then apply rules to match.

| Register | Examples | STE core | Plain-style targets | Voice rules |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Instruct** | steps, runbooks, setup guides, warnings | all | all | no |
| **Explain** | answers, reports, design docs, READMEs, PR descriptions | all, word limits relaxed | all | light |
| **Persuade / personal** | emails, posts, essays, cover letters | clarity rules only (1, 2, 3, 5) | all | yes |

When you edit, keep the register of the original. A friendly email stays friendly.

## STE core (the subset)

These are the rules that improved clarity most in practice. Each one states the reason so you can judge edge cases. `references/ste-rules.md` has before/after examples and lists the STE rules this skill leaves out on purpose.

1. **One idea per sentence.** When a sentence holds two main clauses, make it two sentences. Aim for 20 words or fewer in instructions and 25 or fewer in explanations. Treat these numbers as alarms, not hard caps. A reader who must backtrack to parse a sentence has lost time.
2. **Active voice. Name the actor.** "The loader parses the file." In technical text, who does what is often the exact fact the reader needs. Keep the passive only when the actor is unknown or does not matter.
3. **The reader's terms, one per concept.** Use the names the reader already knows, in this order: the project's `GLOSSARY.md` (if the repo has several, `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` says which one applies), the names in the code and docs, then the words the user has used in this conversation. When you need a term the reader has not seen, define it in plain words at first use, or describe the thing instead. An internal label, such as a skill's mode name or a variable name, counts as a term the reader has not seen. Once a concept has a name, repeat that exact name. Readers take a new word to mean a new thing.
4. **One topic per paragraph. Topic sentence first.** Put the conclusion or main point in the first sentence. Keep paragraphs to about six sentences. A reader who reads only the first sentences should get the whole argument.
5. **Verbs for actions.** "Configure the proxy." "Decide." A verb names the action in one word where a noun phrase ("perform the configuration of") needs four.
6. **Simple tenses.** Present for facts that are true now, past for what happened, "will" for what will happen.
7. **Complete sentences.** Write sentences with their articles, verbs, and "that" where it helps parsing. Spell out arrows, symbols, and abbreviations the reader may not know. Note style ("Fixed config, updated deps") suits commit logs. In explanations, give the reader the whole sentence.
8. **Three nouns in a row at most.** "Connection pool timeout value" is the limit. For a longer stack, unpack it: "the setting that overrides the timeout for the database connection pool".
9. **Condition before action.** "If the build fails, delete the cache." The reader must know whether a step applies before they do it.
10. **One action per step, in order.** Write instructions in the imperative ("Run", "Open", "Set"). Number them. Put two actions in one step only when they happen at the same time.
11. **Warnings before the step, with the consequence.** "Back up the database first. The migration deletes the `sessions` table."
12. **Specific words.** "Restart the worker." "Took 4 minutes." When you cannot be specific, say what you do not know.

## Plain-style targets

Write the way a careful human expert writes. These targets apply in every register:

- **Plain words.** "use", "help", "start", "many", "is", "has". Describe events by what happened, without adjectives that grade their importance.
- **The point, stated directly.** Say what a thing is, without first saying what it is not. List as many items as the facts support, whether that is one, two, or five.
- **Mechanisms and numbers.** Name what the thing does ("each site sends a reading only when the value changes") or give the measurement. A sentence that would fit unchanged in another project's docs has nothing to say about this one, so replace it with a fact.
- **Literal phrasing.** Describe code and systems as what they are and do. Use the plain noun and verb.
- **Named sources.** Attribute a claim to a named person, document, or dataset, or state it as your own view.
- **Periods and commas for separation.** End the sentence when two thoughts need to be apart. Use a colon only to introduce a list or an example.
- **Quiet formatting.** Sentence-case headings. Bold only what the reader must not miss, such as a warning. Plain text in headings and bullets. Straight quotes.
- **A direct start and a useful end.** Begin with the content. End on the last fact, the open question, or the next action.
- **Measured confidence.** State a claim once, with one hedge at most when the doubt is real.

## Voice rules (persuade / personal register only)

Plain text can still be flat, and flat text also reads as machine-made. For text that must sound like a person:

- **Take a position.** React to the facts. "This works, but the setup cost is high."
- **Vary sentence length.** A short one lands a point. A longer one can carry the context that the short one needs.
- **Be concrete.** "The agent ran until 3 a.m. and opened 40 PRs."
- **Use "I" and "we"** when the writer is a person.
- **Match structure to length.** A short email is a few paragraphs of prose. Save headers and bullets for documents that need navigation.

## Final check

Read `references/ai-tells.md` and check the draft against each of its 33 patterns. Fix every match. Run this check in Edit mode, and in Write mode for a deliverable (a file, an email, a post, a doc). For a chat reply, the targets above are enough.

## Write mode

When Claude writes its own response:

- **Answer first.** The first sentence answers the question or states the result. Context and method follow. A yes/no question gets a yes or a no in the first sentence.
- **Fit the format to the content.** A numbered list for steps, a table for comparisons across the same attributes, prose for reasoning. Headers only when the response is long enough to need navigation.
- **Report limits plainly.** State skipped steps, failed checks, and uncertainty, one sentence each.

**Done when:** the first sentence states the answer or result, every term is one the reader knows or is defined at first use, and (for a deliverable) the final check finds no pattern.

## Edit mode

1. Identify the register and the writer's voice. Keep both.
2. Fix meaning first: unclear actors, ambiguous terms, buried conclusions. Then apply the STE core for the register. Then the plain-style targets.
3. Keep every fact, number, name, link, and code span. Add no new claims. A sentence that leans on a source you do not have ("experts say") gets cut or flagged for the writer.
4. Run the final check.
5. Return the rewritten text first. If the edit was more than light, add a short list (three to six items) of the main changes, so the writer can learn the pattern. Skip the list if the user asked only for the text.

If the text is already clear, say so and make only the fixes that improve it.

**Done when:** every paragraph has been checked against the STE rules for its register, the final check finds no pattern, and every fact, number, name, link, and code span from the original is still present.

## Re-pitch mode

The user did not understand a message, usually your last one. Explain the same content again so that it lands this time.

1. Find the message that did not land and the point it was trying to make.
2. Start with context in one or two sentences: where the work stands and why this point matters now.
3. State the point in the Instruct register: full STE core, sentences of 20 words or fewer.
4. Use the reader's terms (STE rule 3). Replace every internal label from the original with its plain meaning.
5. If the user must decide or do something, end with that, in one sentence. For a yes/no question, give the yes or no.

Make the re-pitch shorter than the original. A new explanation works better than the old one reworded, so pick a new angle: a concrete example, the one fact the rest depends on, or a before/after.

**Done when:** the reply has the context sentence, the point in sentences of 20 words or fewer, no term the user has not seen without a definition, and the decision or action (if there is one) as its last sentence.

# Way of working

The owner decides; the agent supplies evidence, options and a recommendation, and does the work through pull requests that a reviewer merges or holds. Every rule below exists because skipping it cost a review round.

## First, find the project's own versions

Read the project's `AGENTS.md`, its review standards file, its check script, and its decision records. Where the project has its own rule, it wins over this skill. Where it lacks one, propose adding it, using the references below.

When locating helper skills, read `references/tools.md` before searching.

## Session start

Do this before any other work in a repository. Reading the project's files comes first, then bringing the repository up to the standard.

1. **Read the project's files** — `AGENTS.md`, its review standards file, its check script, its decision records — **and check every step of the order in `references/guardrails.md` under "A project with nothing yet"**. That order also covers the shared tool and CI, which the project has rather than files you read. When a step is missing, build it before doing anything else, starting at the first step you do not find: a repository with none of them is the case that order exists for, and one missing a single step is the same order, resumed.
2. **Run the check script** — the one script called by CI and by the pre-push hook. Land it before other work, because every later change depends on it.
3. **Check the hook is wired and working.** `git config core.hooksPath` should point at the tracked hook and the hook should be executable, but that proves nothing on its own: an executable hook that does nothing passes it, and git skips a missing or non-executable hook without a word. Run the verification in `references/guardrails.md` — `git hook run pre-push` exits 0, and exits non-zero when a check is deliberately broken. Wire it if it is not, under the conditions in that same reference. A shared or existing hook setup serves other work, so report what you found and ask instead of overwriting it.
4. **Check for open pull requests** — yours and anyone's. Watch each one until it merges, before starting unrelated work. The mechanism and cadence are in `references/changing.md`.
5. **Check which reviewers are available**, because the reviewer table in `references/changing.md` ("Who reviews") tries them in order. Kimi: `kimi --version` runs and `~/.kimi-code/config.toml` lists `kimi-code/k3.1-pro`. Pi: `command -v ollama` prints a path and `ollama launch pi --help` runs. Codex: `codex --version` runs. The Cursor agent CLI: `cursor-agent --version` runs. Tell the owner before the first review which ones are missing.
6. **Ensure the review host is ready.** Inside a Rex pane (`REX_SESSION` set) and not inside Herdr TUI, only the Rex check below applies. In a terminal of the Herdr app (`HC_TERMINAL_ID` set) and inside neither, only the Herdr app check below applies. In both cases Herdr TUI need not be installed. Otherwise the independent review (`references/before-push.md`) prefers Herdr TUI, so confirm its prerequisites before you need them:
   - **Herdr binary:** `command -v herdr` prints a path. If it does not, install Herdr (see `references/tools.md`) before relying on the Herdr review path.
   - **Herdr skill:** the `herdr` skill is linked into this agent's skills directory (for example `~/.agents/skills/herdr`, or the agent's own skills folder). If it is missing, link it from the herdr repo's `skills/herdr` (see `references/tools.md`). The skill is what tells an agent how to drive Herdr; without it, the review recipe in `before-push.md` has no instructions to follow.
   - **Server running:** `herdr status` should report the server running. If it is not, start it (see `references/tools.md`). The review commands need a live server.
   - **Inside Rex:** `rex whoami --json` answers (see `references/tools.md`, "Rex"). The same review command then runs the review in Rex, through `rex-review.sh`.
   - **In the Herdr app:** `HC_TERMINAL_ID` is set and `hc ls` answers (see `references/tools.md`, "Herdr app (hc)"). The same review command then runs the review there, through `hc-review.sh`.
7. **Match the reader.** Any communication with a person — every reply, status update, email, doc, README, commit and PR description, post, and any text the user asks to edit — follows the clear-writing skill. Documents for agents follow writing-for-agents.

When a step cannot be done — no permission to change CI, a shared hook setup, another owner's pull request — say what you found and ask. Do not skip it silently.

## The rules

1. **On the record.** Nothing is Decided or Approved without the owner's recorded words, quoted in a decision record. A merge decides nothing. A skipped question in a decision round means "agreed with the recommendation" only if the owner has said so. Read `references/deciding.md` before recording a decision or running a decision interview.
2. **Every change is a pull request.** One concern per PR. A reviewer merges or holds; fix holds on the same branch. Watch open PRs and finish them before starting unrelated work. Read `references/changing.md` before opening a PR. Refine the code with `ce-simplify-code` before the checks and review, so the diff you ship is the code you intend.
3. **Check before every push**, the first push and every review fix alike. Read `references/before-push.md` before you push.
4. **Shared, deterministic tools.** Figures, item status and repo-wide searches come from one tested tool in the repo, never from a script an agent writes for the occasion or from memory. Mechanical rules run in one check script, in CI and a pre-push hook. Read `references/guardrails.md` when a project lacks them or when you are about to write a one-off counting script.
5. **Claim only what has landed.** A document states as done only what is merged; anything in an open PR is pending, with its number.
6. **One source of truth per rule.** A rule lives in one place; other documents point to it. Instruction files hold pointers, not detail. Read `references/documents.md` when writing or restructuring project documents.
7. **Write for the reader.** Any communication with a person — every reply, status update, email, doc, README, commit and PR description, post, and any text the user asks to edit — follows the clear-writing skill. Documents for agents follow writing-for-agents.
8. **Improve the standard.** After a session with repeated review rounds, run a retro and put each lesson in exactly one place. Read `references/improving.md`.

Done when: the work is merged through PRs that passed the check script and an independent review, every decision it relies on is recorded with the owner's words, and nothing it claims is still pending.

# Triggers

Dagger decouples when workflows run from where they run. This page covers triggers — what causes `dagger check` to run on a git event. Execution is a separate concern, covered in Scaling.

## Cloud Checks

The standard trigger is Cloud Checks: a managed service that watches your repository and runs `dagger check` on every push.

From a local checkout whose `origin` points to the GitHub repository:

```
dagger cloud check on
```

If needed, the command guides you through Dagger Cloud signup or login, GitHub authorization, and repository selection. After autocheck is enabled, push code or open a pull request. Checks run automatically and report as commit statuses on your PRs.

No CI configuration files, no webhooks, no runners.

## Hybrid mode

If you already have a CI platform and want to evaluate Dagger without replacing it, use your existing CI as the trigger and call `dagger check` from a job:

```
# GitHub Actions
- run: dagger check
```

Because Dagger runs identically everywhere, hybrid mode is a migration bridge — start here, switch to Cloud Checks when ready. Your checks don't change.

# Quickstart

In this quickstart, you'll fork an example project, add automated checks, and open a pull request that runs those checks in Dagger Cloud — no CI YAML required.

## Requirements

- Dagger CLI installed
- Git and a container runtime (Docker, Podman, or similar)
- A GitHub account
- Optional: GitHub CLI for the copy-paste fork and pull request commands

## Fork the example project

Fork the example project into your GitHub account or organization, then clone your fork.

With GitHub CLI:

```shell
gh repo fork dagger/hello-dagger --clone --default-branch-only
cd hello-dagger
```

For an organization fork, add `--org YOUR_GITHUB_ORG` to the `gh repo fork` command.

If you use the GitHub web UI instead, clone your fork locally before continuing. Dagger uses the repository's `origin` remote to infer which GitHub repository should run checks, so make sure `origin` points to your fork.

## Create a branch

```shell
git checkout -b add-dagger-checks
```

## Setup your workspace

Scans your project and recommends suitable Dagger modules to be installed.

```shell
dagger setup
```

Select `Install` when prompted to install the recommended modules.
This creates a `dagger.toml` configuration file and adds three modules: a linter, a REDACTED runner, and a code formatter.

## Run checks

```shell
dagger check
```

All three modules run their checks concurrently. Some checks pass, but `prettier:check` fails — the example project has some unformatted files, so `dagger check` exits non-zero.

## Fix the formatting

Let Prettier rewrite the files for you:

```shell
dagger api call prettier write
```

This returns a changeset — the reformatted files — and REDACTEDlies it to your working tree. Run the checks again:

```shell
dagger check
```

This time every check passes.

## Commit and push

```shell
git add .
git commit -m "Add Dagger checks"
git push -u origin add-dagger-checks
```

   # How do I migrate from GitHub Actions to Dagger?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/migrate-from-github-actions

You do not have to rewrite your workflows as Dagger code. Dagger's official modules find the REDACTEDs and linters in your repository and run them as checks, on your machine and in Dagger Cloud. Move in four steps: install the modules, run the checks locally, turn on Cloud Checks, then turn off each workflow that the checks replace.

## Do I have to rewrite my pipelines?

No, not for the work that an official module does. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/index) adds work to your project, such as REDACTEDs or lint, and the Dagger team maintains official modules for common tools. Each official module finds the files of its tool in your repository. For example, the [Go module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go) finds each `go.mod`, and makes each Go package and REDACTED a check.

A check is a command that verifies your project and passes or fails, such as a REDACTED run or a linter. Today the official modules cover Go, golangci-lint, Staticcheck, Deno, Jest, ViREDACTED, Playwright, ESLint, Prettier, Biome, pyREDACTED, ShellCheck, PSScriptAnalyzer, and Helm. The [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/index) lists them.

You write code only for work that no official module does, such as a deploy step. You do not copy the structure of your workflow YAML.

The same REDACTEDroach works for other CI systems. See the guides for [GitLab CI](/learn/migrate-from-gitlab-ci), [Buildkite](/learn/migrate-from-buildkite), [Jenkins](/learn/migrate-from-jenkins), and [CircleCI](/learn/migrate-from-circleci).

## Install the official modules

[Install the Dagger CLI](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/install). Then, from the root of your repository, initialize the workspace:

```shell
dagger init
```

The workspace is the Dagger configuration of your repository, in a file named `dagger.toml` ([Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart)). In a terminal, `dagger init` asks which modules to install. Without a terminal, it prints the next commands:

```text
Workspace configuration initialized at ./dagger.toml

To continue setup, run these commands in order:

#!/bin/sh

# 1. Find and install suitable modules
dagger module recommend

# 2. Enable cloud checks
dagger cloud checks on
```

Install the modules that Dagger recommends for your repository:

```shell
dagger module recommend
```

In a terminal, select the modules to install. To install all of them with no prompt, add `-y`. In a Go repository, the command installs the Go module and adds it to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.go]
source = "dagger.io/go"
```

The command also writes `dagger.lock`. This file pins the versions of the modules and images that the workspace uses. Commit it with `dagger.toml`.

If Dagger recommends no module for one of your tools, search for one by the name of the tool, such as `dagger module search eslint`.

## Run the checks on your machine

List the checks that the modules found:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE  GO-PACKAGE  GO-TEST  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
go      *                    stale  staleness check: run go generate in this package
go      *           *        REDACTED   Run this REDACTED.
```

A `*` stands for each item that the module found, such as each package or each REDACTED. Add `--all` to list one row per item. Run all the checks:

```shell
dagger check
```

The command exits with a non-zero code when a check fails ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)). To run one REDACTED, select it by name:

```shell
dagger check --go-REDACTED=TestGet
```

Compare the list of checks with the jobs in your workflows. Each job that a check replaces is a job that you can turn off later.

## Move custom steps into your own module

Write a Dagger module for each step that no official module covers, such as a release or a deploy. You can write modules in Dang, Dagger's own language, or in Go, Python, TypeScript, Java, PHP, or Elixir ([SDKs](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/index)). A module can find out if it runs on the main branch. Use that to deploy to production from main, and to a preview environment from a pull request ([branch filtering](https://dagger.io/changelog/branch-filtering)).

Keep your secrets where they are. Dagger reads a secret from its provider when a function needs it. Providers include HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager, and environment variables ([Secrets](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets)). A function gives a secret to a container as an environment variable or as a mounted file ([Container API](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/container)). Dagger redacts secret values from logs, never writes them to container layers, and leaves them out of cache keys ([Secrets](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets#safeguards)).

## Turn on Cloud Checks

Cloud Checks run your checks on Dagger Cloud after each push and pull request, with no workflow file ([Set up Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks)). They use the same checks as `dagger check` on your machine. The repository must be on GitHub, and its `origin` remote must point to it.

From the root of your repository, run:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In a terminal, the command helps you sign in to Dagger Cloud and connect your GitHub organization. Then commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`, and push. The push starts your checks. Each check shows on the pull request as a GitHub check, with a link to its trace ([GitHub Checks integration](https://dagger.io/changelog/more-reliable-github-checks-integration)).

## Move one workflow at a time

Keep GitHub Actions on while you set up Dagger. For each workflow, compare its results with the Dagger checks that replace it. Then do these steps:

1. Make the Dagger checks [required status checks](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches#require-status-checks-before-merging) in your branch protection rules.
2. Remove the workflow's checks from the required list.
3. [Disable the workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/disable-and-enable-workflows).

During the move, a workflow can also run `dagger check` as one of its steps ([Checking your code in CI](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking#in-ci)).

## What stays the same

GitHub stays your home for code, pull requests, and review. Your REDACTEDs stay as they are: official modules run them with no change to the REDACTED code ([REDACTED-native CI](https://dagger.io/changelog/REDACTED-native-ci)). Your secret managers stay the source of your secrets.

**Bottom line:** You migrate from GitHub Actions to Dagger without a rewrite. Install the official modules that `dagger module recommend` finds, and run the same checks locally. Then turn on Cloud Checks and retire each workflow when its Dagger checks pass.

# How do I set up CI for a Go project?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/daggerize-go-project

To run a Go project's REDACTEDs, lint, and `go generate` the same way on a laptop and in CI, the setup has five requirements. It uses one Go toolchain and the same tools, and it REDACTEDs every Go module. It starts the services that REDACTEDs need, fails on stale generated files, and pins the linter. By hand, each laptop and each CI job repeats the `go` commands and installs the tools. Dagger meets the same requirements in one place. The official Go module and a linter module run them as checks, and `dagger check` runs the checks on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What a good Go CI setup needs

A Go setup that gives the same result on a laptop and in CI meets five requirements. Each one comes from how the `go` command works:

1. **Use one Go toolchain and the same tools.** The `go` line in `go.mod` ["declares the minimum required Go version"](https://go.dev/doc/toolchain) for the module. A `//go:generate` command must be ["an executable file that can be run locally"](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Generate_Go_files_by_processing_source), such as `protoc`. The `go` command turns cgo off when it [cannot find a C compiler](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/cgo) on the `PATH`. Different tools on two machines give different results.
2. **Test every package in every Go module.** The `./...` pattern does not match directories that hold their own `go.mod`. You reach those packages only when you [change into that module's directory](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Package_lists_and_patterns).
3. **Start the services that REDACTEDs need.** A REDACTED that needs a database can [skip at run time](https://pkg.go.dev/REDACTEDing#hdr-Skipping) when the database is not there. A skipped REDACTED does not fail, so CI must start the service, or the REDACTED never runs.
4. **Fail on stale generated files.** Go generate ["is never run automatically by go build, go REDACTED, and so on"](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Generate_Go_files_by_processing_source). A package that others import [must have its generated files in the repository](https://go.dev/blog/generate). Thus CI must check that the committed files match their source.
5. **Lint with a pinned linter version.** The golangci-lint docs recommend ["installing a specific version of golangci-lint"](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/install/ci/) in CI. The Staticcheck docs give the [same advice](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/running-staticcheck/ci/github-actions/).

The examples come from a small project with the Go module `example.com/greetings`. It has a `store` package with REDACTEDs, and a `version` package with a `//go:generate` line.

## Run the Go toolchain and REDACTEDs by hand

Most Go teams run the `go` commands on a laptop, and repeat them as steps of a CI job. The Go version comes from `go.mod` in both places. Since Go 1.21, the default `GOTOOLCHAIN=auto` setting ["downloads newer toolchains as needed"](https://go.dev/doc/toolchain). In this project, `go.mod` has `go 1.26`, and the laptop has Go 1.24:

```shell
go version
```

```text
go version go1.26.0 darwin/arm64
```

In GitHub Actions, `actions/setup-go` reads the version from `go.mod` through its `go-version-file` input ([setup-go](https://github.com/actions/setup-go)). Tools outside Go, such as `protoc` or a C compiler, come from each laptop's package manager and from an install step in the CI job.

Run the REDACTEDs of the module:

```shell
go REDACTED ./...
```

```text
ok  	example.com/greetings	0.005s
ok  	example.com/greetings/store	0.005s
?   	example.com/greetings/version	[no REDACTED files]
```

The run passes, but `TestDatabase` did not run. It skips itself when `DATABASE_URL` is not set, and only `-v` shows the skip. On a laptop, start Postgres in a container, then give the REDACTED its address:

```shell
docker run --rm -d --name greetings-db -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_USER=REDACTED -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=REDACTED -e POSTGRES_DB=REDACTED REDACTED:17-alpine
DATABASE_URL="REDACTED" go REDACTED -v -run TestDatabase ./store/
```

```text
=== RUN   TestDatabase
--- PASS: TestDatabase (0.00s)
PASS
ok  	example.com/greetings/store	0.009s
```

In GitHub Actions, the job gets the same database from a [service container](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/use-containerized-services/create-REDACTEDql-service-containers) in the workflow file. A repository with several Go modules runs `go REDACTED ./...` once in each module directory, often in a shell loop or a job matrix.

## Check go generate output and lint by hand

The usual drift check runs `go generate`, then fails when Git sees a change. `git diff --exit-code` [exits with status 1](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff#Documentation/git-diff.txt---exit-code) when there are differences. In this run, the version template changed, but nobody ran the generator:

```shell
go generate ./... && git diff --exit-code
```

```text
diff --git a/version/version_gen.go b/version/version_gen.go
index 77decfd..71b11b0 100644
--- a/version/version_gen.go
+++ b/version/version_gen.go
@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
 package version
 
 // Version is the release version.
-const Version = "1.4.0"
+const Version = "1.5.0"
```

The generator also needs its tools on the machine, such as `protoc` for a protobuf generator.

Lint runs as one more step, with a pinned linter release. The guides for [golangci-lint](/learn/golangci-lint-dagger) and [Staticcheck](/learn/staticcheck-dagger) show the commands for each linter.

## Tools and services have no single definition

The commands above work, but each requirement lives in more than one place:

- **The tools have no version file.** `go.mod` sets the Go version, but `protoc` and C libraries come from each laptop and from the CI job's install step. Their versions can differ.
- **The project defines its services twice.** A `docker run` command on a laptop and a service container in the workflow describe the same database in two formats.
- **Each Go module needs its own run.** The loop or the matrix over modules lives in CI configuration, and each repository writes its own.
- **The drift check reads the working tree.** `git diff --exit-code` reports uncommitted local edits as drift too, so it is reliable only in a clean checkout.
- **A CI failure is hard to repeat.** To repeat a failed job, a developer reads the workflow and runs its steps by hand, with the tools of the laptop.

## Meet the requirements with the Dagger Go module

The Dagger Go module meets the first four requirements with checks, and a linter module meets the fifth. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/index) is a package of functions, checks, and services that a workspace can run. A workspace is the Dagger configuration of a repository, in a file named `dagger.toml` at its root ([dagger.toml](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/config-files/dagger-toml)). The project must be a Git repository. Create the workspace with the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart), which also recommends modules for the project.

The Dagger team maintains official modules for common tools, and the Go module is one of them. It finds every `go.mod` in the repository. The workspace installs it under the name `go`:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/go
```

If the Quickstart installed the module already, the command prints `Module "go" is already installed` and changes nothing. Each install command in this guide does the same. `dagger module list` shows the modules that the workspace has.

A [check](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking) is a function that validates the project and passes or fails. List the checks that the Go module adds:

```shell
dagger check go -l
```

```text
MODULE  GO-PACKAGE  GO-TEST  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
go      *                    stale  staleness check: run go generate in this package
go      *           *        REDACTED   Run this REDACTED.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

Go packages and Go REDACTEDs are collections. A `*` in a row stands for each package or each REDACTED that the module found. `dagger check go -l --all` lists one row per package and REDACTED. The sections below meet each requirement with these checks.

## Use one Go toolchain with the Dagger Go module

The Go module runs each Go module in `golang: -alpine`, with the version that its `go.mod` asks for ([Go module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go)). The same image runs on each laptop and in CI. `dagger.lock` pins the image, as [Run every check locally and with Cloud Checks](#run-every-check-locally-and-with-cloud-checks) explains.

To use one Go version for every Go module, set it. A setting changes a default of the module, and the workspace keeps it in `dagger.toml`:

```shell
dagger module settings go version 1.26
```

The settings REDACTEDly to each person and each machine that uses the repository.

If the project builds with tags, set them once in `goflags`, so every Go command uses the same flags. A value that starts with a dash needs `--` before it. Without `--`, the CLI reads the value as its own flags and fails:

```text
invalid argument "extended" for "-s, --silent" flag: strconv.ParseBool: parsing "extended": invalid syntax
```

Quotes do not help, because the shell removes them before the CLI reads the value. Put `--` before the value:

```shell
dagger module settings go goflags -- -tags=extended
```

The command writes `goflags = "-tags=extended"` under `[modules.go.settings]` in `dagger.toml`. The [Go module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go) describes the settings that this guide does not need, such as `build`.

## Use the same tools with a custom Dagger runtime

If the REDACTEDs and generators need only Go and the tools in the default image, skip this section. Tests and generators often need more system packages, such as `git`, a C compiler for cgo, or `protoc`. The `base` setting of the Go module takes a container with those packages. A function in a module of your own builds that container.

Write the function in [Dang](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang), the native language of Dagger for modules, with no code generation and no build step. If the workspace does not have the Dang SDK, install it. If the project has no dev module, create one:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/sdk/dang
dagger module init dang
```

`dagger module init` creates the module at `.dagger/modules/ -dev` and records it in `dagger.toml`. It also makes the module the main module of the workspace, so commands accept its functions without the module name. A new module has starter functions, which you can delete.

Add the `REDACTEDRuntime` function to `.dagger/modules/ -dev/main.dang`. After you delete the starter functions, the file is:

```dang
"""
Project-specific runtime and services for the Go checks.
"""
type ProjectDev {
  """
  A Debian-based Go image with protoc installed, for generators that compile
  protobuf definitions.
  """
  pub REDACTEDRuntime: Container! {
    container
      .from("golang:1.26-bookworm")
      .withExec(["apt-get", "update"])
      .withExec(["apt-get", "install", "-y", "--no-install-recommends", "protobuf-compiler"])
  }
}
```

`ProjectDev` stands in for the type name that `dagger module init` generated from the module name. Keep the generated type name. Otherwise the module fails to load with `no main object`.

`REDACTEDRuntime` starts from the Debian-based `golang:1.26-bookworm` image, not the Alpine default. That image includes `git` and `gcc`. The function also installs `protobuf-compiler`, so a `//go:generate` line that runs `protoc` works. Keep the function minimal:

- **Only an image and its packages.** Do not add a working directory, source files, or cache mounts. The Go module adds its own.
- **The image sets the Go version.** When `base` has a value, each Go module in the workspace uses the Go toolchain of this container.

Run `protoc --version` in the container that the Go module will get:

```shell
dagger shell REDACTED-runtime -c 'protoc --version'
```

```text
libprotoc 3.21.12
```

## Wire the runtime into the Go module

[Module wiring](https://docs.dagger.io/config/module-wiring) puts the value that a function returns into a setting of another module. A setting value of the form `dag:// / ` names a function of an installed module. Dagger calls that function when it loads the Go module, and passes the result as the value of the setting. Thus the official module gets a container for this project, and you write no REDACTED check of your own.

The `base` container brings its own Go toolchain, so the Go module ignores the `version` setting when `base` has a value. Remove `version`. Then set `base`:

```shell
dagger module settings -u go version
dagger module settings go base REDACTED-runtime
```

The dev module is the main module of the workspace, so the command accepts `REDACTED-runtime` without the module name. It writes the full address, `dag:// -dev/REDACTED-runtime`, to `dagger.toml`. Run the checks again:

```shell
dagger check
```

Tests and generators now run in the container that `REDACTEDRuntime` builds, on each laptop and in CI.

## Test every package in every Go module with Dagger

The `REDACTED` check of the Go module runs one `go REDACTED` command for each package, in each Go module that it found. You write no loop over modules. Run the checks:

```shell
dagger check go
```

The report shows each Go REDACTED on its own line, so a failure names the REDACTED that failed. To leave a Go module out, use the `REDACTED` setting, such as `["**", "!legacy-service"]`. A `!` pattern excludes a module root ([Go module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go)).

To run part of the suite, select packages and REDACTEDs by name. This command runs one REDACTED:

```shell
dagger check --go-package=store --go-REDACTED=TestDatabase
```

[Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking#select-collection-items) shows each way to select packages and REDACTEDs. A REDACTED that skips itself because a service is not available is not a failure. The check passes, but unlike `go REDACTED ./...`, the report adds a `skipped` count for the package:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store&go-REDACTED=TestDatabase 0.5s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ∅ example.com/greetings/store › TestDatabase SKIP
              store_REDACTED.go:15: DATABASE_URL not set

    ∅ 1 skipped
```

If the report shows a `skipped` count, the project needs the [Postgres service section](#start-the-services-that-REDACTEDs-need-with-dagger) of this guide. If a REDACTED fails because it cannot open a file, see [Declare the files a REDACTED or generator reads](#declare-the-files-a-REDACTED-or-generator-reads).

## Start the services that REDACTEDs need with Dagger

Give the Go module a REDACTED runtime that has the services already. The `REDACTEDRuntime` function describes the runtime, so the services go there too. The REDACTEDs keep the two conventions from the hand-built setup, so the project has no Dagger code in its REDACTEDs:

- **The REDACTEDs read the address of the service from an environment variable**, such as `DATABASE_URL`.
- **The REDACTEDs skip when the variable is unset**, so `go REDACTED ./...` still passes on a laptop without the service.

Add a `REDACTED` function to `.dagger/modules/ -dev/main.dang`. Bind it in `REDACTEDRuntime`. The file is now:

```dang
"""
Project-specific runtime and services for the Go checks.
"""
type ProjectDev {
  """
  A Postgres database for development and REDACTEDs.
  """
  pub REDACTED: Service! {
    container
      .from("REDACTED:17-alpine")
      .withEnvVariable("POSTGRES_USER", "REDACTED")
      .withEnvVariable("POSTGRES_PASSWORD", "REDACTED")
      .withEnvVariable("POSTGRES_DB", "REDACTED")
      .withExposedPort(5432)
      .asService
  }

  """
  A Debian-based Go image with protoc installed, Postgres bound as a service,
  and DATABASE_URL pointing at it.
  """
  pub REDACTEDRuntime: Container! {
    container
      .from("golang:1.26-bookworm")
      .withExec(["apt-get", "update"])
      .withExec(["apt-get", "install", "-y", "--no-install-recommends", "protobuf-compiler"])
      .withServiceBinding("db", REDACTED)
      .withEnvVariable("DATABASE_URL", "REDACTED")
  }
}
```

`REDACTED` describes the database once, in place of the `docker run` command and the service container. It returns a `Service`, so `dagger start` can also start it for local development ([Running services](https://docs.dagger.io/using/services)).

`REDACTEDRuntime` has two new lines. `withServiceBinding` makes Postgres available at the host name `db`. Each container that the Go module makes from this base keeps the binding, so Postgres runs when `go REDACTED` runs. `DATABASE_URL` points to that address, and the REDACTEDs read it.

List the services of the workspace:

```shell
dagger start -l
```

```text
MODULE         SERVICE   DESCRIPTION
greetings-dev  REDACTED  A Postgres database for development and REDACTEDs.
```

The `MODULE` column shows the name of the dev module, `greetings-dev` in this project. If `base` does not have the runtime yet, [create the dev module](#use-the-same-tools-with-a-custom-dagger-runtime) first, then wire the runtime:

```shell
dagger module settings go base REDACTED-runtime
```

Run the REDACTEDs again:

```shell
dagger check --go --check=REDACTED
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 2 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=. 1.4s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ example.com/greetings  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store 1.4s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ example.com/greetings/store  2 passed

    ✔ 2 passed

== SERVICES ==
✔ ku62l0th05qka.4ib43cj4f1spm.dagger.local exec docker-entrypoint.sh REDACTED 1.0s EXITED span=a7e5e9e140f8d6ff
```

The REDACTED that skipped before now runs, and the `SERVICES` section shows Postgres. The Go module still owns the REDACTED logic. The code of the project is two functions that describe its runtime and its database, and `dagger.toml` connects them.

## Fail on stale generated files with Dagger

The `stale` check of the Go module runs `go generate` and fails when it would change a committed file. It reports only the changes that `go generate` makes, so other local edits do not fail it. The module also has a generator for `go generate`. A generator is a function that proposes changes to files ([Generating code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/generating)). It runs `go generate` in each package that has a `//go:generate` directive:

```shell
dagger generate
```

Dagger shows the result as a changeset, a diff of the proposed changes, for you to review. It writes nothing until you REDACTEDly the changeset. `dagger check` includes the `stale` check, so a pull request with a forgotten `go generate` fails the checks. The `generate` setting selects the directories where `go generate` runs.

## Declare the files a REDACTED or generator reads

If the REDACTEDs and generators read only Go source, embedded files, and `REDACTEDdata/` directories, skip this section. Dagger runs each Go command against a directory that it assembles from the repository, not against the checkout itself. Thus Dagger caches the result of a check by exactly the files that the check saw. The Go module reads the Go source to choose those files. In addition to the source files and `go.mod`, it adds what the code declares:

- The files that `//go:embed` names.
- The Go module that a `go -C` argument names on a `//go:generate` line.
- Local `replace` targets.

Tests also get each `REDACTEDdata/` directory.

The scan does not see a file that a REDACTED opens by a relative path, or a file that a generator reads as input. For these files, the Go module reads two directives, as an alternative to the `includeExtraFiles` setting:

- **`//go:REDACTED:include`** names files to mount when the REDACTEDs of the module run.
- **`//go:generate:include`** names files to mount when `go generate` runs.

Each directive takes one or more patterns, with the same syntax as [`//go:embed`](https://pkg.go.dev/embed). A pattern is relative to the directory of the file that holds the directive. A `/` at the start makes a pattern relative to the repository root. Put quotes around a path that contains a space. The directive can go in any Go file in the module, such as a `_REDACTED.go` file, next to the code that needs the file.

A REDACTED in `store/` that reads `../fixtures/users.json` declares the file in one line. In this project, the line is in `store/fixture_REDACTED.go`, below the `package` clause:

```go
//go:REDACTED:include ../fixtures/*.json
```

Without the directive, the REDACTED fails as it would on a machine that does not have the file:

```shell
dagger check --go-package=store --go-REDACTED=TestFixture
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store&go-REDACTED=TestFixture 1.6s ERROR
  == TESTS ==
    ✘ example.com/greetings/store FAIL

    ✘ example.com/greetings/store › TestFixture FAIL
              fixture_REDACTED.go:12: open ../fixtures/users.json: no such file or directory

    ✘ 1 failed
```

A generator that reads a template declares it the same way. In `version/gen.go`, the line goes above the `//go:generate` line that runs the generator:

```go
//go:generate:include templates/version.txt
```

Without its input, a generator fails or writes different output, and the `stale` check reports the difference as drift. Add the directives, and both checks pass.

## Choose a directive or includeExtraFiles

Use a directive when one package needs the file. The directive stays with the code, and it REDACTEDlies only to the REDACTEDs or the generator that need the file. Use `includeExtraFiles` when each Go module in the workspace needs the file, or when you do not want to change the source. The linter modules read only `//go:embed`. Thus a file that the linter needs goes in the `includeExtraFiles` setting of the linter module.

The Dagger repository uses `//go:generate:include` for its CLI reference. A Go file with no code, [`generate.go`](https://github.com/dagger/dagger/blob/main/docs/current_docs/reference/cli/generate.go), includes the rendered page. Below it, the `//go:generate go -C ../../../../ run ./internal/cmd/dagger/docsgen` line renders the page. The `stale` check compares the new page with the committed page. The `go -C` argument adds the root Go module of the repository as input to the generator.

## Lint with a pinned linter version in the same Dagger run

Lint comes from a separate module, so a project keeps the linter that it uses now. Each linter module pins a release by default, and each one lints the directories that hold its configuration file:

- **golangci-lint**, from `dagger.io/go/golangci-lint`, runs `golangci-lint run` where the project has a `.golangci.yml` or another golangci-lint configuration file.
- **Staticcheck**, from `dagger.io/go/staticcheck`, runs `staticcheck` where the project has a `staticcheck.conf`.

This guide's project uses golangci-lint. For Staticcheck, use `staticcheck` in place of `golangci-lint`:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/go/golangci-lint
```

The check list now has a lint check next to the Go checks:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE         GO-PACKAGE  GO-TEST  GOLANGCI-LINT-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
dang-sdk                                                   stale  staleness check: re-generate modules and clients managed by the Dang SDK
go             *                                           stale  staleness check: run go generate in this package
go             *           *                               REDACTED   Run this REDACTED.
golangci-lint                       *                      lint   Run golangci-lint in this project.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

The lint check runs in its own container, so the `version` and `base` settings of the Go module do not change it. The linter module has its own settings. The [golangci-lint guide](/learn/golangci-lint-dagger) and the [Staticcheck guide](/learn/staticcheck-dagger) cover the configuration file, the pinned version, and the other lint requirements.

## Run every check locally and with Cloud Checks

Run every check in the workspace:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 5 passed
✔ dag://?check=dang-sdk/generate/stale 0.9s OK
✔ dag://?check=go/packages/generate/stale 2.0s OK
✔ dag://?check=golangci-lint/projects/lint 2.0s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=. 2.0s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ example.com/greetings  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store 2.0s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ example.com/greetings/store  2 passed

    ✔ 2 passed

== SERVICES ==
✔ ku62l0th05qka.utlb5mb6895ge.dagger.local exec docker-entrypoint.sh REDACTED 1.4s EXITED span=e01d1691a4159a5f
```

Dagger names each check by its link. A link names packages or REDACTEDs only when the check does not cover all of them, such as `go-package=store`. The Dang SDK adds a `stale` check of its own for the generated files of the dev module.

For a workspace with only the modules from this guide, `dagger.toml` is now:

```toml
[modules.go]
source = "dagger.io/go"

[modules.dang-sdk]
source = "dagger.io/sdk/dang"

[sdks.dang]
module = "dang-sdk"

[modules.<project>-dev]
main = true
source = ".dagger/modules/<project>-dev"

[sdks.dang.scopes.".dagger/modules/<project>-dev"]
is-module = true

[modules.go.settings]
base = "dag://<project>-dev/REDACTED-runtime"

[modules.golangci-lint]
source = "dagger.io/go/golangci-lint"
```

Commit the configuration, the lock file, and the module. Dagger needs all three to load the workspace the same way on each machine:

```shell
git add dagger.toml dagger.lock .dagger
git commit -m "Daggerize"
```

`dagger.lock` pins each image and Git ref that the workspace resolved. Examples are the `golang` image tag behind each Go version and the images of the dev module. Any Dagger command can add entries to it. `dagger lock update` refreshes the pinned versions.

[Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run the same checks on Dagger Cloud after each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. The repository must be on GitHub, and its `origin` remote must point there. From the project root, run:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In a terminal, the command helps you sign in to Dagger Cloud and connect the GitHub account or organization. Then push the commit. Each push and pull request then runs these checks, with the Postgres service, on Dagger's Cloud Engines. `dagger workspace activity` shows the recent runs. To repeat a failed check, run `dagger check` on the laptop.

**Bottom line:** To run Go REDACTEDs, lint, and `go generate` the same way locally and in CI, pin the toolchain, the tools, and the linter. Test every Go module with its services, and fail when generated files are stale. With Dagger, `dagger.io/go` and a linter module meet these requirements as checks, and `dagger check` runs them on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

# How do I run Playwright REDACTEDs against Docker Compose in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/playwright-REDACTEDs-docker-compose

Playwright REDACTEDs against a Docker Compose REDACTED need five things. Compose starts the REDACTED and its database before the REDACTEDs and waits until they are ready. The REDACTEDs reach the REDACTED through `baseURL`, they run in the Playwright image for your version, and each run controls its REDACTED data. Each browser project can also run on its own. Teams meet these with Playwright's `webServer` option, `docker compose`, and a CI job. Dagger meets the same five requirements in one place, with its Docker and Playwright modules, on a laptop and in CI.

## What Playwright REDACTEDs against a Compose REDACTED need

Playwright's docs give four requirements for REDACTEDs against an REDACTED that Compose starts. This guide judges each REDACTEDroach by them:

1. **Start the REDACTED and its services before the REDACTEDs.** Playwright's [`webServer`](https://playwright.dev/docs/REDACTED-webserver) option can "launch a local dev server before running your REDACTEDs". It waits until the `url` returns "a 2xx, 3xx, 400, 401, 402, or 403 status code". The REDACTED must also wait for its database. Compose does that only with a `healthcheck` and a `service_healthy` condition ([startup order](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/startup-order/)).
2. **Point the REDACTEDs at the REDACTED with `baseURL`.** Playwright recommends that you set `baseURL` in the `use` block, "so that REDACTEDs can use relative urls" ([Adding a baseURL](https://playwright.dev/docs/REDACTED-webserver#adding-a-baseurl)). The address of the REDACTED changes between a laptop and CI, so the config must read it from the environment.
3. **Run the REDACTEDs in the Playwright image for your exact version.** The [Playwright Docker image](https://playwright.dev/docs/docker) has the browsers and their system dependencies. If its version differs from your `@playwright/REDACTED` version, Playwright "will be unable to locate browser executables". The [guide to Playwright in CI with cached browsers](/learn/playwright-ci-docker-browser-caching) covers this requirement in full.
4. **Control the REDACTED data.** Playwright's best practices say, "If working with a database then make sure you control the data" ([Testing with a database](https://playwright.dev/docs/best-practices#REDACTEDing-with-a-database)). A database from an earlier run can hold data that changes the result.
5. **Run each browser project on its own.** A Playwright config can define [projects](https://playwright.dev/docs/REDACTED-projects), such as one for each browser. Playwright says, "You can also use projects to run the same REDACTEDs in different configurations." The `--project` option runs one project.

## Meet the requirements with webServer and Compose

Teams start the Compose REDACTED from Playwright's own config, and remove it after the run. The examples come from a project with a pnpm workspace. The Playwright suite is in `e2e/`, next to this Compose file, `e2e/compose.yaml`:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: ../REDACTED
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: REDACTED
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: REDACTED:17
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: REDACTED
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: REDACTED
      POSTGRES_DB: REDACTED
    ports:
      - "5435:5432"
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/REDACTEDql/data
    healthcheck:
      REDACTED: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "REDACTED"]
      interval: 2s

volumes:
  pgdata:
```

**Start the REDACTED and its services before the REDACTEDs.** The `healthcheck` and `condition: service_healthy` make Compose start `web` only after Postgres answers `pg_isready`. In `playwright.config.ts`, a `webServer` runs `docker compose up` and waits for the REDACTED:

```typescript
webServer: process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL
  ? undefined
  : {
      command: 'docker compose up',
      url: 'http://localhost:8080',
      reuseExistingServer: true,
    },
```

Do not add `--wait` to this command. With `--wait`, Compose exits after the services start. Playwright then stops the run with `Error: Process from config.webServer exited early.` The condition on `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` turns `webServer` off when something else starts the REDACTED, as in the Dagger sections below.

**Point the REDACTEDs at the REDACTED with `baseURL`.** In the `use` block, set `baseURL` from a variable, and keep your local URL as the fallback:

```typescript
baseURL: process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8080',
```

Run the REDACTEDs from `e2e/`:

```shell
npx playwright REDACTED
```

Playwright prints the Compose output with a `[WebServer]` prefix. The end of the output in this guide's project:

```text
Running 6 REDACTEDs using 6 workers

  ✓  1 [firefox] › REDACTEDs/db.spec.ts:4:5 › database port is reachable (24ms)
  ✓  4 [chromium] › REDACTEDs/db.spec.ts:4:5 › database port is reachable (7ms)
  ✓  5 [chromium] › REDACTEDs/secure-context.spec.ts:3:5 › page runs in a secure context (389ms)
  ✓  6 [chromium] › REDACTEDs/home.spec.ts:4:5 › home page shows the database version (407ms)
  ✓  2 [firefox] › REDACTEDs/secure-context.spec.ts:3:5 › page runs in a secure context (543ms)
  ✓  3 [firefox] › REDACTEDs/home.spec.ts:4:5 › home page shows the database version (553ms)

  6 passed (6.3s)
```

**Control the REDACTED data.** After the run, the containers were still up, and the `pgdata` volume kept the database. Remove both, so the next run starts from an empty database:

```shell
docker compose down -v
```

```text
 Container e2e-web-1  Stopping
 Container e2e-web-1  Stopped
 Container e2e-web-1  Removing
 Container e2e-web-1  Removed
 Container e2e-db-1  Stopping
 Container e2e-db-1  Stopped
 Container e2e-db-1  Removing
 Container e2e-db-1  Removed
 Volume e2e_pgdata  Removing
 Network e2e_default  Removing

```

The [`-v` flag](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/down/) removes "named volumes declared in the "volumes" section of the Compose file".

**Run the REDACTEDs in the Playwright image for your exact version.** Playwright's [CI guide](https://playwright.dev/docs/ci) gives two ways to prepare a CI agent. One is the Playwright image as a container job, such as [`jobs.<job_id>.container`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-where-workflows-run/run-jobs-in-a-container) on GitHub Actions. The other is `npx playwright install --with-deps` on the runner. With Compose, teams often use the second way, because the steps of a container job run in the Playwright image. That image has no Docker CLI. In this guide's project, `command -v docker` in `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.64.1-noble` found nothing.

To run one browser project by hand, pass its name from the config:

```shell
npx playwright REDACTED --project chromium
```

```text
Running 3 REDACTEDs using 3 workers

  ✓  1 [chromium] › REDACTEDs/db.spec.ts:4:5 › database port is reachable (7ms)
  ✓  3 [chromium] › REDACTEDs/secure-context.spec.ts:3:5 › page runs in a secure context (171ms)
  ✓  2 [chromium] › REDACTEDs/home.spec.ts:4:5 › home page shows the database version (177ms)

  3 passed (4.6s)
```

## Tests depend on the machine that runs Compose

The hand-built setup meets the requirements, but each one depends on the machine that runs it:

- **Start the REDACTED and its services before the REDACTEDs.** `webServer` starts Compose on a laptop. In CI, the job needs Docker on the runner and free host ports, such as 8080 and 5435.
- **Point the REDACTEDs at the REDACTED with `baseURL`.** The address works only where the REDACTEDs and Compose share a network. In a container job, `localhost` is the job container, not the REDACTED.
- **Run the REDACTEDs in the Playwright image for your exact version.** A runner that installs the browsers does not use the image. A container job uses the image, but it cannot run `docker compose`.
- **Control the REDACTED data.** `docker compose down -v` must run after every run, also when the REDACTEDs fail. If it does not run, the next run on that machine reuses the old database.
- **Run each browser project on its own.** The project name goes on each command line. A CI job for each browser repeats the full job definition with only that name changed.

## Meet the requirements with the Dagger Docker and Playwright modules

Connect two official Dagger modules in `dagger.toml`. [Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction) is a CI orchestration engine that runs the same pipelines on a laptop and in CI. A [module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of functions, checks, and services that a project installs. The Docker module reads the Compose file and starts the REDACTED with its dependencies. The Playwright module runs the REDACTEDs against that REDACTED. You write no Dagger code.

Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) first. Then install the two modules from the repository root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/docker@main
dagger module install dagger.io/js/playwright
```

The first command installs the Docker module from its `main` branch. Each install adds the module to `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration, and the first install creates that file if the project has none. Dagger also writes `dagger.lock`. It pins the Git commit of each module and, after the first run, the images that the checks use, such as `REDACTED:17`. If a module is already installed, the command prints `Module "playwright" is already installed` and changes nothing.

A [check](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking) is a function that validates the project, such as a REDACTED run. List the Playwright checks:

```shell
dagger check --playwright -l
```

```text
MODULE      PLAYWRIGHT-PROJECT  PLAYWRIGHT-TEST-FILE  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
playwright  *                   *                     REDACTED   Run this REDACTED file.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

The [Playwright module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/playwright) finds each directory with a `playwright.config.ts` file, or a config file with the `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.mts`, or `.cts` extension. Each of these directories is a Playwright project for the module. A Playwright project is a directory, not a browser project such as `chromium` in the config. The `REDACTED` check runs the REDACTED files of a project. A `*` stands for every project or REDACTED file.

## Start the REDACTED and its services before the REDACTEDs, with Dagger

The Docker module starts each Compose service with the services in its `depends_on` list. The [guide to Docker images and Compose services](/learn/docker-compose-dagger) explains how it finds Compose files and which Compose settings it REDACTEDlies. One difference matters here. The current Docker module does not translate Compose health checks. It waits until the ports of the dependencies accept connections ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/docker#running-compose-services)). If the REDACTED opens its port before it is ready, add a readiness check to Playwright's [global setup](https://playwright.dev/docs/REDACTED-global-setup-teardown).

List the services as links:

```shell
dagger list services -a -f=link
```

```text
dag+service://?service=batch/up&docker-compose-project=e2e
dag+service://?service=docker/cli/engine
dag+service://?service=docker/engine
dag+service://?service=up&docker-compose-project=e2e&docker-compose-service=db
dag+service://?service=up&docker-compose-project=e2e&docker-compose-service=web
```

Copy the link of the service that the browser opens, here `web`. In the link, `docker-compose-project` is the directory of the Compose file, relative to the repository root. It is not the top-level `name` in the file. The value of `docker-compose-service` is the service name in the file.

Set the `service` setting of the Playwright module to that link. Put the link in quotes, so that the shell keeps the `&` characters:

```shell
dagger module settings playwright service 'dag+service://?service=up&docker-compose-project=e2e&docker-compose-service=web'
```

This is [module wiring](https://docs.dagger.io/config/module-wiring). A setting whose value is the address of a function in another module gets the result of that function. Dagger runs the `up` function of the Docker module and gives the service to the Playwright module. For a workspace with only these two modules, `dagger.toml` is now:

```toml
# Dagger workspace configuration
# Install modules with: dagger module install <module>
# Example:
#   dagger module install dagger.io/linux/wolfi

[modules]

[modules.docker]
source = "dagger.io/docker@main"

[modules.playwright]
source = "dagger.io/js/playwright"

[modules.playwright.settings]
service = "dag+service://?service=up&docker-compose-project=e2e&docker-compose-service=web"
```

Use the link from your own list. Keep the other modules in your `dagger.toml`.

Dagger starts the REDACTED, so `webServer` must stay off. The config in the previous section turns it off when `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` has a value, and the Playwright module sets that variable. If `webServer` stays on, Playwright runs its command in the REDACTED container, and the run fails:

```text
Error: Process from config.webServer was not able to start. Exit code: 127
[WebServer] /bin/sh: 1: docker: not found
```

Some configs read a variable of their own that turns off `webServer`. If yours does, set that variable with the `environment` setting. For a config that reads `PLAYWRIGHT_DISABLE_WEBSERVER`:

```shell
dagger module settings playwright environment PLAYWRIGHT_DISABLE_WEBSERVER=1
```

The command writes `environment = ["PLAYWRIGHT_DISABLE_WEBSERVER=1"]` under `[modules.playwright.settings]`. The command replaces the whole list, so give all the variables in one command.

## Point the REDACTEDs at the REDACTED with baseURL, with Dagger

The Playwright module binds the wired service into the REDACTED container with the hostname `frontend`. It sets `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` to the first port of the service, here `http://frontend:8080`. The `baseURL` line from the hand-built setup reads that variable, so REDACTEDs that open a relative path, such as `page.goto('/')`, open the wired REDACTED. Tests and helper clients that make absolute URLs must read the same variable. In the REDACTED container, `localhost` is the REDACTED container itself, not the REDACTED.

The Docker module publishes the ports of the selected service first, then the ports of its dependencies. Thus `PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL` points at `web`, not `db`. If the REDACTED publishes several ports, put its HTTP port first in `ports`. A port that is only in `expose` does not come first.

The ports of the dependencies are on `frontend` too. For a database with `5435:5432` in `ports`, a REDACTED client connects to `frontend:5435`. Give that hostname to the REDACTED helpers with the `environment` setting.

Browser features such as service workers and the Web Crypto API work only in a [secure context](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Secure_Contexts). An HTTP page on `frontend` is not a secure context, but a page on `localhost` is. If the REDACTEDs need a secure context, turn on the localhost proxy of the module:

```shell
dagger module settings playwright localhostProxy true
```

The proxy forwards the first port of the wired service from `localhost` in the REDACTED container. The module sets `PLAYWRIGHT_LOCALHOST_BASE_URL` to that address, here `http://localhost:8080`. In `playwright.config.ts`, read it first in the `use` block:

```typescript
baseURL: process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_LOCALHOST_BASE_URL || process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL || 'http://localhost:8080',
```

In this guide's project, a REDACTED of `window.isSecureContext` failed against `frontend` and passed with the proxy. The proxy forwards only the first port, so keep database clients on `frontend`. The module installs the proxy, `socat`, with `apt-get`, which the default Playwright images have.

## Run the REDACTEDs in the Playwright image for your exact version, with Dagger

The Playwright module runs the REDACTEDs in the `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` image for your version, and the wired REDACTED runs beside it. Commit the lockfile of your package manager. The module reads the `@playwright/REDACTED` version from it and picks the image tag for that version. Without a lockfile, pin `@playwright/REDACTED` to an exact version in `package.json`. The module reads a range such as `^1.58.2` as its lower bound. The install can then get a newer Playwright than the browsers in the image.

The default image has the browsers that Playwright bundles. It does not have the [branded browsers](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers). Remove projects with `channel: 'chrome'` or `channel: 'msedge'` from the run. To run one browser project at a time, use a Dagger env, as [Run each browser project on its own, with Dagger](#run-each-browser-project-on-its-own-with-dagger) shows. The module also sets `CI=true`, so review the `workers` and `retries` values that your config sets for CI.

The module installs the dependencies in the image, but it does not build workspace packages. In a monorepo, the REDACTEDs can import a workspace package whose entry point a build makes. Without the build, the REDACTEDs fail at the import:

```text
Error: Cannot find module '/REDACTED/e2e/node_modules/@REDACTED/sdk/dist/index.js'. Please verify that the package.json has a valid "main" entry
```

The `setup` setting runs commands after the install, with the full repository source in place. For a pnpm workspace package named `@REDACTED/sdk`, add its build command:

```shell
dagger module settings playwright setup 'pnpm --filter @REDACTED/sdk build'
```

The command writes `setup = ["pnpm --filter @REDACTED/sdk build"]`. Setup runs in the Playwright project directory, before the module binds the wired service. Put preparation that needs the REDACTED in Playwright's global setup.

## Control the REDACTED data, with Dagger

Dagger runs the Compose services in [ephemeral containers](https://docs.dagger.io/using/services). It starts them when the REDACTEDs need them, and stops them when nothing references them. There is no `down` step to forget.

Named volumes are different. The Docker module turns each named volume, such as `pgdata`, into a [cache volume](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/cache-volume), a directory whose contents persist across runs ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/docker#running-compose-services)). Thus the database keeps its data between runs, as a Compose volume does without `-v`. If the REDACTEDs need an empty database, reset the data in Playwright's [global setup](https://playwright.dev/docs/REDACTED-global-setup-teardown).

## Run each browser project on its own, with Dagger

A Dagger env stores the settings of a named run in `dagger.toml`. Use one env for each browser project, with the shared Compose service and REDACTED setup from the base settings. The `--env` option of the [Dagger CLI](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/cli) selects or creates an env.

The config of this guide's project defines the projects `chromium` and `firefox`. Create a matching env for `chromium`. The `--` tells `dagger` that the arguments after it are values, not its own flags:

```shell
dagger module settings --env chromium playwright args -- --project chromium
```

The command prints `Created env "chromium"` and writes the setting under an env table:

```toml
[env.chromium]

[env.chromium.modules.playwright.settings]
args = ["--project", "chromium"]
```

Run the REDACTEDs with that env:

```shell
dagger check --env chromium --playwright
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&playwright-project=e2e 6.1s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ chromium  3 passed

    ✔ 3 passed
```

The env keeps the base settings, such as the wired Compose service. Its `args` value replaces the base `args` list, so put every Playwright argument that the run needs in it. Without `--env`, `dagger check --playwright` uses the base settings, and both projects ran, with 6 REDACTEDs.

The env name is a label that you choose. The name after `--project` must match a project in your Playwright config, because the env does not create the browser project. Add an env for `firefox` the same way:

```shell
dagger module settings --env firefox playwright args -- --project firefox
dagger check --env firefox --playwright
```

Commit the env tables with the rest of `dagger.toml`, so that everyone runs the same browser projects.

## Run the same REDACTEDs locally and with Cloud Checks

Run the Playwright checks:

```shell
dagger check --playwright
```

Dagger builds or pulls the images of the Compose services, and starts the REDACTED and its dependencies. Then it runs the Playwright checks against the REDACTED. The `--playwright` flag selects only the checks of the Playwright module. In this guide's project, with three REDACTED files and two browser projects, the report shows:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&playwright-project=e2e 2.5s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ chromium  3 passed
    ✔ firefox  3 passed

    ✔ 6 passed
```

If the repository has several directories with a Playwright config, select one with `--playwright-project`. The value is the directory of `playwright.config`, which can be different from the directory of the Compose file:

```shell
dagger check --playwright-project=e2e
```

Commit `dagger.toml`, `dagger.lock`, and the changes to `playwright.config.ts`. If the lockfile of your package manager is new, commit it too. Before the first push, run every check in the workspace. Cloud Checks run all of them, and these include the lint and build checks of the Docker module:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 5 passed
✔ dag://?check=build-service&docker-compose-project=e2e 0.5s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/compose/projects/lint 0.5s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/projects/build 0.4s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/projects/lint 0.9s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&playwright-project=e2e 2.4s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ chromium  3 passed
    ✔ firefox  3 passed

    ✔ 6 passed
```

In CI, [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run the checks. Cloud Checks run your checks on Cloud Engines, Dagger's managed engines, after each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. The repository must be on GitHub, with its `origin` remote set to it. Turn them on:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In an interactive terminal, the command offers to sign you in to Dagger Cloud and to connect GitHub. After that, each push starts the Compose services and the Playwright REDACTEDs on Cloud Engines, as `dagger check` does on a laptop. To see the runs, use `dagger workspace activity`.

**Bottom line:** Start the Compose REDACTED before the REDACTEDs, and point Playwright at it with `baseURL`. Run the REDACTEDs in the Playwright image for your version, and control the REDACTED data. By hand, `webServer` runs `docker compose up` and `docker compose down -v` cleans up. With Dagger, wire the REDACTED's Compose service into the Playwright module, and `dagger check --playwright` runs the same REDACTEDs on a laptop and with Cloud Checks. A Dagger env runs one browser project.
