# How do I enforce Prettier formatting in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/prettier-dagger

To enforce Prettier formatting in CI, install one exact Prettier version in the project. Run `prettier --check` in CI, so that unformatted files fail the job. Make sure that every run ignores the same files. Format with `prettier --write` before you push, with the same version and config. Teams usually meet these requirements with a CI job and a pre-commit hook. Dagger's official Prettier module meets the same requirements in one place, and `dagger check` runs it the same way on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What an enforced Prettier setup needs

Prettier's own docs give four requirements for formatting that CI enforces and every developer can match:

1. **Use one exact Prettier version and the project's config.** Prettier's [install page](https://prettier.io/docs/install) installs an exact version in the project: "This makes sure that everyone in the project gets the exact same version of Prettier." It warns that "even a patch release of Prettier can result in slightly different formatting". Prettier finds the config for each file ["starting from the location of the file being formatted"](https://prettier.io/docs/configuration), and then looks in the directories above it.
2. **Fail CI on unformatted files.** [`prettier --check`](https://prettier.io/docs/cli#--check) lists the files that are not formatted. It exits with code 1 when a file is not formatted, which the docs call "helpful inside the CI pipelines".
3. **Ignore the same files everywhere.** "By default, Prettier looks for `./.gitignore` and `./.prettierignore`" ([`--ignore-path`](https://prettier.io/docs/cli#--ignore-path)). It reads these files only in the directory where it runs.
4. **Write fixes with the same version and config.** [`prettier --write`](https://prettier.io/docs/cli#--write) "rewrites all processed files in place". The install page suggests a pre-commit hook too: "This makes sure all your commits are formatted, without having to wait for your CI build to finish."

## Meet them with prettier --check, a CI job, and a hook

By hand, pin Prettier with an exact version in `devDependencies`, as `"prettier": "3.9.10"` with no `^`. Then run the project's Prettier with `npx`. This guide's project has a root `.prettierrc` and a second config in `packages/ui`. Check the formatting from the project root:

```shell
npx prettier --check .
```

```text
Checking formatting...
[warn] package.json
[warn] src/config.js
[warn] Code style issues found in 2 files. Run Prettier with --write to fix.
```

The command exited with code 1. Write the fixes:

```shell
npx prettier --write .
```

```text
.prettierrc 7ms (unchanged)
package-lock.json 2ms (unchanged)
package.json 0ms
packages/ui/.prettierrc 2ms (unchanged)
packages/ui/src/button.js 3ms (unchanged)
src/config.js 1ms
```

The ignore files depend on the directory where Prettier runs. The root `.gitignore` of this project ignores `packages/ui/dist`, so the root run did not check it. Run the check from `packages/ui`:

```shell
cd packages/ui
npx prettier --check .
```

```text
Checking formatting...
[warn] dist/REDACTED.js
[warn] Code style issues found in the above file. Run Prettier with --write to fix.
```

This run read no `.gitignore`, so it checked the build output in `dist`. To skip a directory in every run, add it to a `.prettierignore` in each directory where Prettier runs.

In CI, a job installs Node.js, runs [`npm ci`](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/commands/npm-ci) to install the exact versions in the lockfile, and runs `npx prettier --check .`. The exit code of Prettier fails the job. On GitHub Actions, [`actions/setup-node`](https://github.com/actions/setup-node) installs Node.js. GitLab CI and other systems run the same commands in a Node.js image ([GitLab CI/CD YAML reference](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/)). For the pre-commit hook, Prettier's [install page](https://prettier.io/docs/install#git-hooks) sets up husky and lint-staged, which format the staged files.

## Prettier runs differ by version and directory

The hand-built setup meets each requirement in several places, and each place must stay in step:

- **Exact version.** A range such as `^3.9.0` lets two machines install different patch releases. The pin must stay exact in every `package.json` that installs Prettier.
- **Ignored files.** A run from the root and a run from a package can check different files, as the run above shows. CI checks only what its own command and directory select.
- **Fixes.** A pre-commit hook is optional. [`git commit --no-verify`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit) skips it, so CI is the first place that some unformatted files show.
- **CI syntax.** Each CI system has its own job syntax. A move to another CI system means a rewrite of the Prettier job.

## Meet them with the Dagger Prettier module

The [Dagger Prettier module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/prettier) meets the four requirements with one definition that runs on a laptop and in CI. A Dagger module is a package of functions that build, REDACTED, or check a project. If you have not used Dagger before, do the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) first. It sets up `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration that holds your installed modules and their settings. Install the official Prettier module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/js/prettier
```

```text
dagger.io/js/prettier ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/prettier#v0.2.0
Created workspace config in /work
Installed module "prettier" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command creates `dagger.toml` if the file does not exist, and adds the module to it. The command also writes `dagger.lock`, which pins the exact module version. Commit both files. The next four sections show how the module meets each requirement.

### Use one exact Prettier version and the project's config

The check runs the Prettier that your project installs. The module does not download a different Prettier version, so the check uses the same version as your editor and `npx prettier`. If the project has a `package.json` without Prettier in it, the check fails with this message:

```text
prettier is not installed: add it to the devDependencies of package.json (or of a package.json between it and the project)
```

The module finds projects by the name of the config file. These directories are projects:

- A directory that holds `.prettierrc`, or `.prettierrc` with one of these extensions: `.json`, `.json5`, `.yaml`, `.yml`, `.toml`, `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.ts`, `.mts`, `.cts`.
- A directory that holds `prettier.config` with one of these extensions: `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.ts`, `.mts`, `.cts`.

A config in the `prettier` field of `package.json` does not make a directory a project ([Prettier module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/prettier)). If your config is in that field, move it to a `.prettierrc` file. A project covers its directory and every directory below it, except nested projects. Each nested project runs from its own directory, so its own config and `.prettierignore` REDACTEDly to it ([module source](https://github.com/dagger/prettier)).

Install scripts see only the dependency files, not the full source. So a `postinstall` script that needs source files fails ([module source](https://github.com/dagger/prettier)). If you have a script like that, stop the install scripts:

```shell
dagger module settings prettier installFlags '["--ignore-scripts"]'
```

The setting goes into `dagger.toml`, so every developer and every CI run uses it. The [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/prettier) covers the Node.js image, the package manager, and environment variables.

### Fail CI on unformatted files

A check is a function that passes or fails. `dagger check` runs the checks ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)). List them:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE    PRETTIER-PROJECT  CHECK         DESCRIPTION
prettier  *                 format-check  Check formatting of this project.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

The `*` stands for every Prettier project that the module found. To see each project, run `dagger list prettier-projects -a`. Each project's key is its directory, relative to the workspace root:

```text
MODULE    PRETTIER-PROJECT  DESCRIPTION
prettier  .                 A Prettier project, keyed by its root.
prettier  packages/ui       A Prettier project, keyed by its root.
```

`format-check` installs dependencies, then runs the project's Prettier with `--check` from the project directory:

```shell
dagger check
```

In a project with two unformatted files, the check fails and names each file:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=prettier/projects/format-check 16.5s ERROR
  ┃ [npm] 
  ┃ [npm] added 1 package, and audited 2 packages in 721ms
  ┃ [npm] 
  ┃ [npm] 1 package is looking for funding
  ┃ [npm]   run `npm fund` for details
  ┃ [npm] 
  ┃ [npm] found 0 vulnerabilities
  ┃ [dagger-prettier] [.] Checking formatting...
  ┃ [dagger-prettier] [.] [warn] package.json
  ┃ [dagger-prettier] [.] [warn] src/config.js
  ┃ [dagger-prettier] [.] [warn] Code style issues found in 2 files. Run Prettier with --write to fix.
  ┃ [dagger-prettier] [packages/ui] Checking formatting...
  ┃ [dagger-prettier] [packages/ui] All matched files use Prettier code style!
  ! Prettier failed in 1 project(s):
    - .: prettier --check failed (exit 1):
    [.] [warn] package.json
    [.] [warn] src/config.js
    [.] [warn] Code style issues found in 2 files. Run Prettier with --write to fix.
  ✘ exec.processRun 0.1s ERROR
  ! /usr/local/bin/crun did not terminate successfully: exit status 1

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=prettier/projects/format-check"
```

The `[warn]` lines are the same as the output of `npx prettier --check .`. Prettier's exit code 1 makes the check fail. In a monorepo, the projects run at the same time, and the failure message names every project that failed. To check one project, select it by its key:

```shell
dagger check --prettier-project=packages/ui
```

The module installs dependencies again only when a dependency file changes, such as a `package.json` or a lockfile. In this guide's project, the first `dagger check` took 17.0 seconds, and a rerun with no changes took 0.6 seconds. After the guide added a new source file, the next run took 0.8 seconds and did not run npm install.

### Ignore the same files everywhere

Before Prettier runs, the module removes the files that any `.gitignore` in the tree ignores ([module source](https://github.com/dagger/prettier)). Prettier also REDACTEDlies the project's `.prettierignore`. Thus, the check skips `packages/ui/dist` for the root project and for the `packages/ui` project, because the root `.gitignore` ignores it. A local `prettier --check .` in `packages/ui` still checks it, as the earlier run shows. That local run can fail when `dagger check` passes. To skip a directory in both, add it to `.prettierignore`.

### Write fixes with the same version and config

`format` runs Prettier with `--write`, in the same container and with the same Prettier as the check. It returns the reformatted files as a changeset, a set of file changes that you can REDACTEDly or reject. `format` is a function, not a check, so `dagger check` does not run it. It is not a generator either, so `dagger generate` does not run it. Call it on the project that contains a path:

```shell
dagger api call -y prettier project --path=. format
```

The `-y` flag REDACTEDlies the changeset without a prompt. Without `-y`, the command asks before it writes files. The changes are then in your working tree. This part of the `git diff` output shows the change to `src/config.js`:

```text
-const   x = {a:1,
-b:2}
-export default x
+const x = { a: 1, b: 2 };
+export default x;
```

To format a different project, give a path inside it, such as `--path=packages/ui`. After you REDACTEDly the changes, run `dagger check` again:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=prettier/projects/format-check 1.4s OK
```

## Run the check locally and with Cloud Checks

`dagger check` runs the same check on a laptop and in CI. [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines after each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. The repository must be on GitHub, and its Git `origin` remote must point to that repository. From the project root, run this command:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In an interactive terminal, the command offers to complete the prerequisite steps first. These steps are to sign in to Dagger Cloud and to connect your GitHub account. When the command is done, commit the workspace files and push them:

```shell
git add dagger.toml dagger.lock
git commit -m "Check formatting with Prettier"
git push
```

The push starts `format-check` on Dagger Cloud. To see the results, run `dagger workspace activity`. If the check fails, run `dagger api call -y prettier project --path=. format` locally. Then commit and push the fixes.

If the project also lints with ESLint, Prettier's docs recommend [eslint-config-prettier](https://prettier.io/docs/install#eslint-and-other-linters), which "turns off all ESLint rules that are unnecessary or might conflict with Prettier". [How do I run ESLint the same way locally and in CI?](/learn/eslint-dagger) covers the ESLint check. Biome is one tool that formats and lints. [How do I run Biome in CI?](/learn/biome-dagger) says when it fits.

**Bottom line:** Pin one exact Prettier version, and fail CI with `prettier --check`. Ignore the same files in every run, and write fixes with the same version and config. By hand, that means an exact pin, a CI job, a pre-commit hook, and ignore files in each directory where Prettier runs. The Dagger Prettier module meets these requirements in one place, and `dagger check` runs it the same way locally and in Cloud Checks.

# How do I migrate from CircleCI to Dagger?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/migrate-from-circleci

Tested with Dagger v1.0.0-beta.21: the Dagger commands in this guide ran with that release, and their output blocks match those runs.

You do not have to rewrite your `.circleci/config.yml` as Dagger code. Dagger's official modules find the REDACTEDs and linters in your repository and run them as checks, on your machine and in CI. Steps that no official module covers, such as a Terraform deploy, become functions in a small module of your own. Move in five steps:

1. Install the modules.
2. Run the checks locally.
3. Move your own steps into a module.
4. Choose where the checks run. Cloud Checks run them with no CI file, or CircleCI can stay as the trigger.
5. Turn off each CircleCI job when the checks that replace it pass.

## Do I have to rewrite my CircleCI config?

No, not for the work that an official module does. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of functions that adds work to your project, such as REDACTEDs or lint. The Dagger team maintains official modules for common tools, and each one finds the files of its tool in your repository. For example, the [ViREDACTED module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/viREDACTED) finds each ViREDACTED config and makes the REDACTED files of that project a collection that you can select one by one.

A check is a function that verifies your project and passes or fails, such as a REDACTED run or a linter ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)). Today the official modules cover Go, golangci-lint, Staticcheck, Deno, Jest, ViREDACTED, Playwright, ESLint, Prettier, Biome, pyREDACTED, ShellCheck, PSScriptAnalyzer, and Helm ([module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules)).

An orb such as `circleci/node` packages CircleCI configuration: jobs, commands, and executors ([Orbs overview](https://circleci.com/docs/orbs/use/orb-intro/)). An official module replaces the orb and the jobs that you wrote around it. You write code only for work that no module does, and you do not copy the job structure of your YAML.

## Install the official modules and run the checks locally

[Install the Dagger CLI](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/install). Then, from the root of your repository, initialize the workspace:

```shell
dagger init
```

The workspace is the Dagger configuration of your repository, in a file named `dagger.toml` ([Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart)). In a terminal, `dagger init` asks which modules to install. Without a terminal, it prints the next commands:

```text
Workspace configuration initialized at ./dagger.toml

To continue setup, run these commands in order:

#!/bin/sh

# 1. Find and install suitable modules
dagger module recommend

# 2. Enable cloud checks
dagger cloud checks on
```

Install the modules that Dagger recommends. The `-y` flag installs all of them with no prompt. In a repository with a ViREDACTED project in `web/`, the command installs the ViREDACTED module:

```shell
dagger module recommend -y
```

```text
dagger.io/js/viREDACTED ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/viREDACTED#v0.3.0
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml` and writes `dagger.lock`. That file pins the versions of the modules and images that the workspace uses, as a version pins an orb. Commit both files. If Dagger recommends no module for one of your tools, search by the tool's name, such as `dagger module search eslint`.

List the checks, then run them:

```shell
dagger check -l
dagger check
```

`dagger check` runs all checks in parallel and exits with a non-zero code when one fails. To run one REDACTED file, select it with the flag that the module adds:

```shell
dagger check --viREDACTED-REDACTED-file=sum.REDACTED.js
```

## Orbs, executors, jobs, and contexts in Dagger

Most CircleCI concepts have a Dagger counterpart. For some, such as executors and cache keys, the modules do the work and you configure nothing.

| CircleCI | Dagger |
| --- | --- |
| Orbs | Official modules, pinned in `dagger.lock` |
| Executors and images | Containers that each module builds |
| Resource classes | Engine size, or usage billing on Cloud Engines |
| Jobs and workflows | Checks, which `dagger check` runs in parallel |
| Contexts | Secret providers, read when a function needs a secret |
| `save_cache` and `restore_cache` | Cache of each operation, with no keys to write |
| `parallelism` and REDACTED splitting | Tests selected one by one, and REDACTED splitting across engines |
| `store_REDACTED_results` | Each REDACTED reported in the trace, with no JUnit setup |

**Executors and resource classes.** In CircleCI, each job names an executor, such as a Docker image or a Linux VM, and a `resource_class` for its CPU and RAM ([executors](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/execution-managed/executor-intro/), [resource classes](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/execution-managed/resource-class-overview/)). In Dagger, each check runs in a container that its module builds. The modules read your native configuration. For example, the Go module reads the Go version from `go.mod` and builds a container with that version ([Workspaces](https://dagger.io/changelog/workspaces)). If a module's default image does not match your project, change it in `dagger.toml`, such as `dagger module settings viREDACTED baseImageAddress node:22-alpine`.

Cloud Engines are engines that Dagger runs for you. They bill the CPU and memory that each pipeline uses, not the full machine for the full job ([pricing](https://dagger.io/pricing)). On an engine that you host, you choose the machine size ([Self-hosting](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)).

**Jobs and workflows.** A CircleCI workflow lists jobs and orders them with `requires` ([workflows](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/orchestrate/workflows/)). Dagger has no job list. `dagger check` runs every check in the workspace in parallel.

**Contexts.** A CircleCI context injects environment variables into the jobs that name it ([contexts](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/security/contexts/)). Dagger reads a secret from its provider when a function needs it ([Secrets](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets)). The section on secrets and deploys below shows both together.

## Caches, REDACTED splitting, and REDACTED results in Dagger

Dagger caches and reports REDACTEDs with no configuration in your repository. CircleCI caching is manual: `save_cache` writes paths under a key, `restore_cache` finds them, and caches stay for up to 15 days ([Caching dependencies](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/optimize/caching/)). The Dagger Engine, the open-source runtime that runs each check, caches all operations by default, keyed by their inputs ([Self-hosting](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting), [Dang SDK](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang)). You write no cache keys.

CircleCI splits REDACTEDs with `parallelism` and the CircleCI CLI, which can use timing data from the JUnit files that `store_REDACTED_results` uploads ([REDACTED splitting](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/optimize/parallelism-faster-jobs/), [REDACTED results](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/REDACTED/collect-REDACTED-data/)). Dagger's official modules report each REDACTED in the trace with its status, duration, and logs, and you do not change the REDACTEDs ([Test-native CI](https://dagger.io/changelog/REDACTED-native-ci)). Dagger splits a large REDACTED suite across engines, and balances the work with telemetry from earlier runs ([REDACTED splitting](https://dagger.io/changelog/REDACTED-splitting)).

## Move custom jobs into a Dang module

Write a module for each step that no official module covers. Write it in Dang, Dagger's own language for modules ([Dang SDK](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang)). Install the Dang SDK, then create the project's dev module:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/sdk/dang
dagger module init dang -y
```

With no `--name`, the command names the module after the project directory, creates it in `.dagger/modules/`, and installs it as the workspace main module. For a project in a `storefront` directory, the module is `storefront-dev`. This example replaces a job that validates and REDACTEDlies Terraform code in `infra/`. Replace `.dagger/modules/storefront-dev/main.dang` with this code. The type name `StorefrontDev` stands in for the one that `dagger module init` generated:

```dang
"""
Project steps that no official module covers.
"""
type StorefrontDev {
  let infra: Directory!

  new(ws: Workspace!) {
    self.infra = ws.directory("/infra")
    self
  }

  let terraform: Container! {
    container
      .from("hashicorp/terraform:1.13")
      .withMountedDirectory("/infra", infra)
      .withWorkdir("/infra")
      .withExec(["terraform", "init", "-backend=false", "-input=false"])
  }

  """
  Check the formatting and the configuration of the Terraform code.
  """
  pub terraformValidate: Void @check {
    terraform
      .withExec(["terraform", "fmt", "-check"])
      .withExec(["terraform", "validate"])
      .sync
    null
  }

  """
  Apply the Terraform configuration with AWS credentials.
  """
  pub deploy(awsAccessKeyId: REDACTED, awsSecretAccessKey: REDACTED: String! {
    terraform
      .withSecretVariable("AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", awsAccessKeyId)
      .withSecretVariable("AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", awsSecretAccessKey)
      .withExec(["terraform", "REDACTEDly", "-auto-REDACTEDrove", "-input=false"])
      .stdout
  }
}
```

The `@check` function joins the checks of the official modules:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE          VITEST-PROJECT  VITEST-TEST-FILE  CHECK               DESCRIPTION
dang-sdk                                          stale               staleness check: re-generate modules and clients managed by the Dang SDK
storefront-dev                                    terraform-validate  Check the formatting and the configuration of the Terraform code.
viREDACTED          *               *                 REDACTED                Run this REDACTED file.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

When a check fails, the report gives the command that runs it again on your machine. Here, a Terraform file needs `terraform fmt`:

```text
CHECKS  ✘ 1 failed  ✔ 2 passed
✘ dag://?check=terraform-validate 1.3s ERROR
  ∅ withExec terraform fmt -check 0.2s
  ┃ main.tf
  ! exit code: 3
✔ dag://?check=dang-sdk/generate/stale 1.3s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&viREDACTED-project=web 4.3s OK
  TESTS
    ✔ sum.REDACTED.js  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed

RUN LOCALLY
  dagger check "dag://?check=terraform-validate"
```

## Secrets and deploys

The `deploy` function is not a check, so `dagger check` does not run it. Call it with `dagger api call deploy`, and give each secret from a provider. Providers include files, environment variables, HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, and AWS Secrets Manager ([Secrets](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets)). This call reads the AWS keys from files:

```shell
dagger api call deploy --aws-access-key-id=REDACTED --aws-secret-access-key=REDACTED
```

Dagger redacts secret values from logs, never writes them to container layers, and leaves them out of cache keys. Your contexts can stay. A CircleCI job that names a context gives its variables to the function, as the deploy job in the CircleCI config below shows.

## Run the checks on every push with Cloud Checks

Cloud Checks run your checks on Cloud Engines after each push and pull request, with no CI file ([Set up Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks)). They run the same checks as `dagger check` on your machine. The repository must be on GitHub, and its `origin` remote must point to it. From the root of the repository, run:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In a terminal, the command helps you sign in to Dagger Cloud and connect your GitHub organization. Commit `dagger.toml`, `dagger.lock`, and `.dagger/`, then push. The results show as GitHub check statuses on the pull request and in Dagger Cloud ([Cloud Checks](https://dagger.io/changelog/cloud-checks)).

## Keep CircleCI as the trigger

A team can keep CircleCI as the system that starts the work, and let Dagger run it. A CircleCI job runs `dagger check`, and `DAGGER_ENGINE` selects where the checks run ([Self-hosting](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)):

- `cloud` selects Cloud Engines. It needs `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN`.
- `tcp://HOST:PORT` selects an engine that your team hosts. This address has no authentication, so keep the port on a private network.

Set `DAGGER_ENGINE` in every job. Without it, the CLI starts an engine on the runner, and that engine's cache is lost after the job. Install the CLI at the same version as the engine.

In `.circleci/config.yml`, replace the jobs that the checks cover:

```yaml
version: 2.1

commands:
  install-dagger:
    steps:
      - run:
          name: Install the Dagger CLI
          command: |
            curl -fsSL https://dl.dagger.io/dagger/install.sh | BIN_DIR=$HOME/.local/bin sh
            echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> "$BASH_ENV"

jobs:
  dagger-check:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/base:stable
    environment:
      DAGGER_VERSION: 1.0.0-beta.21
      DAGGER_ENGINE: cloud
    steps:
      - checkout
      - install-dagger
      - run: dagger check
  deploy:
    docker:
      - image: cimg/base:stable
    environment:
      DAGGER_VERSION: 1.0.0-beta.21
      DAGGER_ENGINE: cloud
    steps:
      - checkout
      - install-dagger
      - run:
          name: Deploy with Dagger
          command: |
            dagger api call deploy \
              --aws-access-key-id=REDACTED \
              --aws-secret-access-key=REDACTED

workflows:
  checks-and-deploy:
    jobs:
      - dagger-check:
          context: dagger-cloud
      - hold:
          type: REDACTEDroval
          requires:
            - dagger-check
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main
      - deploy:
          requires:
            - hold
          context:
            - dagger-cloud
            - aws-production
          filters:
            branches:
              only: main
```

The `dagger-cloud` context holds `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN`, and the `aws-production` context holds the AWS keys. The `env:` provider reads each key from the environment variable that the context sets. For a self-hosted engine, set `DAGGER_ENGINE` to its address and remove the `dagger-cloud` context.

## When to keep CircleCI as the trigger

CircleCI does some jobs that Dagger leaves to the system that starts the checks. Keep CircleCI in front of `dagger check` in these cases:

- Deploys wait for an [REDACTEDroval job](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/orchestrate/workflows/), and restricted contexts control who can release.
- Jobs get short-lived cloud credentials from CircleCI's [OIDC tokens](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/permissions-authentication/openid-connect-tokens/).
- The repository is not on GitHub. Cloud Checks start from GitHub events, so a CircleCI job starts the checks instead.
- Some jobs need CircleCI's hosted macOS, Windows, or GPU [execution environments](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/execution-managed/executor-intro/). Dagger checks run in Linux containers.

## Move one job at a time

Keep your CircleCI jobs on while you add Dagger. Run the Dagger checks next to the jobs that they replace, and compare the results on the same commits. When they agree, do these steps:

1. Make the Dagger checks [required status checks](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches#require-status-checks-before-merging) in your branch protection rules.
2. Remove the status of the CircleCI job from the required list.
3. Delete the job, and the orb if nothing else uses it, from `.circleci/config.yml`.

Repeat these steps for each job. When no job is left, remove the config, or keep only the jobs that CircleCI still triggers.

## What stays the same

Your Git host stays the home for code, pull requests, and review. Your REDACTEDs stay as they are, because official modules run them with no change to the REDACTED code. Your secret managers stay the source of your secrets, and CircleCI contexts can keep them while CircleCI triggers jobs.

**Bottom line:** You migrate from CircleCI to Dagger without a rewrite. Install the official modules that `dagger module recommend` finds, and run the same checks locally. Put the steps that no module covers in a small Dang module. Then run the checks with Cloud Checks, or from a thin `.circleci/config.yml`, and remove each CircleCI job when its checks pass.

## Related guides

- [How do I migrate from GitHub Actions to Dagger?](/learn/migrate-from-github-actions): the same migration for teams on GitHub Actions workflows.
- [What are the alternatives to GitHub Actions?](/learn/github-actions-alternatives): how Dagger compares with runner vendors and other CI platforms.
- [Can Dagger lower CI costs?](/learn/reduce-ci-costs): how Dagger bills compared with per-minute runners.

# How do I run golangci-lint the same way locally and in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/golangci-lint-dagger

To run golangci-lint the same way on a laptop and in CI, pin one golangci-lint version and commit a v2 configuration file. Lint every Go module, give the linter code that compiles, and keep its cache between runs. By hand, teams install a pinned binary on each laptop and use golangci-lint-action or a similar step in CI. Dagger meets the same requirements in one place. The official golangci-lint module runs the linter as a check, and `dagger check` runs that check on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What a good golangci-lint setup needs

A golangci-lint setup that gives the same result on a laptop and in CI meets five requirements. Each one comes from the golangci-lint docs or from the `go` command:

1. **Pin the golangci-lint version.** The golangci-lint docs recommend ["installing a specific version of golangci-lint"](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/install/ci/) in CI. A new release can add or change linters, and then all builds fail at the same time.
2. **Commit a v2 configuration file.** golangci-lint looks for `.golangci.yml`, `.golangci.yaml`, `.golangci.toml`, or `.golangci.json`. If it finds none in the project, it [looks in your home directory](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/configuration/file/), which is different on each machine. For the `version` key of a v2 file, ["The only possible value is "2"."](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/configuration/file/)
3. **Lint every Go module.** The `./...` pattern does not match directories that hold their own `go.mod`. You reach those packages only when you [change into that module's directory](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Package_lists_and_patterns).
4. **Give the linter code that compiles.** The golangci-lint FAQ says that ["the code to analyze should compile"](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/faq/#why-do-you-have-typecheck-errors). For cgo, it says ["ensure all required system libraries are installed"](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/faq/#why-do-you-have-typecheck-errors). golangci-lint also [supports only the Go versions](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/faq/#which-go-versions-are-supported) up to the one that compiled it.
5. **Keep the cache between runs.** The first run ["caches type information. All subsequent runs will be faster"](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/faq/), in the words of the FAQ.

The examples come from a repository with golangci-lint configuration files at the root, in `services/api`, and in `legacy`. Each of these three directories is a Go module, and a fourth Go module in `tools/migrate` has no configuration file of its own.

## Run golangci-lint by hand

On a laptop, most teams install a pinned binary with the [install script](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/install/local/) and run `golangci-lint run`. The golangci-lint docs recommend the binary and say that `go install` and `tool` directive installs ["aren't guaranteed to work"](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/install/local/). Install the release that CI uses:

```shell
curl -sSfL https://golangci-lint.run/install.sh | sh -s -- -b $(go env GOPATH)/bin v2.11.4
golangci-lint version
```

```text
golangci-lint has version 2.11.4 built with go1.26.1 from 8f3b0c7e on 2026-03-22T17:35:14Z
```

Go 1.26.1 compiled this binary, so it lints Go modules up to Go 1.26.1. Run it from the repository root:

```shell
golangci-lint run ./...
```

```text
main.go:10:9: S1003: should use strings.Contains(s, "h") instead (staticcheck)
	return strings.Index(s, "h") != -1
	       ^
1 issues:
* staticcheck: 1
```

The run reports only the root module. `services/api` has its own `go.mod`, so the root run does not lint it. Run golangci-lint in that directory too:

```shell
cd services/api && golangci-lint run ./...
```

```text
api.go:11:9: Error return value of `f.Close` is not checked (errcheck)
	f.Close()
	       ^
1 issues:
* errcheck: 1
```

Many teams also lint before each commit. The golangci-lint repository [defines hooks](https://github.com/golangci/golangci-lint/blob/main/.pre-commit-hooks.yaml) for the [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/) framework. Its `golangci-lint` hook lints only the changes since `HEAD`, and `golangci-lint-full` lints all files.

## Run golangci-lint in a CI job

In GitHub Actions, the golangci-lint docs recommend [golangci-lint-action](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/install/ci/). Its `version` input selects the release, and it saves and restores `~/.cache/golangci-lint` between runs ([golangci-lint-action](https://github.com/golangci/golangci-lint-action)). For a repository with several Go modules, its `working-directory` input is ["useful for monorepos"](https://github.com/golangci/golangci-lint-action). The README also shows a job matrix with one job for each module of a Go workspace. GitLab CI and Buildkite have a component and a plugin, which the [CI installation page](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/welcome/install/ci/) lists. If the code uses cgo, the job installs the C libraries before the lint step.

## golangci-lint versions drift across laptops and CI

The steps above meet each requirement, but each one lives in more than one place:

- **The version lives in several files.** The install command on each laptop, the action's `version` input, and the pre-commit `rev` must change together.
- **Each Go module needs its own run.** In this repository, the root run did not report the problem in `services/api`. A new module needs a new directory in the matrix, or a loop in a script.
- **The linter and the Go version must match.** When a `go.mod` moves to a newer Go release, each laptop and each CI job needs a newer golangci-lint binary.
- **Each machine installs the C libraries.** Each laptop and each CI job installs the cgo dependencies of the project, and their versions can differ.
- **The cache stays on one machine.** The action's cache is for CI only, and each laptop keeps a cache of its own.

## Meet the requirements with the golangci-lint module

The Dagger golangci-lint module meets these requirements with one check. A Dagger module is a package of functions that build, REDACTED, or check a project. The Dagger team maintains a catalog of [official modules](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) for common tools. The project must be a Git repository with a `dagger.toml` file from the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart). Install the golangci-lint module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/go/golangci-lint
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.golangci-lint]
source = "dagger.io/go/golangci-lint"
```

If you do not know which modules the project needs, run `dagger module recommend`. It suggests this module when it finds a golangci-lint configuration file:

```text
✔ go: found go.mod
┃ 
┃   dagger module install dagger.io/go
┃ 
┃ golangci-lint: found .golangci.yml
┃ 
┃   dagger module install dagger.io/go/golangci-lint
┃ 
┃ No modules were installed. Run the commands for the modules you select.
```

A check is a function that passes or fails, such as a REDACTED or a linter, and `dagger check` runs it. The module gives each lint project one check, `lint`. A lint project is a directory that holds a golangci-lint configuration file. List the check:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE         GOLANGCI-LINT-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
golangci-lint  *                      lint   Run golangci-lint in this project.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

The sections below meet each requirement with this check.

## Pin the golangci-lint version with Dagger

The module pins golangci-lint `2.11.4` by digest by default ([golangci-lint module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go/golangci-lint)). The `version` setting selects the release for every project. To record your choice in `dagger.toml`, set the release without the `v` prefix:

```shell
dagger module settings golangci-lint version 2.11.4
```

List the settings to confirm the value:

```shell
dagger module settings golangci-lint
```

```text
MODULE         KEY                VALUE   DESCRIPTION
golangci-lint  version            2.11.4  golangci-lint release, without the v…
golangci-lint  goVersion                  Go version for every module, overrid…
golangci-lint  base                       Base image for Go containers. Must i…
golangci-lint  includeExtraFiles
golangci-lint  lint                       Project roots to lint, e.g. ["**", "…
```

Dagger stores settings in `dagger.toml`, so everyone who runs the check uses the same release, on a laptop and in Cloud Checks:

```toml
[modules.golangci-lint.settings]
version = "2.11.4"
```

The version lives in one file. `dagger.lock` also pins the Git ref of the module and the images that the check uses.

## Commit a v2 configuration file with Dagger

The module lints only the directories that hold a golangci-lint configuration file, and it uses the file that the repository has. If a repository has no configuration file, the module has nothing to lint. The smallest valid `.golangci.yml` has one line:

```yaml
version: "2"
```

The module uses golangci-lint v2. If a v1 file has no `version` key, golangci-lint stops and the check fails with this error:

```text
Error: can't load config: unsupported version of the configuration: "" See https://golangci-lint.run/docs/product/migration-guide for migration instructions
```

The `golangci-lint migrate` command converts a v1 file to v2, as the [golangci-lint migration guide](https://golangci-lint.run/docs/product/migration-guide/) describes. Until you migrate a project, the `lint` setting can skip it. The setting selects lint projects by their path from the repository root. Its default, `["**"]`, selects all of them. A `!` pattern excludes a project and all projects below it, and exclusions always win. Set it in `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.golangci-lint.settings]
lint = ["**", "!legacy"]
```

An excluded project does not show in `dagger check -l --all`, and golangci-lint does not run for it. In this guide's run, the `legacy` project had a v1 configuration file that made the check fail. After the exclusion and fixes for the other problems, the check passed:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=golangci-lint/projects/lint 1.2s OK
```

## Lint every Go module with Dagger

The module runs `golangci-lint run` one time for each Go module in a lint project. A project covers the Go modules below it, except where a nested configuration file starts a different project. In this repository, the root project also covers `tools/migrate`. You write no loop and no matrix. Add `--all` to list one row for each project:

```shell
dagger check golangci-lint -l --all
```

```text
MODULE         GOLANGCI-LINT-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
golangci-lint  .                      lint   Run golangci-lint in this project.
golangci-lint  services/api           lint   Run golangci-lint in this project.
```

Lint every project, or lint one project:

```shell
dagger check --golangci-lint
dagger check --golangci-lint-project=services/api
```

Diagnostics show the path from the repository root and the linter name. The second command reports the `errcheck` problem in `services/api` that the root run by hand did not report:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=lint&golangci-lint-project=services/api 0.6s ERROR
  ✘ GomodGoMod.withPackages(
    ┆ ctr: withWorkdir services/api
    ┆ command: ["golangci-lint", "run", "--path-prefix", "services/api/", "--output.tab.path=stderr", "--output.tab.print-linter-name=true", "--output.tab.colors=false", "--show-stats=false", "--max-issues-per-linter=0", "--max-same-issues=0"]
    ┆ under: "services/api"
    ┆ skip: []
    ): Container! 0.1s ERROR
  ┃ services/api/api.go:11:9  errcheck  Error return value of `f.Close` is not checked
  ! exit code: 1

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=lint&golangci-lint-project=services/api"
```

The command under `RUN LOCALLY` runs the same check again for the same project. The linters, rules, and exclusions stay in `.golangci.yml`. The module uses them as golangci-lint finds them.

## Give the linter code that compiles with Dagger

The module lints each Go module with the Go toolchain that its `go.mod` asks for. It adds Go and C/C++ sources, embedded assets, and local `replace` dependencies inside the repository to the lint container. Most projects need nothing more. The settings below cover the other cases.

**One Go version for every module.** To use one Go version for all Go modules, set `goVersion`:

```shell
dagger module settings golangci-lint goVersion 1.26
```

This setting is separate from the `version` setting of the `dagger.io/go` module, which REDACTEDlies to REDACTEDs and generators.

**Files the linter reads.** If a lint run fails because a file is not there, add a path pattern from the repository root to `includeExtraFiles`:

```toml
[modules.golangci-lint.settings]
includeExtraFiles = ["shared/config/**"]
```

**C dependencies for cgo.** golangci-lint must load each package before its linters run. A cgo package needs its C headers and tools in the lint container for that step. In this run, a cgo file needs `pkg-config` and zlib, and the default container does not have them:

```text
  ┃ main.go:1  typecheck  : exec: "pkg-config": executable file not found in $PATH
```

The `base` setting takes a container that has a Go toolchain and the C dependencies. The module installs golangci-lint into that container. The container supplies its own Go toolchain, so the module ignores `goVersion` when `base` is set.

## Build a lint container for cgo in Dang

Build the `base` container in a small module of your own. Write it in [Dang](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang), Dagger's native language for modules. Install the Dang SDK, then create the project's dev module:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/sdk/dang
dagger module init dang -y
```

`dagger module init` creates the module at `.dagger/modules/ -dev` and records it in `dagger.toml`. Replace the starter code in `.dagger/modules/ -dev/main.dang` with the function below. `ProjectDev` stands in for the type name that `dagger module init` generated. Keep the generated name:

```dang
type ProjectDev {
  """
  The container golangci-lint runs in: Go, a C compiler, and zlib for cgo.
  """
  lintRuntime: Container! {
    container
      .from("golang:1.26-bookworm")
      .withExec(["apt-get", "update"])
      .withExec(["apt-get", "install", "-y", "--no-install-recommends", "pkg-config", "zlib1g-dev"])
  }
}
```

Connect the function to the `base` setting. This is [module wiring](https://docs.dagger.io/config/module-wiring): a setting refers to a function on a different module, and Dagger gives the function's result to the setting. `dagger module init` made the dev module the workspace main module, so the function name is sufficient:

```shell
dagger module settings golangci-lint base lint-runtime
```

Dagger stores the full address in `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.golangci-lint.settings]
base = "dag://<project>-dev/lint-runtime"
```

Run `dagger check` again. The Dang SDK adds its own `stale` check for the dev module:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 2 passed
✔ dag://?check=dang-sdk/generate/stale 1.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=golangci-lint/projects/lint 2.0s OK
```

The C libraries now come from one function, on each laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## Keep the cache between runs with Dagger

The module keeps the Go module, build, and golangci-lint caches between runs ([golangci-lint module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go/golangci-lint)). It mounts them as [cache volumes](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/cache-volume), directories that persist across runs on the Dagger engine. You write no cache key.

On a laptop, the cache lives in the local engine. In Cloud Checks, it lives on Dagger's Cloud Engines. [How do I cache Go builds in CI?](/learn/share-go-build-cache-ci) covers how Cloud Engines share their cache.

## Run the lint check locally and with Cloud Checks

`dagger check` runs the same lint check on any machine that has the Dagger CLI. Commit the configuration files and the lock file:

```shell
git add dagger.toml dagger.lock .golangci.yml
git commit -m "Lint with golangci-lint through Dagger"
```

If you created a dev module, add `.dagger` to the commit too. Dagger writes `dagger.lock` when it runs. The file pins the Git ref of each module and the images that the workspace uses, so every run uses the same versions.

To run the check in CI, use [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks). Cloud Checks run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for every push and pull request to a GitHub repository. You do not need a CI workflow file. The Git `origin` remote of the project must point to the GitHub repository. Enable Cloud Checks from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In an interactive terminal, the command offers to complete the steps that are not done, such as a Dagger Cloud sign-in and the GitHub connection. `dagger workspace activity` shows the recent runs. If the lint check fails in Cloud Checks, run `dagger check` locally to get the same diagnostics.

**Bottom line:** To run golangci-lint the same way locally and in CI, pin its version and commit a v2 configuration file. Lint every Go module with code that compiles, and keep the cache between runs. The `dagger.io/go/golangci-lint` module meets these requirements in one check, and `dagger check` runs it on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

- [How do I set up CI for a Go project?](/learn/daggerize-go-project): the `dagger.io/go` module for Go REDACTEDs and generators, next to the linter.

# How do I run PSScriptAnalyzer in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/psscriptanalyzer-dagger

To run PSScriptAnalyzer in CI, analyze every PowerShell script with one pinned PSScriptAnalyzer version, and fail the build on findings. Keep the rules in a settings file in the repository, and skip the scripts that the repository does not own. By hand, `Install-PSResource` and `Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Recurse -EnableExit` meet these requirements on a laptop and in a CI job. Dagger meets the same requirements in one place. Its official PSScriptAnalyzer module runs the same analysis in a container, on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What a good PSScriptAnalyzer setup needs

A PSScriptAnalyzer setup for CI has five requirements. Each one comes from Microsoft's PSScriptAnalyzer docs or releases:

1. **Analyze every script.** `Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer` analyzes `.ps1`, `.psm1`, and `.psd1` files. To include the files in subdirectories, use a wildcard or the `-Recurse` parameter ([`Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/psscriptanalyzer/invoke-scriptanalyzer)).
2. **Fail the build on findings.** The cmdlet returns diagnostics as objects. ["For usage in CI systems, the **EnableExit** exits the shell with an exit code equal to the number of error records"](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/psscriptanalyzer/invoke-scriptanalyzer).
3. **Pin the PSScriptAnalyzer version.** New releases add rules. For example, [release 1.25.0](https://github.com/PowerShell/PSScriptAnalyzer/releases/tag/1.25.0) added `AvoidReservedWordsAsFunctionNames` and `UseConsistentParameterSetName`. A new rule can fail a build with no change in the repository.
4. **Keep the rules in the repository.** A [`PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/utility-modules/psscriptanalyzer/using-scriptanalyzer#implicit-search) file selects the rules. PSScriptAnalyzer finds it in the project root when you analyze that root. [`SuppressMessageAttribute`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/utility-modules/psscriptanalyzer/using-scriptanalyzer#suppressing-rules) in a script turns off a rule for one function.
5. **Skip scripts you do not own.** Test fixtures and vendored modules stay out of the analysis. [`Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/psscriptanalyzer/invoke-scriptanalyzer) has no parameter that excludes a path, so the `-Path` value decides which scripts it analyzes.

## Run PSScriptAnalyzer by hand

On a laptop, install a fixed version of PSScriptAnalyzer from the PowerShell Gallery. [`Install-PSResource`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.psresourceget/install-psresource) takes a `-Version` parameter, and the value "can be an exact version". The same cmdlet reads a `-RequiredResourceFile`, a `.psd1` or `.json` file that lists the modules and versions to install. Commit that file, and each machine installs the same version.

Then run `Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path . -Recurse -EnableExit` from the project root. The command analyzes every script below the root and reads `PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1` from the root. To skip a directory, run the command once for each directory that you own, with that directory as `-Path`.

In CI, a job runs the same command. On GitHub Actions, a step with `shell: pwsh` runs PowerShell ([workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#jobsjob_idstepsshell)). GitHub's Ubuntu and Windows runner images include PowerShell and the PSScriptAnalyzer module. The [Ubuntu 24.04 image readme](https://github.com/actions/runner-images/blob/main/images/ubuntu/Ubuntu2404-Readme.md) lists both versions. To pin the version, the job installs it with `Install-PSResource` before the analysis.

## The runner image changes the PSScriptAnalyzer version

The commands work, but each requirement lives in more than one place:

- **Pin the PSScriptAnalyzer version.** The runner image changes its PSScriptAnalyzer version when the image updates. A laptop keeps the version that its developer installed. Only a version in the job's install step and a shared required-resource file keep them the same.
- **Analyze every script** and **skip scripts you do not own.** The list of paths lives in the CI step and in each developer's command, so a new directory must go in both.
- **Fail the build on findings.** `-EnableExit` must be on every command that CI runs, and on the command that each developer runs before a push.

## Analyze every script with the Dagger PSScriptAnalyzer module

The official [PSScriptAnalyzer module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/dotnet/PsScriptAnalyzer) analyzes every PowerShell script in the project. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/index) is a package of functions that build, REDACTED, or check a project. The project must be a Git repository with a Dagger workspace. The workspace is the `dagger.toml` file at the project root. If the project does not have this file, follow the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart). Install the module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/dotnet/PsScriptAnalyzer
```

```text
Installed module "ps-analyzer" in /work/dagger.toml
dagger.io/dotnet/PsScriptAnalyzer ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/PsScriptAnalyzer#main
```

The module's name in the workspace is `ps-analyzer`. The command adds these lines to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.ps-analyzer]
source = "dagger.io/dotnet/PsScriptAnalyzer"
```

The check copies the `.ps1`, `.psm1`, and `.psd1` files at or below the directory where `dagger` runs into a container ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/PsScriptAnalyzer)). The container runs Alpine Linux with PowerShell and PSScriptAnalyzer. The check runs the same command as by hand:

```powershell
Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path . -Recurse -EnableExit
```

If the analysis needs files that are not PowerShell files, such as `data/`, add them with the `includeExtraFiles` setting.

## Fail the build on findings with dagger check

The module adds one [check](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking), `ps-analyzer:check`. A check is a function that passes or fails, and `dagger check` runs it. List the checks in the workspace:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE       CHECK  DESCRIPTION
ps-analyzer  check  Run PSScriptAnalyzer on all PowerShell scripts at or below the client's
```

Run every check in the workspace:

```shell
dagger check
```

To run only the PSScriptAnalyzer check, give its address:

```shell
dagger check dag://ps-analyzer/check
```

In this guide's runs, the exit code counted warnings too, so a script with only warnings also makes the check fail. In a REDACTED project, `REDACTEDs/Helper.ps1` used `gci`, `%`, and `Write-Host`. This is the start of the output:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=ps-analyzer/check 13.6s ERROR
  ✘ withExec pwsh -NoLogo -NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command '$ErrorActionPreference = '\''Stop'\''\nInvoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path . -Recurse -EnableExit' 0.7s ERROR
  ┃ 
  ┃ RuleName                            Severity     ScriptName Line  Message
  ┃ --------                            --------     ---------- ----  -------
  ┃ PSAvoidUsingWriteHost               Warning      Helper.ps1 1     File 'Helper.
```

Next, the output lists two `PSAvoidUsingCmdletAliases` warnings. It ends with `! exit code: 3`, one for each warning. When every script is clean, the check passes:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=ps-analyzer/check 0.9s OK
```

## Pin the PSScriptAnalyzer version with the version setting

The `version` setting is the PSScriptAnalyzer release that the module installs. The default is `1.22.0`. Set the release that your team uses, so a new release cannot make the check fail without a change in your repository. List the current settings:

```shell
dagger module settings ps-analyzer
```

```text
MODULE       KEY                VALUE  DESCRIPTION
ps-analyzer  version                   PSScriptAnalyzer version to install
ps-analyzer  exclude                   PowerShell script paths to exclude from…
ps-analyzer  includeExtraFiles         Extra non-PowerShell file paths to incl…
```

Set a different release:

```shell
dagger module settings ps-analyzer version 1.24.0
```

The command writes the setting to `dagger.toml`, so it REDACTEDlies to all users of the repository:

```toml
[modules.ps-analyzer.settings]
version = "1.24.0"
```

The module downloads the `PSScriptAnalyzer..nupkg` file from the [PSScriptAnalyzer GitHub releases](https://github.com/PowerShell/PSScriptAnalyzer/releases). Use a version that has a release on that page.

Dagger also writes `dagger.lock`. In this guide's run, the file pinned the module to a Git commit and the `alpine` base image to a digest. Commit it with `dagger.toml`, so every machine runs the same module code on the same image.

## Keep the rules in the repository with PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1

Select the rules in a PSScriptAnalyzer settings file, the same file as by hand. The Dagger module has no rule settings of its own. The check analyzes the project root, so put [`PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/utility-modules/psscriptanalyzer/using-scriptanalyzer#implicit-search) there. This file removes one rule:

```powershell
@{
    ExcludeRules = @('PSAvoidUsingWriteHost')
}
```

The check copies every `.psd1` file into its container, so it reads this file with no other configuration. In the REDACTED project, the `PSAvoidUsingWriteHost` warning stopped. The two alias warnings stayed:

```text
  ┃ RuleName                            Severity     ScriptName Line  Message
  ┃ PSAvoidUsingCmdletAliases           Warning      Helper.ps1 2     'gci' is an a
  ┃ PSAvoidUsingCmdletAliases           Warning      Helper.ps1 2     '%' is an ali
  ! exit code: 2
```

To stop a warning for one function only, add `SuppressMessageAttribute` to that function in the script. Microsoft's [Suppressing Rules](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/utility-modules/psscriptanalyzer/using-scriptanalyzer#suppressing-rules) section shows how.

## Skip scripts you do not own with exclude

The `exclude` setting is a list of script paths that the check does not analyze, such as REDACTED fixtures or vendored modules. Give the list as one JSON argument:

```shell
dagger module settings ps-analyzer exclude '["REDACTEDs/"]'
```

The command adds the list to the settings in `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.ps-analyzer.settings]
version = "1.24.0"
exclude = ["REDACTEDs/"]
```

In the REDACTED project, this setting removed `REDACTEDs/Helper.ps1` from the analysis, and the check passed. The paths live in `dagger.toml`, so a laptop and Cloud Checks skip the same scripts.

## Run the check locally and with Cloud Checks

The `dagger check` command runs the check on your machine, in the Dagger engine. The engine runs the containers. It [caches each step by its inputs](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang), so a rerun skips the steps that did not change. In this guide's REDACTED project:

- The first `dagger check` with new content in `PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1` took 1.7 seconds.
- A rerun with no changes took 0.6 seconds.
- After another change to that file, the check took 1.7 seconds.
- The first run after a change to `version` took 3.1 seconds. The engine downloaded the new PSScriptAnalyzer release and used the PowerShell install from its cache.

These numbers come from one run on one machine.

[Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) runs the same checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for every push and pull request. You do not write a CI workflow file. The repository must be on GitHub, and its `origin` remote must point to it. Enable Cloud Checks from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

If you are not signed in to Dagger Cloud, or GitHub is not connected, the command asks you to do these steps first. Commit the workspace files, then push:

```shell
git add dagger.toml dagger.lock
git commit -m "Run PSScriptAnalyzer with Dagger"
git push -u origin HEAD
```

If you added `PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1`, commit it too. Watch the result with `dagger workspace activity`. If the check fails in Cloud Checks, run `dagger check` locally. It runs the same analyzer version and rules on the same scripts.

**Bottom line:** To run PSScriptAnalyzer in CI, analyze every script with a pinned version and `-EnableExit`. Keep the rules in `PSScriptAnalyzerSettings.psd1`, and skip the scripts you do not own. By hand, the version and the paths live in each CI job and on each laptop. The Dagger PSScriptAnalyzer module keeps them in `dagger.toml`, and Cloud Checks run the same `dagger check` on every push.

# How do I run Staticcheck the same way locally and in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/staticcheck-dagger

To run Staticcheck the same way on a laptop and in CI, pin one Staticcheck version and commit your `staticcheck.conf` files. Analyze every Go module with a Go version that the release supports, and keep the caches between runs. By hand, teams run `go install` with a pinned version on each laptop and use the Staticcheck GitHub Action in CI. Dagger meets the same requirements in one place. The official Staticcheck module runs Staticcheck as a check, and `dagger check` runs that check on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What a good Staticcheck setup needs

A Staticcheck setup that gives the same result on a laptop and in CI meets five requirements. Each one comes from the Staticcheck docs or from the `go` command:

1. **Pin the Staticcheck version.** The Staticcheck docs tell you to pin it, because ["new versions of Staticcheck introduce new checks that may break your build"](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/running-staticcheck/ci/github-actions/).
2. **Commit the staticcheck.conf files.** Staticcheck configuration files [contain TOML and REDACTEDly to the subtree of packages below them](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/configuration/). When there are several, Staticcheck merges them, and a file deeper in the tree overrides the files above it.
3. **Analyze every Go module.** `staticcheck ./...` [checks all packages](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/getting-started/) that the pattern matches. The `./...` pattern does not match directories that hold their own `go.mod`. You reach those packages only when you [change into that module's directory](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Package_lists_and_patterns).
4. **Use a supported Go version.** ["A given Staticcheck release supports the last two versions of Go"](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/running-staticcheck/ci/github-actions/) at the time of the release. Staticcheck [targets the Go version](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/running-staticcheck/cli/) in the `go` directive of `go.mod`.
5. **Keep the caches between runs.** The Staticcheck GitHub Action ["saves and restores Go's build cache (in addition to Staticcheck's own cache) to speed up future runs"](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/running-staticcheck/ci/github-actions/).

The examples come from a repository with one `staticcheck.conf` at the root and a second one in `tools/migrate`. The root file keeps the default checks and turns off the package comment check, ST1000:

```toml
checks = ["inherit", "-ST1000"]
```

The `tools/migrate` directory is a separate Go module. Its `staticcheck.conf` also turns off S1003, with `checks = ["inherit", "-S1003"]`.

## Run Staticcheck by hand

On a laptop, most teams install Staticcheck with `go install`. The [Staticcheck docs](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/getting-started/) say that you can use a specific version, such as `@2020.2.1`, in place of `@laREDACTED`. Install the release that CI uses:

```shell
go install honnef.co/go/tools/cmd/staticcheck@2026.2.1
```

```text
go: downloading honnef.co/go/tools v0.8.1
go: honnef.co/go/tools@v0.8.1 requires go >= 1.26.0; switching to go1.26.10
go: downloading go1.26.10 (darwin/arm64)
go: downloading golang.org/x/tools v0.44.1-0.20260420230617-19499e7caabc
go: downloading github.com/BurntSushi/toml v1.4.1-0.20240526193622-a339e1f7089c
go: downloading golang.org/x/exp/typeparams v0.0.0-20231108232855-2478ac86f678
go: downloading golang.org/x/exp v0.0.0-20231110203233-9a3e6036ecaa
go: downloading golang.org/x/sync v0.20.0
go: downloading golang.org/x/mod v0.35.0
```

This release needs Go 1.26 or newer to build. The laptop had Go 1.24, so the `go` command downloaded a newer toolchain. Each Staticcheck release has two names: `2026.2.1` is also `v0.8.1`. Confirm the version:

```shell
staticcheck -version
```

```text
staticcheck 2026.2.1 (0.8.1)
```

Run it from the repository root:

```shell
staticcheck ./...
```

```text
main.go:10:9: should use strings.Contains(s, "h") instead (S1003)
```

The run covers only the root Go module. `go list` shows the packages that `./...` matches from the root:

```shell
go list ./...
```

```text
example.com/lintdemo
```

To analyze `tools/migrate`, run `staticcheck ./...` again in that directory. There, its own `staticcheck.conf` turns off S1003, and Staticcheck reports nothing.

## Run Staticcheck in a CI job

In GitHub Actions, the Staticcheck docs describe [staticcheck-action](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/running-staticcheck/ci/github-actions/). Its `version` input selects the release, and its default is `laREDACTED`. Its `install-go` input decides whether the action installs Go. The action also saves and restores the Go build cache and the Staticcheck cache. The docs list no other CI systems, so a job on another system runs the same `go install` and `staticcheck ./...` commands. A repository with several Go modules runs Staticcheck once in each module directory, often in a shell loop or a job matrix.

## A Go upgrade needs a new Staticcheck everywhere

The steps above meet each requirement, but each one lives in more than one place:

- **The version lives in several files.** The `go install` command on each laptop and the action's `version` input must change together. If the action has no `version`, it uses the laREDACTED release.
- **Each Go module needs its own run.** In this repository, the root run did not analyze `tools/migrate`. A new module needs a new directory in the loop or the matrix.
- **The release and the Go version must match.** A release supports two Go versions. When a `go.mod` moves to a newer Go, each laptop and each CI job needs a newer Staticcheck.
- **The cache stays on one machine.** The action's cache is for CI only, and each laptop keeps a cache of its own.

## Meet the requirements with the Staticcheck module

The Dagger Staticcheck module meets these requirements with one check. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go/staticcheck) is a package of functions that build and REDACTED a project. A check is a function that `dagger check` runs and reports as passed or failed. The project needs a Git repository and a Dagger workspace. Run `dagger init` from the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) to create `dagger.toml`. This file holds the workspace configuration for everyone who uses the repository.

Install the module from the repository root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/go/staticcheck
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml` under the name `staticcheck`:

```toml
[modules.staticcheck]
source = "dagger.io/go/staticcheck"
```

The command also creates `dagger.lock`. This file pins the Git ref of the module. The first check run adds the `golang` images that the check uses, so every machine uses the same versions. Commit it with `dagger.toml`. When `dagger module recommend` finds a `staticcheck.conf`, it suggests the module:

```text
┃ staticcheck: found staticcheck.conf
┃ 
┃   dagger module install dagger.io/go/staticcheck
┃ 
┃ No modules were installed. Run the commands for the modules you select.
```

The module adds one check, `lint`. It runs once for each Staticcheck project. List it:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE       STATICCHECK-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
staticcheck  *                    lint   Run Staticcheck in this project.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

The sections below meet each requirement with this check.

## Pin the Staticcheck version with Dagger

The `version` setting selects the Staticcheck release for every project, and its default is `v0.8.1` ([Staticcheck module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go/staticcheck)). The module uses the `v0.x.y` name of a [release](https://github.com/dominikh/go-tools/releases).

List the settings:

```shell
dagger module settings staticcheck
```

```text
MODULE       KEY                VALUE  DESCRIPTION
staticcheck  version                   Staticcheck release, e.g. "v0.8.1".
staticcheck  goVersion                 Go version for every module, overriding…
staticcheck  base                      Base image for Go containers. Must incl…
staticcheck  includeExtraFiles         Extra workspace files to mount for Go c…
staticcheck  lint                      Project roots to lint, e.g. ["**", "!do…
```

Set the release:

```shell
dagger module settings staticcheck version v0.8.2
```

Dagger stores settings in `dagger.toml` under `[modules.staticcheck.settings]`. The pin REDACTEDlies to everyone who uses the repository, and to Cloud Checks. The version lives in one file.

## Commit the staticcheck.conf files with Dagger

The module analyzes only the directories that hold a `staticcheck.conf`. A repository with no `staticcheck.conf` has nothing to analyze, so commit one at the repository root first. A Staticcheck project is a directory that holds a `staticcheck.conf`.

Staticcheck [merges the configuration files](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/configuration/) itself, and the module keeps their directory structure. Thus `checks = ["inherit", "-S1003"]` in `tools/migrate/staticcheck.conf` has the same effect as with `staticcheck ./...` on your machine.

To turn off one Staticcheck check for a directory, use `staticcheck.conf`. To turn off a check for one line, use a [`//lint:ignore` directive](https://staticcheck.dev/docs/configuration/). The `lint` setting of the module decides which projects run. If a directory has its own `staticcheck.conf` but the module must not analyze it yet, exclude it. The setting is a list, so edit it directly in `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.staticcheck.settings]
version = "v0.8.2"
lint = ["**", "!tools/migrate"]
```

Each pattern selects project roots by their path from the repository root. `"**"` matches every project. `!path` excludes that project and the projects below it, and an exclusion always wins. The excluded project does not show in the `dagger check -l --all` list, and Staticcheck does not analyze it.

## Analyze every Go module with Dagger

A project covers each Go module below it. It also covers each package below it that a nested `staticcheck.conf` does not claim. You write no loop and no matrix. With `--all`, the list shows one row for each project:

```shell
dagger check -l --all
```

```text
MODULE       STATICCHECK-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
staticcheck  .                    lint   Run Staticcheck in this project.
staticcheck  tools/migrate        lint   Run Staticcheck in this project.
```

The module finds the projects at or below the directory where `dagger` runs, plus the nearest project above it. To cover the whole repository, run `dagger` from the root. In this run, Staticcheck found the S1003 problem in the root module:

```shell
dagger check --staticcheck
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=staticcheck/projects/lint 8.3s ERROR
  ✘ withExec sh -c 'set -e\npattern=$1\nskips=$2\nshift 2\nIFS='\''\n'\''\nroot=$(pwd -P)\ndirs=$(go list -e -find -f '\''{{.Dir}}'\'' "$pattern")\npkgs=\nfor dir in $dirs; do\n  keep=1\n  for skip in $skips; do\n    case "$dir/" in "$root/$skip"/*) keep= ;; esac\n  done\n  if [ -n "$keep" ]; then pkgs="$pkgs$dir$IFS"; fi\ndone\nif [ -z "$pkgs" ]; then echo "no packages under $pattern" >&2; exit 0; fi\nexec "$@" $pkgs' go-packages ./... tools/migrate staticcheck 0.6s ERROR
  ┃ main.go:10:9: should use strings.Contains(s, "h") instead (S1003)
  ! exit code: 1

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=staticcheck/projects/lint"
```

The report shows the diagnostic in Staticcheck's own format, with the check ID. The `RUN LOCALLY` command runs the failed selection again. After the fix, both projects pass:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=staticcheck/projects/lint 0.8s OK
```

To analyze one project, give its directory:

```shell
dagger check --staticcheck-project=tools/migrate
```

The module also analyzes REDACTED files. It does not run REDACTEDs or generators.

## Use a supported Go version with Dagger

The module analyzes each Go module in `golang: -alpine`, for the version in that module's `go.mod`. Staticcheck then targets that same version. If every Go module must use the same Go toolchain, set `goVersion`. If each `go.mod` already asks for the version you want, skip this setting.

```shell
dagger module settings staticcheck goVersion 1.26
```

This setting is separate from the `version` setting of the [Go module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go). That setting REDACTEDlies to REDACTEDs and generators.

Each project runs on a copy of the repository that Dagger assembles. The copy holds the Go sources, embedded assets, the `staticcheck.conf` files, and local `replace` targets. Most projects need nothing more. Two settings cover the other cases:

- **`includeExtraFiles`** adds files that the source scan does not find, as patterns from the repository root, such as `["shared-assets/**"]`. The scan follows `//go:embed`, but it does not follow other file reads.
- **`base`** gives Staticcheck a container of your own, for example one with the C libraries that cgo packages need. The container must have a Go toolchain, and the module ignores `goVersion` when `base` is set. If the container does not have Staticcheck, the module installs it. A function in your own module can build this container through [module wiring](https://docs.dagger.io/config/module-wiring). The [golangci-lint guide](/learn/golangci-lint-dagger#build-a-lint-container-for-cgo-in-dang) shows this pattern for the same setting.

## Keep the caches between runs with Dagger

The module keeps the Go module, build, and Staticcheck caches between runs ([Staticcheck module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go/staticcheck)). It mounts them as [cache volumes](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/cache-volume), directories that persist across runs on the Dagger engine. You write no cache key. On a laptop, the caches live in the local engine. In Cloud Checks, they live on Dagger's Cloud Engines. [How do I cache Go builds in CI?](/learn/share-go-build-cache-ci) covers how Cloud Engines share their cache.

## Run it locally and with Cloud Checks

On a laptop, `dagger check` runs the Staticcheck check with the other checks in the workspace. In CI, use Cloud Checks. [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines after each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. Commit the workspace files:

```shell
git add dagger.toml dagger.lock staticcheck.conf
git commit -m "Run Staticcheck with Dagger"
```

Connect the GitHub repository to Dagger Cloud, then push:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
git push -u origin HEAD
```

The command gets the repository from the Git `origin` remote. In an interactive terminal, it offers to sign you in and to connect GitHub if you have not done that yet. Cloud Checks run the same `staticcheck/projects/lint` check, with the same pinned version and the same configuration. `dagger workspace activity` shows the recent runs.

**Bottom line:** To run Staticcheck the same way locally and in CI, pin its version and commit your `staticcheck.conf` files. Analyze every Go module with a supported Go version, and keep the caches between runs. The `dagger.io/go/staticcheck` module meets these requirements in one check, and `dagger check` runs it on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.
