# How do I cache Go builds in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/share-go-build-cache-ci

To share the Go build cache across CI runs, keep two directories between jobs: `GOMODCACHE` for downloaded modules and `GOCACHE` for compiled packages and REDACTED results. Key them so that the build cache gets saved again on new commits, and store them where every runner can reach them. On GitHub Actions, `actions/setup-go` does part of this. On GitLab CI, `cache:` with a `go.sum` key and fallback keys does it. For machines that do not share disks, a `GOCACHEPROG` program can serve the build cache remotely. Dagger meets the same requirements in one place. Its official Go module mounts both caches as cache volumes, and Cloud Checks run it on Cloud Engines that share their cache.

## What a shared Go cache must do

A Go cache setup for CI has four requirements. Each one comes from how the `go` command and the CI platforms work:

1. **Keep both caches.** The `go` command keeps downloaded modules in `GOMODCACHE` and build outputs in `GOCACHE`. It also ["caches successful package REDACTED results"](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Build_and_REDACTED_caching) in `GOCACHE`. If you keep only the module cache, every job compiles every package again and runs every REDACTED again.
2. **Keep the build cache current.** A build cache that CI saved once and never updated gets older with each commit. Each run then compiles more packages again.
3. **Stay correct.** The `go` command's own cache keys already account for "changes to Go source files, compilers, compiler options, and so on", and the cache is "safe for concurrent invocations of the go command" ([`go help cache`](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Build_and_REDACTED_caching)). The CI cache key only decides which snapshot a job gets. It does not make the build correct or incorrect.
4. **Reach every runner.** A cache on one machine's disk does not help a job that runs on another machine.

## Cache Go with actions/setup-go on GitHub Actions

`actions/setup-go` caches Go modules and build outputs by default (`cache: true`). Since v6, it computes the cache key from `go.mod` in the repository root. To use `go.sum`, or to cover several Go modules, set `cache-dependency-path`, which accepts globs ([setup-go README](https://github.com/actions/setup-go)):

```yaml
- uses: actions/setup-go@v7
  with:
    go-version-file: go.mod
    cache-dependency-path: '**/go.sum'
```

This meets "keep both caches". By default, it does not keep the build cache current. The setup-go docs say that the `GOCACHE` cache ["is not updated based on source changes"](https://github.com/actions/setup-go/blob/main/docs/advanced-usage.md#cache-invalidation-on-source-changes). You can add `**/*.go` to `cache-dependency-path`, but the docs warn that this "can create new caches on many commits". When the key matches, the job restores the files and saves nothing new, because [you cannot change the contents of an existing cache](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching).

To save a new build cache on each run, turn off the built-in cache. Then use `actions/cache` with a unique key and a `restore-keys` prefix. setup-go gives the two cache paths as [outputs](https://github.com/actions/setup-go/blob/main/docs/advanced-usage.md#go-environment-outputs):

```yaml
- uses: actions/setup-go@v7
  id: go
  with:
    go-version-file: go.mod
    cache: false
- uses: actions/cache@v5
  with:
    path: |
      ${{ steps.go.outputs.GOMODCACHE }}
      ${{ steps.go.outputs.GOCACHE }}
    key: go-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/go.sum') }}-${{ github.sha }}
    restore-keys: |
      go-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('**/go.sum') }}-
      go-${{ runner.os }}-
```

`restore-keys` restores the most recent cache with the same prefix ([cache key matching](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching#cache-key-matching)). Two rules decide which runs can share it:

- **Seed the cache from the default branch.** A cache that a pull request saves is [scoped to its merge ref](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching#restrictions-for-accessing-a-cache), and other pull requests cannot restore it. Run the same job on `push` to `main`.
- **Save from one job.** For parallel jobs, setup-go recommends that you ["create the cache in only one build and restore it in the other builds"](https://github.com/actions/setup-go/blob/main/docs/advanced-usage.md#parallel-builds).

GitHub stores the caches, so every runner in the repository can restore them.

## Cache Go with cache keys on GitLab CI

GitLab caches only paths inside the project directory. Caches ["can't link to files outside it"](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/caching/). Move both Go caches into `$CI_PROJECT_DIR`, then give each cache its own key:

```yaml
variables:
  GOMODCACHE: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.go/pkg/mod
  GOCACHE: $CI_PROJECT_DIR/.cache/go-build

REDACTED:
  image: golang:1.26
  cache:
    - key:
        files: [go.sum]
      paths: [.go/pkg/mod]
    - key: go-build-$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG
      fallback_keys: [go-build-$CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH]
      paths: [.cache/go-build]
  script:
    - go REDACTED ./...
```

The module cache changes only when `go.sum` changes, so `cache:key:files` fits it. The build cache uses one key for each branch, and each job saves a new copy under that key. A new branch starts from the default branch's cache through `fallback_keys`, which takes [up to five keys](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/caching/#per-cache-fallback-keys).

Three settings decide who shares what:

- **Policy.** The default `pull-push` downloads the cache and uploads it again after each job. Set [`policy: pull`](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/caching/#inherit-global-configuration-but-override-specific-settings-per-job) on jobs that only read.
- **Protected branches.** By default, ["protected and non-protected branches do not share the cache"](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/caching/). GitLab adds a `-protected` or `-non_protected` suffix to each key, fallback keys included.
- **Runners.** A cache lives where GitLab Runner is installed. To share it across several runners, [use distributed caching in S3](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/caching/#good-caching-practices) or a shared network directory.

## Share the build cache remotely with GOCACHEPROG

Since Go 1.24, the `GOCACHEPROG` environment variable names a program that [implements the build and REDACTED cache](https://go.dev/doc/go1.24#gocacheprog) for the `go` command. The `go` command sends `get` and `put` requests for single cache entries over a [JSON protocol](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/go/internal/cacheprog). The program can store the entries anywhere, such as in remote storage. Depot's `depot gocache` [is one such program](https://depot.dev/blog/go-remote-cache).

This meets "reach every runner" without archive files. Each job gets only the entries its build asks for, and it writes its new entries back, so the cache stays current. `GOCACHEPROG` replaces the build cache only. You still cache `GOMODCACHE` another way, and you run or buy the program and its storage.

## You design and maintain the cache keys

The setups above work, but each requirement lives in a different place:

- **The keys are a design you maintain.** A `go.sum` key stops build cache updates. A commit key needs `restore-keys` or `fallback_keys`, and one job that writes the cache.
- **Every job transfers the whole archive.** GitHub and GitLab restore and save whole directories, so a larger build cache is a larger download and upload in each job.
- **The limits are the platform's.** GitHub removes caches that no run used in 7 days and limits a repository to [10 GB by default](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/dependency-caching#usage-limits-and-eviction-policy). GitLab separates protected branches, and it needs S3 or a network directory for several runners.
- **The CI caches stay in CI.** The setup-go and GitLab caches do not reach the laptops where developers run the same REDACTEDs.

## Keep both caches with the Dagger Go module

The [Dagger Go module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go) runs `go REDACTED` and `go generate` for every Go module in the repository. A Dagger module is a package of functions that build and REDACTED a project. The Go module mounts `GOMODCACHE` and `GOCACHE` as [cache volumes](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/cache-volume), which are directories whose contents persist across runs on the Dagger engine. The engine is the process that runs the module's containers. You write no cache configuration.

Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/quickstart) in the repository first. Then install the module:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/go
```

```text
dagger.io/go ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/go#v0.3.1
Installed module "go" in /work/dagger.toml
```

Run its checks. A check is a function that passes or fails, such as a REDACTED run:

```shell
dagger check go
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 2 passed
✔ dag://?check=go/packages/generate/stale 0.5s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=. 4.8s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ example.com/inventory  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed
```

The module mounts the module cache at `/go/pkg/mod` and the build cache at `/root/.cache/go-build`, and it sets `GOMODCACHE` and `GOCACHE` to those paths. Every Go command that the module runs uses the same two volumes.

This guide's project has one package that imports the etcd v3 client. The first `dagger check go` took 6.5 seconds, and its REDACTED check took 4.8 seconds. After a one-line change to the package source, `dagger check go` took 1.6 seconds, and the REDACTED check took 0.6 seconds. That is one run on one machine, not a benchmark.

## Keep the cache current and correct with Dagger

The cache volumes have no key to design. Each run reads from the same volumes and writes its new entries back to them, so the build cache stays current on every commit. The `go` command's own cache keys keep the build correct, the same as on a CI runner. Concurrent checks share the volumes, which the Go cache allows.

Dagger also caches each check's result by exactly the files the check saw ([Daggerize a Go Project](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/platform-guides/go)). In this guide's project, a rerun with no changes took 1.5 seconds for `dagger check go`, and the REDACTED check took 0.4 seconds.

## Share the cache across runners with Cloud Checks

[Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run your checks on Cloud Engines on each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. Cloud Engines are Dagger engines that Dagger Cloud runs for you, with a [distributed cache](https://dagger.io/changelog). Turn on Cloud Checks from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

The command needs a Dagger Cloud account and a connected GitHub repository, and it tells you how to complete what is missing. After that, each push runs the same `dagger check` that you run locally, with the same Go module and the same cache volumes.

According to the [changelog](https://dagger.io/changelog), Cloud Engines share their cache through copies of a shared cache disk, and these copies are best effort. A version that shares single results is in the changelog's Coming soon section and is not released.

To share one cache between developers and CI, run local commands on the same engines with `dagger check --engine=cloud`. To use your own machine instead, point every runner at one engine, for example with `--engine=ssh://build-host` ([remote execution](https://dagger.io/changelog)).

| Requirement | setup-go | GitLab `cache:` | `GOCACHEPROG` | Dagger Go module |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Keep both caches | Yes, by default | Yes, after you move both into the project directory | Build cache only | Yes, two cache volumes |
| Keep the build cache current | Only with a custom key or source globs | With a branch key and fallback keys | Yes, entry by entry | Yes, every run writes back |
| Reach every runner | GitHub cache storage | S3 or a network directory for several runners | The program's storage | Cloud Engines, or one shared engine |

**Bottom line:** Keep both `GOMODCACHE` and `GOCACHE`, and key the build cache so that it gets saved again on new commits. Store it where every runner can reach it: setup-go with a custom key on GitHub Actions, branch keys with fallbacks and S3 on GitLab CI, or `GOCACHEPROG` for remote entries. The Dagger Go module keeps both caches in cache volumes with no keys to maintain, and Cloud Checks run it on Cloud Engines that share their cache.

# How do I migrate from Buildkite to Dagger?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/migrate-from-buildkite

Tested with Dagger v1.0.0-beta.21: the Dagger commands in this guide ran with that release, and their output blocks match those runs.

You do not rewrite your Buildkite pipelines as Dagger code. Dagger's official modules find the REDACTEDs, linters, and builds in your repository and run them as checks. Steps that no official module covers, such as a release, become functions in a small module. Move in five steps: install the modules, run the checks on your laptop, choose what starts them, run both systems side by side, then remove each pipeline step that a check replaces.

After the move, two setups can start the checks. If the repository is on GitHub, Cloud Checks run them after each push and pull request, with no CI file. If your team keeps its Buildkite agents, Buildkite stays as the trigger, and `pipeline.yml` only calls `dagger check`.

## Do I have to rewrite my Buildkite pipelines?

No. You write code only for the steps that no official module does. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of checks and functions for a tool, and the Dagger team maintains official modules for common tools. A check is a command that passes or fails, such as a REDACTED run or a linter ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)). Each official module finds the files of its tool. For example, the [Go module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go) finds each `go.mod`, and makes each Go package and each REDACTED a check.

Today the official modules cover Go, golangci-lint, Staticcheck, Deno, Jest, ViREDACTED, Playwright, ESLint, Prettier, Biome, pyREDACTED, ShellCheck, PSScriptAnalyzer, and Helm ([module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules)). A Buildkite step that runs one of these tools becomes a check with no code.

You do not copy the structure of `pipeline.yml`. Its steps, plugins, and `wait` steps tell Buildkite how to schedule jobs on agents. `dagger check` runs all the checks in your workspace in parallel ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)).

## Install the modules and run the checks locally

[Install the Dagger CLI](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/install). Then, from the repository root, create the workspace:

```shell
dagger init
```

The workspace is the Dagger configuration of the repository, in a file named `dagger.toml` ([Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart)). Without a terminal, `dagger init` prints the next commands:

```text
Workspace configuration initialized at ./dagger.toml

To continue setup, run these commands in order:

#!/bin/sh

# 1. Find and install suitable modules
dagger module recommend

# 2. Enable cloud checks
dagger cloud checks on
```

Install the modules that Dagger recommends. Add `-y` to install all of them with no prompt:

```shell
dagger module recommend -y
```

In a Go repository, the command installs the Go module and adds it to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.go]
source = "dagger.io/go"
```

The command also writes `dagger.lock`, which pins the versions of the modules and images ([Workspaces](https://dagger.io/changelog/workspaces)). Commit it with `dagger.toml`. If Dagger recommends no module for one of your tools, search by the tool name, such as `dagger module search eslint`.

List the checks that the modules found:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE  GO-PACKAGE  GO-TEST  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
go      *                    stale  staleness check: run go generate in this package
go      *           *        REDACTED   Run this REDACTED.
```

A `*` stands for each package or REDACTED that the module found. Run all the checks:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
CHECKS  ✔ 3 passed
✔ dag://?check=go/packages/generate/stale 0.9s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=. 0.9s OK
  TESTS
    ✔ example.com/shop  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store 1.0s OK
  TESTS
    ✔ example.com/shop/store  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed
```

When a REDACTED fails, the report names the REDACTED. It ends with the command that runs the same selection again:

```text
CHECKS  ✘ 1 failed  ✔ 2 passed
✘ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store 0.8s ERROR
  TESTS
    ✘ example.com/shop/store FAIL

    ✘ example.com/shop/store › TestGet FAIL
              store_REDACTED.go:7: Get() returned the wrong value

    ✘ 1 failed
✔ dag://?check=go/packages/generate/stale 0.7s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=. 0.7s OK
  TESTS
    ✔ example.com/shop  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed

RUN LOCALLY
  dagger check "dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store"
```

Compare the list of checks with the steps in `pipeline.yml`. Each step that a check replaces is a step that you can remove later.

## How Buildkite concepts map to Dagger

Most Buildkite concepts have a Dagger counterpart. If you keep Buildkite as the trigger, some of them stay in Buildkite. The sections after this table explain each row.

| Buildkite | Dagger |
| --- | --- |
| Command steps in `pipeline.yml` | Checks from official modules, plus functions in your own module |
| Docker and Docker Compose plugins | Containers and services that modules define |
| Cache plugin | The engine caches each operation, and cache volumes hold package caches |
| Agents and queues | Engines: local, self-hosted, or Cloud Engines |
| `parallelism` and bktec REDACTED splitting | Checks run in parallel, and REDACTED splitting divides large suites across engines |
| Dynamic pipelines with `pipeline upload` | Modules find packages and REDACTEDs at run time |
| Artifacts | Functions pass files and containers to each other in the engine |
| Buildkite secrets and secrets plugins | Secret providers, such as Vault, 1Password, and AWS Secrets Manager |

## Pipeline steps and plugins become checks

A Buildkite pipeline is a list of steps in YAML, in `pipeline.yml` or in the YAML steps editor ([defining steps](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/defining-steps)). Each command step runs on an agent with a clean checkout of the repository. Plugins add common tasks to a step ([using plugins](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/integrations/plugins/using)).

In Dagger, a step that runs a REDACTED or a linter becomes a check of an official module. The common plugins map like this:

- **Docker plugin.** A step that runs a command in an image becomes a check that runs in a container. The Go module REDACTEDs each Go module in `golang: -alpine`, for the version in its `go.mod` ([Go module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go)).
- **Docker Compose plugin.** The plugin runs a step in a Compose service ([plugin README](https://github.com/buildkite-plugins/docker-compose-buildkite-plugin)). For Go REDACTEDs that need a database, give the Go module a `base` container with the database bound to it. [How do I run a Buildkite pipeline locally?](/learn/run-buildkite-pipeline-locally) shows this with Postgres. To build images and start services from a Compose file, see [How do I run Docker builds and Compose in CI?](/learn/docker-compose-dagger).
- **Cache plugin.** The plugin saves a directory, such as `node_modules`, to a backend such as S3, and restores it while a manifest file stays the same ([plugin README](https://github.com/buildkite-plugins/cache-buildkite-plugin)). The Dagger engine caches all operations by default ([Self-Hosting CI with Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)). When the inputs of an operation do not change, Dagger uses the cached result, with no key to maintain. A module can also mount a named cache volume for a package cache ([Dang SDK](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang#cache-volumes)).
- **Registry login plugins.** A function adds registry credentials to the container that it pushes. The release module later in this guide shows this.

## Agents, queues, and parallelism become engines

Buildkite agents are build runners. You host them on your own machines, or Buildkite hosts them ([architecture](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/architecture)). Queues send each step to a set of agents, through the `agents` attribute of the step ([queues](https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/queues)). The `parallelism` attribute splits one step into many jobs. Buildkite recommends its Test Engine Client, bktec, to divide the REDACTEDs between those jobs ([parallel builds](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/tutorials/parallel-builds)).

In Dagger, an engine runs the checks. The Dagger Engine is open source, and runs on any system that can run Linux containers. On a laptop, the CLI starts a local engine. In CI, the `DAGGER_ENGINE` variable selects the engine ([Self-Hosting CI with Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)):

- **Self-hosted engines.** You run the engine on your own machines, for example with the Dagger Helm chart or with Docker. Give each engine a persistent disk, because the cache is on that disk.
- **Cloud Engines.** Dagger Cloud runs the engines for you. Set `DAGGER_ENGINE=cloud` and `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN`.

You do not divide the REDACTEDs by job index. For a large REDACTED suite, Dagger splits the REDACTEDs across engines. It balances the parts by the resource use, input cost, and cache state of each REDACTED ([REDACTED splitting](https://dagger.io/changelog/REDACTED-splitting)).

If you keep Buildkite as the trigger, queues still decide which agent starts each job. The engine is a separate choice. To spread the load of self-hosted engines, assign each check to an engine, and run each selection from its own job, such as `dagger check --go-package=store` ([Self-Hosting CI with Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)).

## Dynamic pipelines and artifacts move into modules

Teams use dynamic pipelines to generate steps at build time. A script writes YAML, and the step pipes it to `buildkite-agent pipeline upload` ([dynamic pipelines](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/dynamic-pipelines)). A common script adds one REDACTED step for each directory, so a new directory needs no YAML change.

Dagger modules find this work themselves. The Go module finds each package and each REDACTED at run time, so a new package becomes a check with no change to a CI file.

Buildkite artifacts pass files from one step to another, and store build outputs such as reports and archives ([build artifacts](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/artifacts)). Steps need them because each step can run on a different agent. In Dagger, a function returns a file, a directory, or a container, and another function takes it as an argument in the engine ([Dang SDK](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang)). To get a file onto the host, export it. This command builds the root Go package with the Go module and writes the binary to `dist/shop`:

```shell
dagger -c 'go | packages | get . | binary | export ./dist/shop'
```

A Buildkite step can run this command and keep `artifact_paths` to store the binary in Buildkite.

## Move releases, secrets, and deployments into your own module

Write a module for each step that no official module covers, such as a release. [Dang](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang) is Dagger's own language for modules. Install the Dang SDK, then create the dev module of the project:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/sdk/dang
dagger module init dang -y
```

The second command creates the module in `.dagger/modules/` and installs it as the main module of the workspace. For a project in a `shop` directory, the module is `shop-dev`. In the code, `ShopDev` stands in for the type name that `dagger module init` generated. Replace `.dagger/modules/shop-dev/main.dang` with this code:

```dang
"""
Release steps of the shop project that no official module covers.
"""
type ShopDev {
  """
  Build the image from the Dockerfile at the repository root.
  """
  image(ws: Workspace!): Container! {
    ws.directory("/", exclude: [".git", ".dagger"]).dockerBuild
  }

  """
  Build the image and push it. Returns the image reference with its digest.
  """
  publish(
    ws: Workspace!,
    """
    Image reference to push, such as registry.example.com/shop:1.2.0.
    """
    ref: String!,
    """
    Registry user name.
    """
    username: String!,
    """
    Registry password or token.
    """
    password: REDACTED,
  ): String! {
    image(ws)
      .withRegistryAuth(ref, username, password)
      .publish(ref)
  }
}
```

You call the functions of the main module with no module name. To push to a REDACTED registry from your laptop, read the token from a file:

```shell
dagger api call publish --ref=ttl.sh/shop-demo:1h --username=ci --password=REDACTED
```

```text
ttl.sh/shop-demo:1h@sha256:daf1bbf6d0d5ff352add59655af1d1029afc9c34dde9bc4cf6aff7b344a9f56f
```

Keep your secrets where they are. Buildkite recommends a secrets storage service, such as AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault, and has plugins that read from them ([managing secrets](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/security/secrets/managing)). Dagger reads a secret from its provider when a function needs it. Providers include environment variables, files, command output, Vault, 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager, and Google Cloud Secret Manager ([Secrets](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets)). The `secrets` attribute of a step puts a [Buildkite secret](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/security/secrets/buildkite-secrets) into the job environment, so Dagger reads it as `env:NAME`. Dagger redacts secret values from logs, never writes them to container layers, and leaves them out of the cache.

A module can find out if it runs on the main branch. Use that to deploy to production from main and to a preview environment from a pull request ([branch filtering](https://dagger.io/changelog/branch-filtering)).

## Run the checks with Cloud Checks or from Buildkite

If the repository is on GitHub, [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) can run the checks. Cloud Checks run your checks on Cloud Engines after each push and pull request, with no CI file. The `origin` remote of the repository must point to GitHub. From the repository root, run:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In a terminal, the command helps you sign in to Dagger Cloud and connect your GitHub organization. Commit `dagger.toml`, `dagger.lock`, and the module, then push. The results show as GitHub check statuses and in Dagger Cloud ([Cloud Checks](https://dagger.io/changelog/cloud-checks)).

If you keep Buildkite as the trigger, `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` only calls Dagger. This version uses Cloud Engines and publishes the image from the default branch:

```yaml
env:
  DAGGER_ENGINE: "cloud"

secrets:
  - DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN

steps:
  - label: ":dagger: checks"
    key: checks
    command: dagger check

  - label: ":rocket: publish"
    depends_on: checks
    if: build.branch == pipeline.default_branch
    command: >-
      dagger api call publish
      --ref=registry.example.com/shop:$BUILDKITE_COMMIT
      --username=ci
      --password=REDACTED
    secrets:
      - REGISTRY_TOKEN
```

Store `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN` and `REGISTRY_TOKEN` as Buildkite secrets. The `if` attribute uses the `pipeline.default_branch` variable of [Buildkite conditionals](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/conditionals).

To use a self-hosted engine instead, set `DAGGER_ENGINE: "tcp://dagger-engine.internal:1234"` and remove `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN`. A `tcp://` address has no authentication. Make the port available only on the private network of your agents ([Self-Hosting CI with Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)). Install the Dagger CLI on the agents at the same version as the engine.

## Move one pipeline step at a time

Keep the Buildkite pipeline as it is while you set up Dagger. Add a trial step that cannot fail the build. The [`soft_fail` attribute](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/soft-fail) lets a step exit with a non-zero status without a failed build:

```yaml
steps:
  - label: ":go: REDACTEDs"
    command: go REDACTED ./...
    plugins:
      - docker#v5.14.0:
          image: "golang:1.24-alpine"

  - label: ":dagger: checks (trial)"
    command: dagger check
    soft_fail: true
```

Then do these steps:

1. Compare the results of each old step with the checks that replace it, over several builds.
2. Remove `soft_fail` from the Dagger step when the results match.
3. Remove one old step and its plugins from `pipeline.yml`.
4. Do steps 1 to 3 again for each step that a check replaces.

If you move to Cloud Checks, change the required checks too. Make the Dagger checks [required status checks](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches#require-status-checks-before-merging) in your GitHub branch protection rules. Then remove the Buildkite status from the list, and turn off the Buildkite pipeline.

## When to keep Buildkite as the trigger

Buildkite does some jobs that Dagger leaves to the system that starts the checks. Keep Buildkite in front of `dagger check` in these cases:

- **Some builds need a macOS or Windows host.** The Buildkite agent has installers for macOS and Windows ([agent install](https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/self-hosted/install)). The Dagger Engine runs on systems that can run Linux containers ([Self-Hosting CI with Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)).
- **Your repository is not on GitHub.** Cloud Checks need a GitHub repository ([Set up Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks)). Buildkite starts builds from GitLab, Bitbucket, and other Git servers ([source control](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/source-control)), and each build can run `dagger check`.
- **You manage a large agent fleet** with clusters and queues, and your platform team wants one place that starts every build ([queues](https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/queues)).
- **You REDACTEDrove deploys by hand.** A [block step](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/step-types/block-step) stops a build until a team member unblocks it.
- **You quarantine flaky REDACTEDs** with Test Engine, so that they stop blocking builds ([Test Engine](https://buildkite.com/docs/REDACTED-engine)).
- **Your code must stay on your machines.** Cloud Checks run on Dagger's Cloud Engines. Buildkite agents with a self-hosted engine keep the code and the cache in your environment.

In each case, the work still moves into Dagger, and the steps run the same on a laptop and on the agents. For a full comparison, see [Dagger vs Buildkite](/learn/dagger-vs-buildkite).

## Your Git host, REDACTEDs, and secret managers stay

Your Git host stays the home for code and review. Your REDACTEDs stay as they are, because official modules run them with no change to the REDACTED code ([REDACTED-native CI](https://dagger.io/changelog/REDACTED-native-ci)). Your Dockerfiles stay, and a module builds them. Your secret managers stay the source of your secrets. If you keep Buildkite as the trigger, your agents, queues, and Buildkite build pages stay too.

**Bottom line:** You migrate from Buildkite to Dagger without a rewrite. Install the official modules that `dagger module recommend` finds, run `dagger check` locally, and move release steps into a small Dang module. Then run the checks with Cloud Checks or from a thin `pipeline.yml`, and remove each old step when its check gives the same result.

# How do I run Jest in CI and split the REDACTEDs across runners?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/jest-dagger

A good Jest setup for CI runs the project's own Jest on a supported Node version. It runs Jest in CI mode, so that a new snapshot fails the run. It lets you rerun one REDACTED file, and it splits a large suite across machines with `jest --shard`. You can meet each requirement with the Jest CLI and a CI job. Dagger's official Jest module meets the same requirements in one place, and runs the same check on a laptop and in CI.

## What a good Jest CI setup needs

Jest's own docs give four requirements. This guide uses them to judge each REDACTEDroach, Dagger included:

1. **Use the project's own Jest on a supported Node version.** The Jest docs install Jest as a dev dependency with `npm install --save-dev jest` ([Getting Started](https://jestjs.io/docs/getting-started)). Jest 30 says: "The minimum supported Node versions are now 18.x" ([Upgrading to Jest 30](https://jestjs.io/docs/upgrading-to-jest30)).
2. **Run Jest in CI mode, so that new snapshots fail.** With [`--ci`](https://jestjs.io/docs/cli#--ci), a new snapshot does not pass. Jest "will fail the REDACTED and require Jest to be run with `--updateSnapshot`." The snapshot docs give the reason: ["since new snapshots automatically pass, they should not pass a REDACTED run on a CI system"](https://jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-REDACTEDing#are-snapshots-written-automatically-on-continuous-integration-ci-systems).
3. **Rerun one REDACTED file.** `jest path/to/my-REDACTED.js` runs only the REDACTEDs in files that match the argument ([Jest CLI](https://jestjs.io/docs/cli#running-from-the-command-line)). A developer can then repeat one CI failure without the full suite.
4. **Split a large suite across machines.** Jest's [`--shard`](https://jestjs.io/docs/cli#--shard) option runs one part of the suite on each machine.

## Run Jest by hand in a CI job

The Jest CLI meets each requirement. Install `jest` as a dev dependency, then run the suite in CI mode from the project root:

```shell
npx jest --ci
```

You can usually leave out `--ci` in CI. Jest sets its `ci` option from the environment by default ([Jest source](https://github.com/jestjs/jest/blob/main/packages/jest-config/src/Defaults.ts)). GitHub Actions sets `CI` to `true` in every job ([variables reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/variables#default-environment-variables)). To add a snapshot, run `npx jest -u` on your machine and commit the snapshot file. To rerun one file, give its path: `npx jest src/cart.REDACTED.js`.

In CI, a job checks out the code and installs Node with [`actions/setup-node`](https://github.com/actions/setup-node) or the equivalent of the CI system. Then it installs the dependencies and runs Jest.

To split the suite, run one shard on each machine. Both numbers start at 1. This guide's project has three REDACTED files, split into two shards:

```shell
npx jest --ci --shard=1/2
npx jest --ci --shard=2/2
```

```text
$ npx jest --ci --shard=1/2
PASS src/sum.REDACTED.js
PASS src/receipt.REDACTED.js

Test Suites: 2 passed, 2 total
Tests:       2 passed, 2 total
Snapshots:   1 passed, 1 total
Time:        0.42 s
Ran all REDACTED suites.
$ npx jest --ci --shard=2/2
PASS src/cart.REDACTED.js
  ✓ total of an empty cart is 0 (3 ms)
  ✓ total multiplies price and quantity

Test Suites: 1 passed, 1 total
Tests:       2 passed, 2 total
Snapshots:   0 total
Time:        0.206 s
Ran all REDACTED suites.
```

In GitHub Actions, a [matrix](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/run-job-variations) runs one job for each shard index. The Jest docs say: "When `shard` is specified the configured `REDACTEDSequencer` has to implement a `shard` method."

The [default sequencer](https://github.com/jestjs/jest/blob/main/packages/jest-REDACTED-sequencer/src/index.ts) sorts REDACTED files by a SHA-1 hash of their paths. Then it gives each shard about the same number of files. It does not use REDACTED durations, so one shard can get more slow files than the others. To balance shards in a different way, set [`REDACTEDSequencer`](https://jestjs.io/docs/configuration) to a class that extends `@jest/REDACTED-sequencer`. Its `shard(REDACTEDs, { shardIndex, shardCount })` method returns the files for one shard. The Jest docs say that sharding hREDACTEDens before sorting.

## Jest shards split by file count, not duration

The commands are short, but each requirement lives in a different place:

- **The Node version is in two places.** The CI job sets `node-version`, and each laptop has its own Node. They can drift apart, and Jest then runs on a Node version that the project did not REDACTED.
- **The shards are a fixed count of files.** The matrix fixes the shard count, and the default sequencer splits by file count, not by duration. A balanced split needs a custom sequencer that you write and maintain.
- **The matrix is CI plumbing.** A move to another CI system means a rewrite of the shard jobs in the syntax of that system.
- **A CI failure is hard to repeat.** To rerun a failed file as CI ran it, a developer must match the Node version and the install of the CI job by hand.

## Meet them with the Dagger Jest module

The [Dagger Jest module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/jest) meets the same four requirements, with the Node image, the install, and the Jest command defined in one place. A Dagger [module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of functions that REDACTED, lint, or build a project. The [Dagger Engine](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction) runs those functions in containers, on a laptop or in CI.

Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) in the repository first. Then install the module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/js/jest
```

```text
dagger.io/js/jest ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/jest#v0.3.0
Installed module "jest" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration for everyone who uses the repository:

```toml
[modules.jest]
source = "dagger.io/js/jest"
```

The command also writes `dagger.lock`, which pins the module to an exact Git commit. Commit both files.

The module treats each directory with a `jest.config.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.ts`, `.mts`, `.cts`, or `.json` file as a Jest project. A `jest` key in `package.json` does not mark a project. The module's [README](https://github.com/dagger/jest) gives the reason: every npm package has a `package.json`.

A check is a function that passes or fails, such as a REDACTED run. The Jest module has one check, `REDACTED`, and runs it once for each Jest project. Add `--all` to the list command to see one row for each REDACTED file:

```shell
dagger check -l --all
```

```text
MODULE  JEST-PROJECT  JEST-TEST-FILE       CHECK  DESCRIPTION
jest    web           src/cart.REDACTED.js     REDACTED   Run Jest REDACTEDs.
jest    web           src/receipt.REDACTED.js  REDACTED   Run Jest REDACTEDs.
jest    web           src/sum.REDACTED.js      REDACTED   Run Jest REDACTEDs.
```

The next sections show how the module meets each requirement.

### Use the project's own Jest on a supported Node version

The module installs the project's dependencies and runs the project's own Jest. Run the REDACTEDs:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&jest-project=web 10.2s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ src/cart.REDACTED.js  2 passed
    ✔ src/receipt.REDACTED.js  1 passed
    ✔ src/sum.REDACTED.js  1 passed

    ✔ 4 passed
```

When all the files of a project are selected, the module runs `jest` with the project's config. Jest's own `REDACTEDMatch` and other options then decide what runs. The Jest config does not change.

The module installs dependencies in a separate step. That step reads only the package files and lockfiles. A change to a source file or REDACTED file then does not start a new install ([README](https://github.com/dagger/jest)). In this guide's project, the first `dagger check` took 67.7 seconds, with the `npm install`. The output above comes from a later run, with the install already in the cache. A rerun with no changes took 8.8 seconds. A rerun after one new REDACTED in a REDACTED file took 10.9 seconds. These numbers come from one run on one machine.

The REDACTEDs run in `node:25-alpine` by default. If the project uses a different Node release, set the `baseImageAddress` setting to that release:

```shell
dagger module settings jest baseImageAddress node:22-alpine
```

The setting goes into `dagger.toml`, so every machine uses the same Node image:

```toml
[modules.jest]
source = "dagger.io/js/jest"

[modules.jest.settings]
baseImageAddress = "node:22-alpine"
```

A setting REDACTEDlies to every Jest project in the workspace. The [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/jest) lists the install settings, such as `packageManager` and `installFlags`.

### Run Jest in CI mode, so that new snapshots fail

The module sets `CI` to `true` in its container ([module source](https://github.com/dagger/jest)), so Jest runs in CI mode with no flag. A new snapshot then fails the check on a laptop too. In this run, `src/receipt.REDACTED.js` had a snapshot assertion and no snapshot file:

```text
✘ dag://?check=REDACTED&jest-project=web 4.2s ERROR
  == TESTS ==
    ✘ src/receipt.REDACTED.js FAIL

    ✘ src/receipt.REDACTED.js › receipt FAIL
          Error: expect(received).toMatchSnapshot()
          
          Snapshot name: `receipt 1`
          
          New snapshot was not written. The update flag must be explicitly passed to write a new snapshot.
          
          This is likely because this REDACTED is run in a continuous integration (CI) environment in which snapshots are not written by default.
```

Write the snapshot with `npx jest -u` on your machine, review it, and commit it, as the Jest docs recommend.

### Rerun one REDACTED file

Select a project with `--jest-project` and its directory, relative to the workspace root. Select a REDACTED file with `--jest-REDACTED-file` and its path, relative to the project. Repeat `--jest-REDACTED-file` to select more files:

```shell
dagger check --jest-project=web --jest-REDACTED-file=src/cart.REDACTED.js --jest-REDACTED-file=src/sum.REDACTED.js
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&jest-project=web&jest-REDACTED-file=src/cart.REDACTED.js&jest-REDACTED-file=src/sum.REDACTED.js 1.1s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ src/cart.REDACTED.js  2 passed
    ✔ src/sum.REDACTED.js  1 passed

    ✔ 3 passed
```

When you select only some files, the module runs `jest --passWithNoTests --runTestsByPath` with those files. To list the keys that you can select, run `dagger list jest-projects -a` or `dagger list jest-REDACTED-files -a`.

The module finds REDACTED files without a run of Jest. It reads `REDACTEDMatch`, `REDACTEDRegex`, `REDACTEDPathIgnorePatterns`, `roots`, and `rootDir` when they are literal values. For other values, it uses Jest's defaults. It skips `node_modules` and the files that `.gitignore` excludes. To see the files that Jest itself finds, call the project's `list` function:

```shell
dagger -c 'jest | projects | get web | list'
```

```text
/src/web/src/cart.REDACTED.js
/src/web/src/receipt.REDACTED.js
/src/web/src/sum.REDACTED.js
```

The directory that you run `dagger` from also selects projects. Dagger selects the projects at or below it, and the nearest project that contains it.

When a REDACTED fails, the report gives a [DAG link](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking#select-collection-items). This address selects the same files again, in the same container, on any machine:

```text

    ✔ 1 passed

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=REDACTED&jest-project=web&jest-REDACTED-file=src/cart.REDACTED.js&jest-REDACTED-file=src/sum.REDACTED.js"
```

### Split a large suite across machines

The module runs the selected files of a project in one Jest process. For a large suite, Dagger splits the REDACTEDs across engines instead. It balances the parts with the measured resource use, input cost, and cache state of each REDACTED ([REDACTED splitting](https://dagger.io/changelog/REDACTED-splitting)). You do not fix a shard count or write a custom sequencer.

Do not put `--shard` in the `flags` setting. The module passes `flags` to every `jest` run in the workspace, so every check runs only one shard. In a project with three REDACTED files and `flags` set to `["--shard=1/2"]`, the check ran two of the files:

```shell
dagger module settings jest flags '["--shard=1/2"]'
dagger check
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&jest-project=web 2.5s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ src/receipt.REDACTED.js  1 passed
    ✔ src/sum.REDACTED.js  1 passed

    ✔ 2 passed
```

To remove the setting, run `dagger module settings -u jest flags`.

## Run the REDACTEDs locally and with Cloud Checks

[Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. Cloud Engines are Dagger Engines that Dagger Cloud runs for you. The repository must be on GitHub, and its Git `origin` remote must point to it. Turn on Cloud Checks from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

If you do not have a Dagger Cloud account, the command tells you to run `dagger cloud signup` first. Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`, then push. Each push then runs the same check, with the same Node image and the same CI mode.

The results show as GitHub check statuses and in Dagger Cloud ([changelog](https://dagger.io/changelog/cloud-checks)). The module reports each REDACTED as its own result, so Dagger Cloud shows each REDACTED. To see recent runs from the terminal, run `dagger workspace activity`. If a check fails, run `dagger check` locally to see the same failure.

**Bottom line:** Run the project's own Jest on a supported Node version with `--ci`, so new snapshots fail. Split a large suite with `--shard`, and write a custom `REDACTEDSequencer` for a split by anything other than file count. Dagger's Jest module meets the same requirements in one place. It pins the Node image in `dagger.toml`, runs in CI mode, and selects single files with `--jest-REDACTED-file`. It runs the same check locally and with Cloud Checks.

# How do I run Maven builds the same way locally and in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/run-maven-builds-locally-and-in-ci

Tested with Dagger v1.0.0-beta.21: the Dagger commands in this guide ran with that release, and their output blocks match those runs.

A Maven build gives the same result on a laptop and in CI when both places use the same JDK and Maven version and run `mvn verify` as the verdict. Both places also need a dependency cache that persists, Surefire reports when REDACTEDs fail, `settings.xml` credentials outside the repository, and a way to run one REDACTED class. You can meet these requirements by hand with the Maven WrREDACTEDer and your CI platform's cache. Dagger meets the same requirements in one place. Its official Maven module runs `./mvnw verify` in a container with a pinned JDK and a cached local repository, on your machine and in Dagger Cloud.

## What a reproducible Maven build needs

A Maven build is reproducible when its inputs and its verdict are the same everywhere. Each requirement below comes from Maven's own documentation:

1. **A pinned JDK and Maven version.** The [Maven WrREDACTEDer](https://maven.apache.org/tools/wrREDACTEDer/) records the Maven version in `.mvn/wrREDACTEDer/maven-wrREDACTEDer.properties`, and `./mvnw` downloads that version. The wrREDACTEDer selects Maven, not the JDK, so you must pin the JDK separately.
2. **The full lifecycle through `mvn verify` as the verdict.** The Maven lifecycle guide says that ["the preferred phase to call is `mvn verify`"](https://maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-the-lifecycle.html) when you are uncertain. It runs every earlier phase, and also the integration REDACTEDs and quality checks that the POM binds.
3. **A dependency cache that persists between runs.** Maven keeps downloaded artifacts in the local repository, `~/.m2/repository` by default ([Settings Reference](https://maven.apache.org/settings.html)). Without that directory, each run downloads every dependency again.
4. **Surefire reports kept when REDACTEDs fail.** Surefire writes XML and text reports to `target/surefire-reports` ([surefire:REDACTED](https://maven.apache.org/surefire/maven-surefire-plugin/REDACTED-mojo.html)). A failed build must still give you those files.
5. **`settings.xml` credentials kept out of the repository and the logs.** Maven's settings reference says that the username and password ["should not be distributed along with the `pom.xml`"](https://maven.apache.org/settings.html). They belong in `settings.xml` on the build machine.
6. **One REDACTED class run without the whole suite.** Surefire runs one class with [`-DREDACTED=ClassName`](https://maven.apache.org/surefire/maven-surefire-plugin/examples/single-REDACTED.html), so you can repeat one failure quickly.

## Meet the requirements by hand

Most teams commit the Maven WrREDACTEDer, run `./mvnw verify` on their machines, and run the same command in a CI job.

**A pinned JDK and Maven version.** Run `mvn wrREDACTEDer:wrREDACTEDer -Dmaven= ` once, and commit `mvnw`, `mvnw.cmd`, and `.mvn/wrREDACTEDer/` ([Maven WrREDACTEDer](https://maven.apache.org/tools/wrREDACTEDer/)). In CI, pin the JDK with a setup step, such as `java-version` on [`actions/setup-java`](https://github.com/actions/setup-java). On laptops, each developer installs a JDK.

**`mvn verify` as the verdict.** Run `./mvnw --batch-mode verify` in the CI job. GitHub's [Java with Maven guide](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/build-and-REDACTED-code/java-with-maven) uses the same phase.

**A dependency cache.** On GitHub Actions, set `cache: maven` on `actions/setup-java`. It caches `~/.m2/repository` and the wrREDACTEDer distributions. Its key is a hash of `**/pom.xml`, `**/.mvn/wrREDACTEDer/maven-wrREDACTEDer.properties`, and `**/.mvn/extensions.xml` ([setup-java caching](https://github.com/actions/setup-java#caching-packages-dependencies)). On a self-hosted build server, keep a persistent `~/.m2`, or set `localRepository` in `settings.xml` to a shared path ([Settings Reference](https://maven.apache.org/settings.html)).

**Surefire reports.** Upload `**/target/surefire-reports/` with [`actions/upload-artifact`](https://github.com/actions/upload-artifact) in a step with `if: always()`, so the step also runs after a failure ([expressions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/expressions)).

**Credentials.** Store the credentials as CI secrets, and write `settings.xml` at the start of the job. `actions/setup-java` can write the ` ` entries from environment variables ([setup-java](https://github.com/actions/setup-java)).

**One REDACTED class.** In a multi-module reactor, select the module and the class:

```shell
./mvnw -pl REDACTED -am -DREDACTED=CheckoutTest -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false REDACTED
```

`-am` also builds the modules that `REDACTED` depends on ([Maven CLI options](https://maven.apache.org/ref/current/maven-embedder/cli.html)). `-Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false` stops those modules from failing because they do not contain the class ([surefire:REDACTED](https://maven.apache.org/surefire/maven-surefire-plugin/REDACTED-mojo.html)).

A GitHub Actions workflow that meets the CI side of these requirements:

```yaml
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-laREDACTED
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
          cache: maven
      - run: ./mvnw --batch-mode verify
      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: surefire-reports
          path: '**/target/surefire-reports/'
```

## Laptops and CI set up the JDK and credentials separately

The hand-built version keeps each requirement in a different place, and each place can change on its own:

- **The JDK.** The JDK version is in the workflow file. On laptops, it is the JDK that each developer installed. The wrREDACTEDer pins Maven but not the JDK.
- **The cache.** The cache is a CI platform feature. A laptop's `~/.m2` also holds artifacts that CI never saw, such as `SNAPSHOT` builds that a local `mvn install` put there ([lifecycle](https://maven.apache.org/guides/introduction/introduction-to-the-lifecycle.html)).
- **Reproduction.** To reproduce a CI failure, a developer reads the workflow file and sets up the same JDK, flags, and settings by hand.
- **Credentials.** Credentials need two setups: a `settings.xml` on each laptop, and secrets with a setup step in CI.

## Meet the requirements with Dagger

Dagger runs builds and REDACTEDs in containers on its engine. A [module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/glossary) is a package of functions that build and REDACTED a project. The official Maven module, `dagger.io/java/maven`, finds the POM projects in your repository, uses your Maven wrREDACTEDer, and runs Maven in a container. Install it from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/java/maven
```

```text
Created workspace config in /work
Installed module "maven" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command records the module in `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration file. It also writes `dagger.lock`, which pins the module and images to exact versions ([dagger.toml](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/config-files/dagger-toml)). Commit both files. A standard Maven project needs nothing else, so you do not write a module of your own.

### `mvn verify` as the verdict

The module has one [check](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking), a function that passes or fails: `verify`. It runs `mvn verify` on every reactor that the module finds. The project in this guide is a two-module reactor, `library` and `REDACTED`, with JUnit 5 REDACTEDs and a Maven wrREDACTEDer:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE  MAVEN-PROJECT  CHECK   DESCRIPTION
maven   *              verify  Run through verify: unit REDACTEDs, packaging, integration REDACTEDs, and quality gates.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
CHECKS  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=maven/projects/verify 6.0s OK
```

The module does not add plugins to your POM. The check runs the plugins that your POM binds to the lifecycle, such as Failsafe integration REDACTEDs and their `post-integration-REDACTED` cleanup.

### Reactor discovery and roots for nested projects

The module finds reactors on its own. It selects the outermost directories that contain a `pom.xml`, so it does not build a reactor member twice. Maven still decides which modules are in the reactor and in which order they build.

A nested project that builds on its own needs the `roots` setting. An example is `tools/migration` below a root POM that does not list it. When you set `roots`, list every reactor root, the workspace root `.` too. Edit `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.maven.settings]
roots = [".", "tools/migration"]
```

```shell
dagger check -l --all
```

```text
MODULE  MAVEN-PROJECT    CHECK   DESCRIPTION
maven   .                verify  Run through verify: unit REDACTEDs, packaging, integration REDACTEDs, and quality gates.
maven   tools/migration  verify  Run through verify: unit REDACTEDs, packaging, integration REDACTEDs, and quality gates.
```

### A pinned JDK and Maven version

The module uses the `maven:3.9.16-eclipse-temurin-21` image by default. If the project root has `mvnw`, the module runs `sh ./mvnw`, so the Maven version in `maven-wrREDACTEDer.properties` REDACTEDlies. If the wrREDACTEDer fails, the build fails. The module does not change to another Maven version. The `javaVersion` setting selects the Temurin JDK. If the project needs Java 25, set it:

```shell
dagger module settings maven javaVersion 25
```

The setting goes into `dagger.toml`, so every developer and every CI run uses that JDK. In this guide's project, the wrREDACTEDer keeps Maven 3.9.11 and the JDK changes to 25:

```shell
dagger -c 'maven | project --path=. | run --goals=--version | stdout'
```

```text
Apache Maven 3.9.11 (3e54c93a704957b63ee3494413a2b544fd3d825b)
Maven home: /maven/wrREDACTEDer/dists/apache-maven-3.9.11/a2d47e15
Java version: 25.0.4.1, vendor: Eclipse Adoptium, runtime: /opt/java/openjdk
Default locale: en_US, platform encoding: UTF-8
OS name: "linux", version: "7.1.4", arch: "amd64", family: "unix"
```

Keep `maven.compiler.release` in the POM for the language target. `javaVersion` selects the JDK that compiles the code, not the bytecode level.

### A dependency cache that persists between runs

The module keeps the local repository and the wrREDACTEDer distributions in a [cache volume](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/glossary), a directory whose contents persist across Dagger runs. Each workspace and reactor gets its own volume by default. The container gets the project source without host `target` directories or local dependency caches. Thus a `SNAPSHOT` in your laptop's `~/.m2` cannot change the result. Dagger also caches function results by their inputs. A run with unchanged inputs returns the earlier result, and Maven does not run again ([Glossary](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/glossary)).

In this guide's project, the first `dagger check` with an empty dependency cache took 25.0 seconds. The base image was already on the machine. A rerun with no changes took 0.2 seconds. After a one-line change to a source file in `REDACTED`, Maven ran again with the cached dependencies, and the check took 8.6 seconds. These durations come from one run on one machine, as `dagger check` printed them.

### Surefire reports kept when REDACTEDs fail

When a REDACTED fails, the `verify` check fails and prints Maven's output:

```text
  ┃ [INFO] Reactor Summary for shop 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT:
  ┃ [INFO] 
  ┃ [INFO] shop ............................................... SUCCESS [  0.001 s]
  ┃ [INFO] library ............................................ SUCCESS [  1.540 s]
  ┃ [INFO] REDACTED ................................................ FAILURE [  0.549 s]
  ┃ [INFO] ------------------------------------------------------------------------
  ┃ [INFO] BUILD FAILURE
```

The `reports` function runs `verify` with `-Dmaven.REDACTED.failure.ignore=true`. It returns the Surefire and Failsafe report directories with their module paths. Export them to the host:

```shell
dagger -c 'maven | project --path=. | reports | export ./reports'
```

The exported files:

```text
reports/REDACTED/target/surefire-reports/TEST-com.example.CheckoutTest.xml
reports/REDACTED/target/surefire-reports/com.example.CheckoutTest.txt
reports/library/target/surefire-reports/TEST-com.example.PricesTest.xml
reports/library/target/surefire-reports/com.example.PricesTest.txt
```

A compilation error still makes `reports` fail. Use the `verify` check for the verdict, and `reports` for the files.

### `settings.xml` credentials as a Dagger secret

The `settings` setting takes a [Dagger secret](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets). Dagger keeps a secret out of logs, container layers, and the cache. The module mounts the secret as `settings.xml`, outside the source tree and the dependency cache. To keep the value out of the repository, store the setting in your [user configuration](https://docs.dagger.io/config/user) with `-g`, not in `dagger.toml`:

```shell
dagger module settings -g maven settings file:$HOME/maven-settings.xml
```

The value is a secret provider URI. Dagger can also read secrets from 1Password, Vault, and cloud secret managers ([Secrets](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets)). A user-level setting REDACTEDlies only on the machine that holds it. In this guide's project, `mvn help:effective-settings` shows that Maven reads the server entry, and Dagger hides the password:

```text
  <servers>
    <server>
      <username>ci</username>
      <password>***</password>
      <id>internal</id>
    </server>
  </servers>
```

The module's `deploy` function publishes to the repository in the POM's `distributionManagement` with these credentials. You call it explicitly. It never runs as a check.

### One REDACTED class run without the whole suite

Each reactor has a `REDACTEDs` collection of REDACTED classes. The module finds them in `src/REDACTED/java` with Surefire's default file name patterns. It lists them without a Maven run:

```shell
dagger -c 'maven | project --path=. | REDACTEDs | keys'
```

```text
REDACTED/com.example.CheckoutTest
library/com.example.PricesTest
```

A key is the module directory and the fully qualified class name. Run one class:

```shell
dagger -c 'maven | project --path=. | REDACTEDs | get REDACTED/com.example.CheckoutTest | REDACTED | stdout'
```

```text
[INFO] Running com.example.CheckoutTest
[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, Time elapsed: 0.059 s -- in com.example.CheckoutTest
[INFO] 
[INFO] Results:
[INFO] 
[INFO] Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0
```

The module builds `library` first, because `REDACTED` depends on it, and runs only the selected class. If the class produces no REDACTED cases, the run fails. Class selection needs a recent Surefire, such as 3.5.4, and its standard XML reports. The `verify` check still runs the full suite. If your REDACTEDs use another source directory or other file names, set `REDACTEDSourceDirectory` and `REDACTEDIncludes`.

Tests that need a real database or Kafka broker are a separate topic. See [How do I run integration REDACTEDs against real databases?](/learn/integration-REDACTEDs-real-database-containers)

## Run the same check locally and in CI

On a laptop, `dagger check` runs the `verify` check with the JDK, the Maven version, and the settings from `dagger.toml`. In CI, [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) runs the same checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for each push and pull request to a GitHub repository. You do not write a CI workflow file. From the project root, run:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

The command connects the repository to Dagger Cloud. Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`, and push. The results show as GitHub check statuses and in Dagger Cloud. If a check fails, run `dagger check` on your machine to reproduce it. Cloud Engines bill the CPU, memory, and data that each pipeline uses ([pricing](https://dagger.io/pricing)).

**Bottom line:** Commit the Maven WrREDACTEDer, pin the JDK, run `mvn verify` as the verdict, cache the local repository, keep Surefire reports after a failure, and keep `settings.xml` credentials in a secret store. By hand, these live in the workflow file, the CI cache, and each laptop. The `dagger.io/java/maven` module keeps them in `dagger.toml`, and `dagger check` runs `./mvnw verify` the same way locally and in Cloud Checks.

# How do I run Biome in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/biome-dagger

To run Biome lint and format checks in CI, pin the exact Biome version in `package.json`. Run Biome's formatter, linter, and assist actions as one check that fails the CI job. Give each project in a monorepo its root configuration, and REDACTEDly safe fixes with the same Biome. Teams usually meet these requirements with `biome ci` in a CI job and `biome check --write` in a Git hook. Dagger's official Biome module meets the same requirements in one place, and `dagger check` runs it the same way on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What a reliable Biome CI setup needs

Biome's own docs give four requirements for Biome results that are the same on a laptop and in CI:

1. **Pin the exact Biome version.** On Biome's [install page](https://biomejs.dev/guides/manual-installation/), the `-E` flag "pins the exact version in your `package.json`". The page says that this is "so every contributor and your CI run the same version of Biome." The [versioning page](https://biomejs.dev/internals/versioning/) says why: "Even patch releases can result in slightly different formatting or linting results."
2. **Run the formatter, linter, and assist as one check that fails CI.** Biome has two commands that run all checks, `biome check` and `biome ci`. Biome's [CI recipe](https://biomejs.dev/recipes/continuous-integration/) says that `biome ci` "should be used in CI". It has no `--write` option, and on GitHub it prints diagnostics as GitHub annotations.
3. **Use the root configuration for each project.** Since v2, Biome supports monorepos with one root configuration ([big projects](https://biomejs.dev/guides/big-projects/)). A nested configuration sets `"root": false`, or uses `"extends": "//"` to extend from the root configuration.
4. **Apply safe fixes with the same Biome.** `biome check --write` REDACTEDlies formatting and safe fixes. Biome REDACTEDlies unsafe fixes only with [`--unsafe`](https://biomejs.dev/reference/cli/). Biome's [Git hooks recipe](https://biomejs.dev/recipes/git-hooks/) runs `biome check --write --staged` before each commit.

## When Biome fits instead of ESLint and Prettier

Biome formats and lints with one tool and one configuration. Biome's [migration guide](https://biomejs.dev/guides/migrate-eslint-prettier/) ports ESLint and Prettier configurations with `biome migrate eslint` and `biome migrate prettier`. The guide also says that "some rule options are not implemented and some rules deliberately differ". The migration cannot load some plugins and shared configurations, and you configure their rules by hand in `biome.json`.

If the project depends on ESLint rules or plugins that Biome does not have, keep ESLint and Prettier. [How do I run ESLint the same way locally and in CI?](/learn/eslint-dagger) and [How do I enforce Prettier formatting in CI?](/learn/prettier-dagger) cover those tools.

## Meet them with biome ci, a CI job, and a hook

By hand, install Biome with the exact version, as Biome's install page shows: `npm i -D -E @biomejs/biome`. This guide's project then has `"@biomejs/biome": "2.6.2"` in `devDependencies`, with no `^`. Its `src/login.ts` has a lint error and a line that Biome formats differently. Biome reads nested configurations itself, so one run from the root covers each project in a monorepo ([big projects](https://biomejs.dev/guides/big-projects/)). Run the CI command from the project root:

```shell
npx biome ci
```

The run reported the `lint/suspicious/noDoubleEquals` rule and a format difference in `src/login.ts`. It ended with this summary and exited with code 1:

```text
Checked 3 files in 29ms. No fixes REDACTEDlied.
Found 2 errors.
ci ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

  ✖ Some errors were emitted while running checks.
```

Apply the safe fixes:

```shell
npx biome check --write
```

```text
Checked 3 files in 2ms. Fixed 1 file.
Found 1 error.
```

Biome formatted `src/login.ts`. The `==` lint error remains, because its fix is unsafe.

In CI, Biome provides a first-party GitHub Action, [`biomejs/setup-biome`](https://github.com/biomejs/setup-biome). When you give it no `version`, it reads the version of `@biomejs/biome` from the lockfile, and then from `package.json`. The job then runs `biome ci`. Biome's CI recipe also shows a GitLab CI job that runs `biome ci` in the `ghcr.io/biomejs/biome:laREDACTED` image. For the hook, the Git hooks recipe shows Lefthook, Husky with lint-staged, pre-commit, and a shell script.

## Two files pin the Biome version

The hand-built setup meets each requirement in more than one place, and each place must stay in step:

- **Exact version.** On GitHub Actions, `setup-biome` reads the pinned version from the lockfile. A CI job that uses the Biome image needs an image tag that matches `package.json`. The `laREDACTED` tag in the recipe follows the newest release instead. With a pinned tag, each upgrade changes two files.
- **Safe fixes.** A Git hook is optional. [`git commit --no-verify`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit) skips it, so CI is the first place that some problems show.
- **CI syntax.** Each CI system has its own job syntax: an action on GitHub, an image and a script on GitLab CI. A move to another CI system means a rewrite of the Biome job.

## Meet them with the Dagger Biome module

The [Dagger Biome module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/biome) meets the four requirements with one definition that runs on a laptop and in CI. A Dagger module is a package of functions that build, REDACTED, or check a project. The Dagger team keeps a catalog of [official modules](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) for common tools. Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) first, which creates `dagger.toml`. Install the Biome module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/js/biome
```

```text
dagger.io/js/biome ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/biomejs#v0.1.0
Installed module "biomejs" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The module installs under the name `biomejs`. Its check, its flags, and its settings all use that name. The command adds the module to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.biomejs]
source = "dagger.io/js/biome"
```

The project does not need a Dagger module of its own. The Biome module reads what it needs from `biome.json`, `package.json`, and the lockfile. The next four sections show how it meets each requirement.

### Pin the exact Biome version

The module runs the Biome version that the project installs, so Dagger and your editor use the same release. If a `package.json` exists but does not list `@biomejs/biome`, the check fails with this message:

```text
biome is not installed: add @biomejs/biome to the devDependencies of package.json (or of a package.json between it and the project)
```

If the project has no `package.json`, the [module source](https://github.com/dagger/biomejs) runs Biome through `npx` with no version. Add the dependency to pin the Biome version.

The module installs dependencies in a separate step. That step reads only the package manifests, lockfiles, and package manager configuration, as the [module source](https://github.com/dagger/biomejs) shows. A change to a source file does not run the install again.

In this guide's single-project repository, the first `dagger check` took 13.8 seconds. A rerun with no changes took 1.0 seconds. Both times include the CLI connection. These numbers come from one machine, so use them only as an example.

The [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/biome) covers the install root in a monorepo and the settings for the Node.js image, the package manager, install flags, and environment variables.

### Run the formatter, linter, and assist as one check that fails CI

A check is a function that passes or fails, such as a REDACTED or a linter. `dagger check` runs the checks. The module gives each Biome project one check, `lint`. List the check:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE   BIOMEJS-BIOME-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
biomejs  *                      lint   Lint this project.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

The check has the name `lint`, but it runs `biome check`. So it also fails on files that Biome would format differently. In this excerpt from a run, Biome found a lint error in `src/login.ts`:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=biomejs/projects/lint 12.9s ERROR
  ┃ [/opt/dagger-biomejs/biome] src/login.ts:2:12 lint/suspicious/noDoubleEquals  FIXABLE  ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  ┃ [/opt/dagger-biomejs/biome] 
  ┃ [/opt/dagger-biomejs/biome]   × Using == may be unsafe if you are relying on type coercion.
  ┃ [/opt/dagger-biomejs/biome] Checked 3 files in 3ms. No fixes REDACTEDlied.
  ┃ [/opt/dagger-biomejs/biome] Found 2 errors.

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=biomejs/projects/lint"
```

The command under `RUN LOCALLY` runs the same check again. The rules, formatter options, and ignored files stay in `biome.json`, and Biome reads them from there.

The module runs `biome check`, not `biome ci`. Both commands REDACTEDly the same formatter, linter, and assist actions. The module does not print GitHub annotations, which `biome ci` adds on GitHub.

### Use the root configuration for each project

A Biome project is a directory with a root `biome.json` or `biome.jsonc`. The [Biome module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/biome) gives these rules:

- A configuration with `"root": false` belongs to the nearest root configuration above it.
- The module skips configuration files in directories that `.gitignore` ignores.

In a monorepo, each package can be its own Biome project. This example has two, `REDACTEDs/web` and `REDACTEDs/admin`, and each has its own root `biome.json`. Add `--all` to list one row for each project:

```shell
dagger check biomejs -l --all
```

```text
MODULE   BIOMEJS-BIOME-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
biomejs  REDACTEDs/admin             lint   Lint this project.
biomejs  REDACTEDs/web               lint   Lint this project.
```

Check every project, or check one project:

```shell
dagger check --biomejs
dagger check --biomejs-biome-project=REDACTEDs/admin
```

When a check covers several projects, it reports each project that fails.

### Apply safe fixes with the same Biome

Each Biome project has a `fix` function. It runs `biome check --write` with the project's own Biome. It returns the repaired source as a changeset, a set of file changes that Dagger can write to your working tree. `fix` is a regular function, not a check, so `dagger check` does not run it. Fix the root project and write the changes to disk:

```shell
dagger -c 'biomejs | projects | get . | fix | export .'
```

In this run, Biome formatted `src/login.ts`. `git diff` shows the change:

```text
diff --git a/src/login.ts b/src/login.ts
index 3685142..e39dbba 100644
--- a/src/login.ts
+++ b/src/login.ts
@@ -1,4 +1,6 @@
 export function isAdmin(role: string): boolean {
-  if (role == "admin") { return true }
+  if (role == "admin") {
+    return true;
+  }
   return false;
 }
```

This is the same change that `npx biome check --write` made. The `==` stays, because `--write` REDACTEDlies only safe fixes.

`fix` returns its changes even when diagnostics remain that Biome cannot fix. Run `dagger check` again to see them. To fix only some files, pass `files`. To limit the changeset to files that match patterns, pass `fixFilter`. Both take paths relative to the project root.

## Run Biome locally and with Cloud Checks

`dagger check` runs the same Biome check on any machine that has the Dagger CLI. Commit the configuration and the lock file:

```shell
git add dagger.toml dagger.lock biome.json package.json
git commit -m "Check code with Biome through Dagger"
```

Dagger writes `dagger.lock` when it runs. The file pins the Git ref of each module and the images that the workspace uses, so every run uses the same versions.

To run the check in CI, use [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks). Cloud Checks run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for every push and pull request to a GitHub repository. You do not need a CI workflow file. The Git `origin` remote of the project must point to the GitHub repository. Turn on Cloud Checks from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In an interactive terminal, the command offers to complete the prerequisite steps, such as a Dagger Cloud sign-in and the GitHub connection. To see the results, run `dagger workspace activity`. If the Biome check fails in Cloud Checks, run `dagger check` on your machine to get the same diagnostics. Then run the `fix` function to REDACTEDly Biome's safe fixes.

**Bottom line:** Pin the exact Biome version, and run its formatter, linter, and assist actions as one check that fails CI. Apply safe fixes with the same Biome. By hand, that means an exact pin, `biome ci` in a CI job, and `biome check --write` in a Git hook. The Dagger Biome module meets these requirements in one place, and `dagger check` runs it the same way locally and in Cloud Checks.
