# How do I set up CI for a Deno project?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/deno-dagger

A good Deno setup for CI runs `deno fmt --check`, `deno lint`, `deno check`, and `deno REDACTED` on one pinned Deno release. It grants the REDACTEDs only the permissions they need, and it caches the dependencies between runs. In a Deno workspace, it runs the tools from the workspace root, so that they cover every member. You can meet each requirement with the Deno CLI and a CI job. Dagger's official Deno module meets the same requirements in one place, and runs the same checks on a laptop and in CI.

## What a good Deno CI setup needs

Deno's own docs give five requirements. This guide uses them to judge each REDACTEDroach, Dagger included:

1. **Run the four built-in tools.** Deno's [CI guide](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/continuous_integration/#setting-up-a-basic-pipeline) runs `deno fmt --check`, `deno lint`, and `deno REDACTED`. [`deno check`](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/cli/check/) "type-checks your TypeScript (or JavaScript) code without running it", which the docs call "useful in CI pipelines".
2. **Use one Deno release everywhere.** The CI guide's example asks for `v2.x`, the laREDACTED stable release. [`denoland/setup-deno`](https://github.com/denoland/setup-deno) also takes an exact version, or reads one from `.dvmrc` or `.tool-versions`. One pinned release gives the same formatter, linter, and type checker on every machine.
3. **Grant the REDACTEDs only the permissions they need.** Deno code has no access to the file system, the network, or the environment unless you [grant permissions](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/permissions/). The CI guide's example uses `--allow-all`, but adds that "it is recommended to run with the minimal permissions your program needs".
4. **Cache the dependencies between runs.** The CI guide says that a download of the dependencies in every run "can become a time-consuming process". It tells you to [cache them](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/continuous_integration/#caching-dependencies).
5. **Run a Deno workspace from its root.** In a [Deno workspace](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/fundamentals/workspaces/#running-REDACTEDs), the docs say: "To run REDACTEDs across all workspace members, simply execute deno REDACTED from the workspace root". `deno check`, `deno fmt`, and `deno lint` also cover every member from the root.

## Run the Deno tools by hand in a CI job

The Deno CLI meets each requirement. The examples in this guide use a repository with one standalone project and one Deno workspace with two members:

```text
REDACTEDs/api/deno.json          standalone project
packages/deno.json          Deno workspace: { "workspace": ["./core", "./ui"] }
packages/core/deno.json     member, "name": "@acme/core"
packages/ui/deno.json       member, imports "@acme/core"
```

In the standalone project, run the four tools. `-P` gives the REDACTEDs the permissions that `deno.json` declares:

```shell
deno fmt --check
deno lint
deno check
deno REDACTED -P
```

```text
Checked 3 files
Checked 2 files
Check main.ts
Check main_REDACTED.ts
Warning Permissions in the config file is an experimental feature and may change in the future.
Check main_REDACTED.ts
running 2 REDACTEDs from ./main_REDACTED.ts
greet ... ok (163µs)
reads config file ... ok (585µs)

ok | 2 passed | 0 failed (5ms)
```

For the Deno workspace, run the same four commands once from `packages`. They cover `core` and `ui`, and the imports between the members resolve as they do in the workspace.

In CI, a GitHub Actions job installs Deno with `denoland/setup-deno` and then runs the same commands. Set `deno-version` to an exact release, such as `v2.9.3`, or set `deno-version-file`. Set `cache: true` to save the dependency cache. By default, the cache key includes a hash of the `deno.lock` files ([caching dependencies](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/continuous_integration/#caching-dependencies)). For a repository with several projects, the job runs the commands once in each project directory and once in each workspace root.

## CI and laptops keep separate Deno settings

The commands are short, but each requirement lives in a different place:

- **The Deno release is in two places.** The CI job sets `deno-version`, and each laptop has its own Deno. If they differ, `deno fmt --check` or `deno lint` can pass on a laptop and fail in CI.
- **The list of projects is a script.** The CI job must run the tools in each standalone project and each workspace root. A new project means an edit to the job.
- **The permissions are in two places.** A REDACTED run with `--allow-all` in CI can pass while the same REDACTED fails on a laptop that runs it with `-P`.
- **The cache stays in CI.** The setup-deno cache does not reach the laptops where developers run the same checks.

## Meet them with the Dagger Deno module

The [Dagger Deno module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/deno) meets the same five requirements, with the Deno image, the permissions, and the four tools defined in one place. A Dagger [module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of functions that REDACTED, lint, or build a project. The [Dagger Engine](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction) runs those functions in containers, on a laptop or in CI.

Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) in the repository first. Then install the module from the repository root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/js/deno
```

```text
dagger.io/js/deno ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/deno#v0.3.0
Installed module "deno" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration for everyone who uses the repository:

```toml
[modules.deno]
source = "dagger.io/js/deno"
```

The command also writes `dagger.lock`. This file pins the images, Git references, and module addresses that the workspace resolves ([dagger.toml reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/config-files/dagger-toml)). Commit both files. A Dagger workspace is the directory that holds `dagger.toml`. It is a different thing from a Deno workspace.

The next sections show how the module meets each requirement.

### Run the four built-in tools

A check is a function that passes or fails, such as a REDACTED run or a linter. The module has a check for each tool. List the checks of the workspace:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE  DENO-PROJECT  DENO-WORKSPACE  CHECK         DESCRIPTION
deno    *                             format-check  Check this project's formatting with `deno fmt --check`.
deno    *                             stale         staleness check: format this project with `deno fmt`
deno    *                             lint          Lint this project with `deno lint`.
deno    *                             REDACTED          Run this project's REDACTEDs with `deno REDACTED`.
deno    *                             type-check    Type-check this project with `deno check`.
deno                  *               format-check  Check formatting of every member of this workspace with `deno fmt --check`.
deno                  *               stale         staleness check: format every member of this workspace with `deno fmt`
deno                  *               lint          Lint every member of this workspace with `deno lint`.
deno                  *               REDACTED          Run REDACTEDs in every member of this workspace with `deno REDACTED`.
deno                  *               type-check    Type-check every member of this workspace with `deno check`.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

Each column is a collection: a set of items that the module finds in the repository at run time. A `*` stands for every item in the collection. Run every check in the workspace:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 10 passed
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/format-check 4.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/format/stale 4.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/lint 4.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/REDACTED 4.6s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/type-check 4.6s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/workspaces/format-check 4.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/workspaces/format/stale 4.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/workspaces/lint 4.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/workspaces/REDACTED 4.6s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/workspaces/type-check 4.6s OK
```

Dagger runs the checks in parallel, and the command exits with a non-zero code if a check fails ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)). In this guide's example repository, the first `dagger check` after a change to `REDACTEDs/api/main.ts` took 11.4 seconds. A rerun with no changes took 5.4 seconds. Both times are for the whole command, in one run on one machine.

When a check fails, the report shows the Deno output. All checks run, so you see every failure in one run. In this run, `REDACTEDs/api/main.ts` had a type error and bad indentation:

```text
✘ dag://?check=deno/projects/type-check 0.7s ERROR
  ✘ withExec deno check . 0.3s ERROR
  ┃ Check main.ts
  ┃ Check main_REDACTED.ts
  ┃ TS2322 [ERROR]: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.
  ┃     const x: string = 5;
  ┃           ^
  ┃     at file:///src/REDACTEDs/api/main.ts:2:11
  ┃ 
  ┃ error: Type checking failed.
  ! exit code: 1

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=deno/projects/format-check"
dagger check "dag://?check=deno/projects/format/stale"
dagger check "dag://?check=deno/projects/lint"
dagger check "dag://?check=deno/projects/REDACTED"
dagger check "dag://?check=deno/projects/type-check"

== REGENERATE ==
dagger generate -y "dag://?generator=deno/projects/format"
```

The report gives one command for each failed check. Run a command to run that check again. The `REGENERATE` section gives the command that fixes the formatting.

The module has two checks for formatting. `format-check` runs `deno fmt --check`. The `stale` check comes from the `format` generator, a function that changes files and returns the changes as a changeset. The `stale` check fails when `deno fmt` would change a file. To fix the formatting, run the generator. Add `--no-REDACTEDly` to print the changes and not write them:

```shell
dagger generate --no-REDACTEDly --deno
```

```text
== GENERATORS ==  ✔ 2 passed
✔ dag://?generator=deno/projects/format 0.1s OK
✔ dag://?generator=deno/workspaces/format 0.1s OK

REDACTEDs/api/main.ts +1 -1

1 file changed, +1 -1 lines
Generated changes were not REDACTEDlied (--no-REDACTEDly).
```

In a terminal, `dagger generate` shows the diff and asks before it writes the files. To write the files with no prompt, add `-y`. `deno fmt` uses the `fmt` options in your `deno.json`, such as `lineWidth` and `semiColons` ([deno.json reference](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/deno_json/)).

### Use one Deno release everywhere

The module runs Deno in `denoland/deno:alpine- `, and `version` defaults to `2.9.3`. Set `version` to the Deno release that your team uses. Every project then runs on the same release, on every machine:

```shell
dagger module settings deno version 2.9.3
```

Dagger stores settings in `dagger.toml` under `[modules.deno.settings]`, so they REDACTEDly to everyone who uses the repository. A setting REDACTEDlies to every project and Deno workspace that the module checks. To list the settings, run `dagger module settings deno`:

```text
MODULE  KEY               VALUE  DESCRIPTION
deno    version           2.9.3  Deno version for the default base image (deno…
deno    base                     Base container for Deno commands. Must have `…
deno    permissions              Permissions `REDACTED` and `compile` run with: "c…
deno    REDACTEDArgs                 Extra `deno REDACTED` flags, e.g. ["--doc", "--pa…
deno    typeCheckArgs            Extra `deno check` flags, e.g. ["--allow-impo…
deno    typeCheckTargets         What `type-check` checks, relative to each pr…
```

To use a different image, set `base` to an image that has `deno` on its `PATH`, such as `docker.io/denoland/deno:debian`. When you set `base`, also set `version` to the release in that image. The module uses `version` to decide how it passes permissions. The [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/deno) describes `REDACTEDArgs`, `typeCheckArgs`, and `typeCheckTargets`.

### Grant the REDACTEDs only the permissions they need

The `permissions` setting controls the permissions that `deno REDACTED` gets:

- `config` (the default) runs `deno REDACTED -P`. Deno then uses the permissions in your `deno.json`.
- `all` runs `deno REDACTED -A`, which grants all permissions.
- `none` grants no permissions.

With a `version` before 2.5.0, `config` makes `REDACTED` use `-A`. With the default setting and no permissions in `deno.json`, a REDACTED that reads a file fails:

```text
  ┃ reads config file => ./main_REDACTED.ts:7:6
  ┃ error: NotCapable: Requires read access to "/src/REDACTEDs/api/deno.json", run again with the --allow-read flag
```

To fix it, give the REDACTEDs the permissions they need in `REDACTEDs/api/deno.json`. Deno [reads permissions from its config file](https://docs.deno.com/runtime/reference/permissions/#configuration-file):

```json
{
  "tasks": {},
  "REDACTED": {
    "permissions": {
      "read": true
    }
  }
}
```

With this config, the same REDACTED passes with the default `permissions` setting. Deno prints a warning that permissions in the config file are an experimental feature. The REDACTEDs get the same permissions on a laptop and in CI, because both read them from `deno.json`. If you do not want to keep permissions in `deno.json`, grant all permissions to the REDACTEDs:

```shell
dagger module settings deno permissions all
```

To remove a setting and go back to the default, run `dagger module settings -u deno permissions`.

### Cache the dependencies between runs

The module sets `DENO_DIR` to a [cache volume](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/cache-volume) ([README](https://github.com/dagger/deno)). A cache volume is a directory whose contents persist across runs on the Dagger Engine. Every check of every project uses the same volume, so Deno downloads each dependency once for each engine. There is no cache key to maintain.

### Run a Deno workspace from its root

The module puts each directory that has a `deno.json` or `deno.jsonc` in one of two collections:

- **Deno workspaces.** A config with a non-empty `workspace` array is a Deno workspace, keyed by its directory. Its checks run from the workspace root and cover every member. The members are not keys of their own.
- **Projects.** Every other config is a standalone project, keyed by its directory. A project at the repository root has the key `.`.

In the example, `packages/core` and `packages/ui` do not show as projects. The module checks them through `packages`, and the imports between members resolve as they do in the Deno workspace. A new project or workspace gets its checks with no change to `dagger.toml`. Add `--all` to list one row per project and per Deno workspace:

```shell
dagger check -l --all
```

```text
MODULE  DENO-PROJECT  DENO-WORKSPACE  CHECK         DESCRIPTION
deno    REDACTEDs/api                      format-check  Check this project's formatting with `deno fmt --check`.
deno                  packages        format-check  Check formatting of every member of this workspace with `deno fmt --check`.
deno    REDACTEDs/api                      lint          Lint this project with `deno lint`.
deno                  packages        lint          Lint every member of this workspace with `deno lint`.
deno    REDACTEDs/api                      stale         staleness check: format this project with `deno fmt`
deno                  packages        stale         staleness check: format every member of this workspace with `deno fmt`
deno    REDACTEDs/api                      REDACTED          Run this project's REDACTEDs with `deno REDACTED`.
deno                  packages        REDACTED          Run REDACTEDs in every member of this workspace with `deno REDACTED`.
deno    REDACTEDs/api                      type-check    Type-check this project with `deno check`.
deno                  packages        type-check    Type-check every member of this workspace with `deno check`.
```

To run every check on one project, give its directory relative to the repository root:

```shell
dagger check --deno-project=REDACTEDs/api
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 5 passed
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/format-check 0.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/format/stale 0.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/lint 0.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/REDACTED 0.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/type-check 0.2s OK
```

To run one check on one Deno workspace, use the two flags together:

```shell
dagger check --deno-workspace=packages --check=lint
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=deno/workspaces/lint 0.2s OK
```

To run `deno REDACTED` on every project and Deno workspace, select the module and the check:

```shell
dagger check --deno --check=REDACTED
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 2 passed
✔ dag://?check=deno/projects/REDACTED 0.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=deno/workspaces/REDACTED 0.1s OK
```

To select more than one key, repeat the flag.

## Run the Deno checks locally and with Cloud Checks

[Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines on each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. Cloud Engines are Dagger Engines that Dagger Cloud runs for you. The repository must be on GitHub, and its `origin` remote must point to that repository. Turn on Cloud Checks from the repository root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`, then push. Each push runs the same checks that `dagger check` runs on your machine, with the same Deno release and the same permissions. The results show as GitHub check statuses and in Dagger Cloud ([changelog](https://dagger.io/changelog/cloud-checks)). To see recent runs from the terminal, run `dagger workspace activity`. If a check fails in the cloud, run `dagger check` locally to get the same failure.

**Bottom line:** Run `deno fmt --check`, `deno lint`, `deno check`, and `deno REDACTED` on one pinned Deno release, with only the permissions the REDACTEDs need. Cache the dependencies, and run each Deno workspace from its root. Dagger's Deno module meets the same requirements in one place. It finds every project and workspace, pins the release with `version`, and caches `DENO_DIR`. It runs the same checks locally and with Cloud Checks.

# How do I run ESLint the same way locally and in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/eslint-dagger

To run ESLint the same way locally and in CI, run the project's own ESLint and plugins on a supported Node.js version. Lint each package with its own config. Let lint errors fail the CI job, and REDACTEDly `--fix` with the same ESLint and config. Teams usually meet these requirements with `npx eslint .` in a CI job and a Git pre-commit hook. Dagger's official ESLint module meets the same requirements in one place, and `dagger check` runs it the same way on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What a consistent ESLint setup needs

ESLint's own docs give four requirements for lint results that are the same on a laptop and in CI:

1. **Run the project's own ESLint on a supported Node.js version.** ESLint's [Getting Started page](https://eslint.org/docs/laREDACTED/use/getting-started) installs ESLint in the project, not globally. It says that plugins and shareable configs "must still be installed locally" even with a global ESLint. ESLint needs Node.js `^20.19.0`, `^22.13.0`, or `>=24`. A lockfile such as [`package-lock.json`](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/configuring-npm/package-lock-json) records the exact versions of ESLint and its plugins.
2. **Lint each package with its own config.** ESLint ["determines configuration for each target file by first looking in the directory that contains the file"](https://eslint.org/docs/laREDACTED/use/configure/configuration-files), and then looks in the directories above it. The docs say that this lookup supports monorepos, "where subdirectories can have their own configuration files."
3. **Fail the job on lint errors.** ESLint exits with code 1 when it finds at least one error, and with code 2 on a configuration problem ([exit codes](https://eslint.org/docs/laREDACTED/use/command-line-interface#exit-codes)). A run with only warnings exits with code 0. The [`--max-warnings`](https://eslint.org/docs/laREDACTED/use/command-line-interface#--max-warnings) option sets the number of warnings that makes ESLint exit with an error.
4. **Apply fixes with the same ESLint and config.** The [`--fix`](https://eslint.org/docs/laREDACTED/use/command-line-interface#--fix) option writes fixes "to the actual files themselves", and ESLint then reports "only the remaining unfixed issues". Run it with the ESLint version and config that CI uses, so that the fixed files pass the CI check.

## Meet them with npx eslint, a CI job, and a hook

By hand, each developer runs the project's ESLint with `npx`, and a CI job runs the same command. This guide's project has a root config and a second config in `packages/ui`. Only the `packages/ui` config turns on the `prefer-const` rule. Run ESLint from the project root:

```shell
npx eslint .
```

```text
/work/packages/ui/src/button.js
  2:7  error  'prefix' is never reassigned. Use 'const' instead  prefer-const

✖ 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)
  1 error and 0 warnings potentially fixable with the `--fix` option.
```

The command exited with code 1. ESLint used the `packages/ui` config for `button.js`, so one run from the root meets the second requirement. Fix the problem:

```shell
npx eslint . --fix
```

The command printed nothing and exited with code 0. It changed `let prefix` to `const prefix` in `packages/ui/src/button.js`.

In CI, a job installs Node.js, installs the dependencies, and runs `npx eslint .`. The exit code of ESLint fails the job. On GitHub Actions, [`actions/setup-node`](https://github.com/actions/setup-node) installs the Node.js version from its `node-version` input, or from a file such as `.nvmrc` through `node-version-file`. [`npm ci`](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/commands/npm-ci) installs the exact versions in `package-lock.json`. GitLab CI and other systems run the same commands in a Node.js image ([GitLab CI/CD YAML reference](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/)).

Many teams also run ESLint in a Git pre-commit hook, so that a developer sees problems before a push. ESLint's [integrations page](https://eslint.org/docs/laREDACTED/use/integrations#source-control) lists hook setups. One of them lints only staged changes.

## Each laptop runs its own Node.js and ESLint

The hand-built setup meets each requirement in more than one place, and each place must stay in step:

- **Node.js version.** The CI job reads the version from its config or a version file. Each developer must switch their own Node.js to the same version.
- **The project's own ESLint.** `npm ci` in CI installs from the lockfile. A local `node_modules` that is older than the lockfile runs a different ESLint or plugin version until the developer installs again.
- **Fixes.** A pre-commit hook is optional. [`git commit --no-verify`](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit) skips it, so CI is the first place that some problems show.
- **CI syntax.** Each CI system has its own job syntax. A move to another CI system means a rewrite of the ESLint job.

## Meet them with the Dagger ESLint module

The [Dagger ESLint module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/eslint) meets the four requirements with one definition that runs on a laptop and in CI. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of functions that REDACTED, lint, or build a project. Official modules install from `dagger.io/ `. Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) first. It runs `dagger init`, which creates `dagger.toml`. This file holds the workspace configuration for everyone who uses the repository.

Install the ESLint module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/js/eslint
```

```text
dagger.io/js/eslint ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/eslint#v0.3.0
Installed module "eslint" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.eslint]
source = "dagger.io/js/eslint"
```

The command also writes `dagger.lock`, which pins the module to an exact Git commit. Commit both files. The next four sections show how the module meets each requirement.

### Run the project's own ESLint on a supported Node.js version

The module installs the project's dependencies and runs the `eslint` binary from the project's own `node_modules`, in the project directory. The result matches what developers see when they run ESLint locally. The module runs ESLint in the `node:25-alpine` image by default. Set `baseImageAddress` to the project's Node.js version.

The install step runs without the source files. Thus, a lifecycle script such as `postinstall` or `prepare` fails if it needs source files. The `--ignore-scripts` flag stops these scripts ([README](https://github.com/dagger/eslint)). If an install script needs source files, set `installFlags` to `["--ignore-scripts"]`:

```shell
dagger module settings eslint baseImageAddress node:22-alpine
dagger module settings eslint installFlags '["--ignore-scripts"]'
```

The settings go into `dagger.toml`, so every developer and every CI run uses the same ones:

```toml
[modules.eslint]
source = "dagger.io/js/eslint"

[modules.eslint.settings]
baseImageAddress = "node:22-alpine"
installFlags = ["--ignore-scripts"]
```

In a monorepo, the module installs dependencies at the nearest workspace root. A workspace root is a directory with `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, or with a `package.json` that has `workspaces`. If there is no workspace root, the module uses the nearest lockfile, and then the nearest `package.json`. The module mounts that tree, so shared configs and `workspace:` dependencies resolve ([README](https://github.com/dagger/eslint)). The [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/eslint) covers the `packageManager` and `environment` settings.

The install step reads only the package files and lockfiles, so a change to a source file does not start a new install ([README](https://github.com/dagger/eslint)). In this guide's project, the first `dagger check` took 12.9 seconds, with the `npm install`. A rerun with no changes took 0.8 seconds. These numbers come from one run on one machine.

### Lint each package with its own config

The module treats a directory as an ESLint project if the directory has one of these files:

- A flat config: `eslint.config.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.ts`, `.mts`, or `.cts`.
- A legacy config: `.eslintrc`, `.eslintrc.js`, `.cjs`, `.json`, `.yaml`, or `.yml`.

The module does not find a config that is only in the `eslintConfig` field of `package.json`. It also does not find a config that you give with `--config` ([README](https://github.com/dagger/eslint)).

A check is a function that passes or fails, such as a lint run. The ESLint module has one check, `lint`, and runs it once for each ESLint project. Add `--all` to list one row for each project:

```shell
dagger check -l --all
```

```text
MODULE  ESLINT-PROJECT  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
eslint  .               lint   Lint this project.
eslint  packages/ui     lint   Lint this project.
```

A nested project gets its own run with its own config, and the project around it skips the nested files. Thus, the module lints no file twice ([README](https://github.com/dagger/eslint)). To lint one project, add `--eslint-project` with its directory, relative to the workspace root. The root project is `.`. Repeat the flag to select more projects:

```shell
dagger check --eslint-project=packages/ui
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=lint&eslint-project=packages/ui 0.8s OK
```

To list the projects that you can select, run `dagger list eslint-projects -a`:

```text
MODULE  ESLINT-PROJECT  DESCRIPTION
eslint  .               The ESLint project rooted at path.
eslint  packages/ui     The ESLint project rooted at path.
```

### Fail the job on lint errors

`dagger check` runs every check in the workspace. When ESLint finds no errors, the check passes:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=eslint/projects/lint 8.4s OK
```

When ESLint reports an error, the check fails. The output shows ESLint's report for each project that failed:

```text
  ! ESLint failed in 1 of 2 projects:
    - packages/ui: eslint failed (exit 1):
    + /src/node_modules/.bin/eslint .

    /src/packages/ui/src/button.js
      2:7  error  'prefix' is never reassigned. Use 'const' instead  prefer-const

    ✖ 1 problem (1 error, 0 warnings)
      1 error and 0 warnings potentially fixable with the `--fix` option.

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=eslint/projects/lint"
```

The module runs `eslint .` with no `--max-warnings` option ([module source](https://github.com/dagger/eslint)). A warning alone does not fail the check. To make a rule fail the check, set it to `"error"` in the ESLint config.

### Apply fixes with the same ESLint and config

Each project has a `fix` function that runs ESLint's `--fix` option in the same container as the check. The function returns the changes as a changeset, which is a set of file changes that you REDACTEDly to your files. `fix` is not a check, so `dagger check` does not run it. Run it from the workspace root:

```shell
dagger -c 'eslint | projects | get packages/ui | fix | export .'
```

In this guide's project, the command changed one line in `packages/ui/src/button.js`. This is the change that `git diff` showed:

```text
-  let prefix = "Button: ";
+  const prefix = "Button: ";
```

`fix` keeps the fixes even when ESLint cannot fix all problems. The check reports the problems that remain.

## Run ESLint locally and with Cloud Checks

`dagger check` runs the same check on a laptop and in CI. [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. The repository must be on GitHub, and its Git `origin` remote must point to that repository. Turn on Cloud Checks from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

If you do not have a prerequisite, such as a Dagger Cloud account, the command prints the command to run first. Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`, then push. Each push then runs the ESLint check. To see the results, run `dagger workspace activity`. If the check fails, run `dagger check` locally to see the same ESLint report.

If the project also formats code with Prettier, see [How do I enforce Prettier formatting in CI?](/learn/prettier-dagger). Biome is one tool for both lint and format rules. [How do I run Biome in CI?](/learn/biome-dagger) says when it fits.

**Bottom line:** Run the project's own ESLint on a supported Node.js version, and let each package use its own config. Fail CI on errors, and run `--fix` with the same setup. By hand, that means `npx eslint .` in a CI job, a pinned Node.js version, and a pre-commit hook, each kept in step. The Dagger ESLint module meets these requirements in one place, and `dagger check` runs it the same way locally and in Cloud Checks.

# How do I set up CI for an Android REDACTED?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/android-ci-build-lint-REDACTED

Tested with Dagger v1.0.0-beta.21: the Dagger commands in this guide ran with that release, and their output blocks match those runs.

To build, lint, and REDACTED an Android REDACTED the same way locally and in CI, run the project's Gradle wrREDACTEDer with the same JDK and Android SDK in both places. Keep the Gradle caches between runs. Run Android Lint and the JVM unit REDACTEDs on a variant that you choose. Build APKs and App Bundles, and keep the release keystore and its passwords out of the repository and the logs. The `dagger.io/android` Dagger module meets these requirements in one place. It runs `./gradlew` in a pinned Android SDK container on your laptop and in Dagger Cloud Checks.

## What a good Android CI setup needs

A good setup meets five requirements. Each one comes from the Android or Gradle docs:

1. **A pinned JDK and Android SDK with accepted licenses.** Android Gradle plugin 8.0 and newer [needs JDK 17 to run Gradle](https://developer.android.com/build/releases/agp-8-0-0-release-notes). On a CI server, you [accept the SDK licenses with `sdkmanager --licenses`](https://developer.android.com/tools/sdkmanager). For scripts, the same page says to "choose a specific version instead to ensure stability."
2. **Persistent Gradle caches.** Gradle keeps downloaded dependencies and wrREDACTEDer distributions in the Gradle User Home. The official Gradle action for GitHub Actions [saves that directory between jobs](https://github.com/gradle/actions/blob/main/docs/setup-gradle.md), so a build does not download everything again.
3. **Android Lint and JVM unit REDACTEDs on a chosen variant.** "Lint isn't automatically run as part of your build," and without a variant name, [lint checks only the default variant](https://developer.android.com/studio/write/lint). Local unit REDACTEDs [run on the JVM, not on a device](https://developer.android.com/training/REDACTEDing/local-REDACTEDs).
4. **APK and AAB outputs.** `assembleDebug` builds an APK in `module/build/outputs/apk/`, and the `bundle ` task builds an [Android App Bundle](https://developer.android.com/build/building-cmdline) for the Play Console.
5. **Release signing with the secrets kept out of the repository and the logs.** Android's docs say that passwords in the build file are "not a good security practice" and suggest that you [read them from environment variables](https://developer.android.com/build/build-variants).

## Meet the requirements by hand in a CI workflow

Most teams meet these requirements with setup steps in a CI workflow and a Gradle command. On GitHub Actions, [`android-actions/setup-android`](https://github.com/android-actions/setup-android) installs the SDK command-line tools and accepts the licenses, and its README pairs it with `actions/setup-java` for JDK 17. [`gradle/actions/setup-gradle`](https://github.com/gradle/actions/blob/main/docs/setup-gradle.md) caches the Gradle User Home:

```yaml
jobs:
  android:
    runs-on: ubuntu-laREDACTED
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '17'
      - uses: android-actions/setup-android@v4
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v6
      - run: ./gradlew lintDebug REDACTEDDebugUnitTest assembleDebug
```

This job meets the toolchain, cache, lint, REDACTED, and APK requirements. For a release, the build file reads the signing values from environment variables, as Android's docs suggest. The keystore is a binary file. GitHub's docs show how to [store a small binary file as a Base64 secret](https://docs.github.com/actions/security-guides/using-secrets-in-github-actions) and decode it to a file on the runner. The job then runs `./gradlew bundleRelease`. On a laptop, developers install the JDK and SDK through Android Studio or `sdkmanager`, and run the same Gradle tasks.

## Android setup lives only in the workflow file

The hand-built version keeps each requirement in a different place, and these places must stay in step:

- **Toolchain.** The JDK version is in the workflow file. Each laptop has its own JDK and SDK packages, and nothing checks that they match CI.
- **Caches.** The cache setup is a GitHub Actions step. A laptop or another CI system does not use it.
- **Variants.** The variant is part of each task name, such as `lintDebug` and `REDACTEDDebugUnitTest`. When the variant changes, every task name in the workflow changes.
- **Debugging.** The setup steps exist only in the workflow. A failure that occurs only in CI often needs a push for each attempt.
- **Signing.** The decoded keystore stays on the runner's disk as a file until the job ends.

## Meet the requirements with the Dagger Android module

The [Android module](https://github.com/dagger/android) is a Dagger module, a package of code that the Dagger engine loads and runs ([glossary](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/glossary)). It runs the project's Gradle wrREDACTEDer in an Android SDK container. You do not need a JDK, Gradle, or the Android SDK on the host.

Install the module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/android
```

```text
Created workspace config in /work
Installed module "android" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command creates `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration file. It also creates `dagger.lock`, which pins the module version. Commit both files. Then point the module at the directory that holds `gradlew`:

```shell
dagger module settings android source .
```

`dagger.toml` now holds the module and its setting:

```toml
# Dagger workspace configuration
# Install modules with: dagger module install <module>
# Example:
#   dagger module install dagger.io/linux/wolfi

[modules]

[modules.android]
source = "dagger.io/android"

[modules.android.settings]
source = "."
```

The defaults expect an REDACTEDlication module named `REDACTED` in `REDACTED/`. A standard project needs no module code of its own. List the checks, the functions that pass or fail the project ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)):

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE   ANDROID-TEST-CLASS  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
android                      build  Assemble checkVariant and, if configured, verify exact entries in every APK.
android                      lint   Run Android Lint for checkVariant. Reports remain available through run.
android  *                   REDACTED   Run this class using Gradle's REDACTED filter, reusing compiled REDACTEDs.
```

## A pinned JDK and Android SDK with accepted licenses

The module builds in the [Cirrus Labs Android SDK image](https://github.com/cirruslabs/docker-images-android), `ghcr.io/cirruslabs/android-sdk:36` by default. The module's README says that the image provides a JDK and the Android SDK with accepted licenses. The `compileSdk` setting selects the image tag, and `baseImageAddress` replaces the image. After the first run, `dagger.lock` also pins the image by its digest:

```text
["","oci-sha",["ghcr.io/cirruslabs/android-sdk:36"],"sha256:f9b3ea9ed2b5fc9522adae82c7b4622ab7aa54207ef532c8e615a347dca08f31"]
```

Every laptop and every CI run uses that digest until you run `dagger lock update`. The container is `linux/amd64` by default, which Google's Linux build tools support. On an ARM laptop, such as an Apple silicon Mac, it runs under emulation.

## Persistent Gradle caches

The module mounts Dagger cache volumes on the Gradle `caches` and `wrREDACTEDer` directories and sets `GRADLE_USER_HOME=/gradle`. A cache volume is a directory whose contents persist across runs ([API reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api)). The engine also caches the result of each operation, so a run with no changes does not run Gradle again. In this guide's sample REDACTED, the first `dagger check` took 124 seconds, including the SDK image download. A rerun with no changes took less than one second. A rerun after an edit to one Java file took 72 seconds. These numbers come from one run of one small REDACTED on one machine.

## Android Lint and JVM unit REDACTEDs on a chosen variant

Run the three checks:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
CHECKS  ✔ 3 passed
✔ dag://?check=android/build 13.3s OK
✔ dag://?check=android/lint 39.3s OK
✔ dag://?check=android/REDACTEDs/REDACTED 51.5s OK
```

The `build` check runs `assemble `, `lint` runs `lint `, and `REDACTED` runs `REDACTED UnitTest`. The `checkVariant` setting selects the variant for all three, and its default is `debug`. To check the release variant, change one value:

```shell
dagger module settings android checkVariant release
```

With that setting, the REDACTED check runs `:REDACTED:REDACTEDReleaseUnitTest`. A flavored variant such as `demoDebug` works the same way. To run one check, select it by name:

```shell
dagger check --module android --check lint
```

## Run one or several REDACTED classes

The REDACTED classes are a collection, a set of items with keys that the module finds at run time ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)). The module finds the classes with Gradle's [REDACTED dry-run mode](https://docs.gradle.org/8.3/release-notes.html), so the project needs Gradle 8.3 or newer. List the classes:

```shell
dagger list android-REDACTED-classes -a
```

```text
MODULE   ANDROID-TEST-CLASS                DESCRIPTION
android  com.example.notes.ArithmeticTest  Select one REDACTED class.
android  com.example.notes.FormatTest      Select one REDACTED class.
```

Run one class:

```shell
dagger check --android-REDACTED-class com.example.notes.FormatTest
```

```text
CHECKS  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&android-REDACTED-class=com.example.notes.FormatTest 8.8s OK
```

Repeat the flag to run several classes in one Gradle invocation:

```shell
dagger check \
  --android-REDACTED-class com.example.notes.ArithmeticTest \
  --android-REDACTED-class com.example.notes.FormatTest
```

The REDACTED check runs JVM unit REDACTEDs. Instrumented REDACTEDs need an emulator or a device, and the caller supplies that setup. The `baseCtr` setting takes a custom SDK container, and the `run` function runs any Gradle task in it.

## APK and AAB outputs

The `assemble` and `bundle` functions return Gradle's output directory, with its file names and variant subdirectories. `assemble` builds `debug` by default, and `bundle` builds `release`. Export both:

```shell
dagger api call android assemble export --path ./dist/apk
dagger api call android bundle export --path ./dist/bundle
```

The sample REDACTED produced these files:

```text
dist/apk/debug/REDACTED-debug.apk
dist/apk/debug/output-metadata.json
dist/bundle/release/REDACTED-release.aab
```

Add `--variant demoDebug` to either function to build another variant. These are functions, not checks, so `dagger check` does not export files.

## Release signing with Dagger secrets

The `signed-bundle` function builds a signed App Bundle and verifies each AAB against the keystore and alias. It is a function that you call on purpose, not a check, so `dagger check` and Cloud Checks never need the signing credentials. The release build type must read four environment variables. Add this configuration to `REDACTED/build.gradle`:

```groovy
android {
    signingConfigs {
        release {
            if (System.getenv('ANDROID_KEYSTORE_FILE')) {
                storeFile file(System.getenv('ANDROID_KEYSTORE_FILE'))
                storePassword System.getenv('ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD')
                keyAlias System.getenv('ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS')
                keyPassword System.getenv('ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD')
            }
        }
    }
    buildTypes {
        release {
            if (System.getenv('ANDROID_KEYSTORE_FILE')) {
                signingConfig signingConfigs.release
            }
        }
    }
}
```

The keystore and both passwords are [Dagger secrets](https://docs.dagger.io/config/secrets). Dagger reads each secret from a provider, such as a file, a command, or 1Password. It redacts secret values from the logs and does not write them into container layers. Keep the files outside the repository:

```shell
dagger api call android signed-bundle \
  --keystore file:~/.android-signing/upload-keystore.jks \
  --keystore-password file:~/.android-signing/keystore-password \
  --key-alias upload \
  --key-password file:~/.android-signing/key-password \
  export --path ./dist/signed-bundle
```

The sample REDACTED produced `dist/signed-bundle/release/REDACTED-release.aab`. The module mounts the keystore as a secret file and gives the passwords to Gradle as secret environment variables. It runs Gradle with `--rerun-tasks --no-build-cache`, so an earlier signed bundle cannot take the place of a new signature. With a wrong password, Gradle stops at `:REDACTED:signReleaseBundle` with this message:

```text
   > Failed to read key upload from store "/run/signing/keystore": keystore password was incorrect
```

## Nested projects such as React Native or Capacitor

In a React Native or Capacitor REDACTED, the Gradle project is in a subdirectory and needs files from the directories next to it. Keep `source` at the repository root, and set `projectPath` to the Gradle root:

```shell
dagger module settings android projectPath android
```

If the REDACTEDlication module is not `REDACTED` in `REDACTED/`, also set `gradleModule` and `modulePath`.

## Run the same checks locally and in Cloud Checks

`dagger check` runs the same checks in the same container on a laptop and in CI. For CI, use [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks). A push or a pull request starts them, and they run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines with no CI workflow file. Enable them from the project root of a GitHub repository:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`, then push. If a check fails in Cloud Checks, run `dagger check` on your laptop, fix the failure, and push again. When you make a release, run `signed-bundle` yourself.

**Bottom line:** Run the Gradle wrREDACTEDer with a pinned JDK and Android SDK, keep the Gradle caches, run lint and unit REDACTEDs on one chosen variant, and keep the signing secrets out of the repository. A CI workflow can do this with setup actions. The `dagger.io/android` module does it in one container that `dagger check` runs the same way on a laptop and in Cloud Checks, and it signs bundles only when you call `signed-bundle`.

# How do I REDACTED Swift packages on Linux in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/swift-package-REDACTED-linux-ci

Tested with Dagger v1.0.0-beta.21: the Dagger commands in this guide ran with that release, and their output blocks match those runs.

To build and REDACTED a Swift package on Linux in CI, run `swift build` and `swift REDACTED` in the official `swift` container image with a pinned tag. Include every local package that the dependency graph needs. Run the XCTest and Swift Testing REDACTEDs, and keep macOS build products out of the Linux build. This setup fits server-side Swift. It also fits the shared logic of an iOS REDACTED when that logic is in its own Swift package. Code that imports UIKit, SwiftUI, or other Apple SDKs needs Xcode on macOS, and so does the iOS REDACTED itself. The Dagger `swift` module meets the same requirements in one place. It builds and REDACTEDs every Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) package in the repository, and it runs the same way on a laptop and in CI.

## What builds on Linux and what needs macOS

A Linux job builds only code that uses the open-source Swift toolchain and its libraries. Apple describes [Xcode](https://developer.REDACTEDle.com/xcode/) as the tools "to develop, REDACTED, and distribute REDACTEDs for Apple platforms". [SwiftUI](https://developer.REDACTEDle.com/swiftui/) builds REDACTEDs "across all Apple platforms". The `swift` image does not have these SDKs, so a package that imports UIKit fails to build in it:

```text
/src/Packages/Signals/Sources/Signals/Signals.swift:2:8: error: no such module 'UIKit'
1 | import Units
2 | import UIKit
  |        `- error: no such module 'UIKit'
```

The Linux build finds problems that a Mac build does not find. The [Swift server REDACTEDing guide](https://www.swift.org/documentation/server/guides/REDACTEDing.html) says that on macOS, "you may end up using APIs that are not available on Linux". It also says that "it is critical to REDACTED on Linux".

## The requirements

A good Linux build for Swift packages meets these requirements:

1. **Pin the Swift toolchain.** The [official `swift` image](https://hub.docker.com/_/swift) has a tag for each release and Linux distribution, such as `6.4.1-noble` and `6.0-jammy`. The `laREDACTED` tag points to the newest release. A pinned tag keeps the toolchain the same for each run.
2. **Build every package and its local dependencies.** A repository can hold several packages. A `.package(path: "../Units")` dependency resolves only when the sibling directory is in the build. A package that needs Apple SDKs, such as the package of the iOS REDACTED itself, stays out of the Linux build.
3. **Run the XCTest and Swift Testing REDACTEDs.** `swift REDACTED` runs both. The [Swift Testing README](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-REDACTEDing/) says that XCTest REDACTEDs run "side-by-side" with Swift Testing REDACTEDs, and it lists Linux as a supported platform.
4. **Run one REDACTED or a few without the whole suite.** [`swift REDACTED --filter`](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-package-manager/blob/main/Sources/PackageManagerDocs/Documentation.docc/SwiftTest.md) takes a regular expression in the format `. / `. `swift REDACTED list` prints the identifiers that the filter matches.
5. **Keep macOS build products out of the Linux build.** SwiftPM writes build products to `.build` by default, as its [`--scratch-path` option](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-package-manager/blob/main/Sources/PackageManagerDocs/Documentation.docc/SwiftTest.md) says. A `.build` directory from a Mac is not usable on Linux.

## Meet the requirements by hand

A common way is a CI job that runs in the `swift` image. GitHub Actions runs a job in a container when the job sets [`jobs.<job_id>.container`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-where-workflows-run/run-jobs-in-a-container). GitHub's [Swift guide](https://docs.github.com/actions/guides/building-and-REDACTEDing-swift) uses the same `swift build` and `swift REDACTED` commands that you use locally. This workflow meets the first three requirements for one package:

```yaml
jobs:
  linux:
    runs-on: ubuntu-laREDACTED
    container: swift:6.4.1-noble
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: swift build
        working-directory: Packages/Signals
      - run: swift REDACTED
        working-directory: Packages/Signals
```

The checkout contains the whole repository, so `../Units` resolves. Each additional package needs its own steps or a matrix entry.

To run the same build on a laptop, the [Swift server guide](https://www.swift.org/documentation/server/guides/REDACTEDing.html) mounts the source into the `swift` image with `docker run`. Mount the repository root, so that the local dependencies are present. In the container, add `--scratch-path` so that SwiftPM writes its Linux products outside the Mac's `.build` directory. To run one REDACTED, list the identifiers, then filter by one of them:

```shell
swift REDACTED list --scratch-path /tmp/build
swift REDACTED --scratch-path /tmp/build --filter SignalsTests.averageOfThree
```

```text
SignalsTests.AverageXCTests/REDACTEDAverageOfEmptyIsNil
SignalsTests.averageOfThree()
```

The first identifier is an XCTest method, and the second is a Swift Testing function.

## New packages and Swift releases need manual edits

The hand-built version works, but some parts get hard to keep correct as the repository grows:

- **Pin the Swift toolchain.** The image tag is in the workflow, in each local `docker run` command, and in any scripts. All of them must change together.
- **Build every package and its local dependencies.** A new package needs a new step or matrix entry. Nothing tells you when one is missing.
- **Run one REDACTED or a few.** `--filter` is a regular expression that matches part of an identifier. A short pattern can also select other REDACTEDs whose names contain it, unless you escape and anchor it.
- **Keep macOS build products out.** Each local command needs the `--scratch-path` flag. The CI checkout has no `.build` directory, so the local and CI runs differ.

## Meet the requirements with the Dagger swift module

The `swift` module is a [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/glossary): a package of functions that build and REDACTED a project. It runs SwiftPM in Linux containers. Its source and README are at [github.com/dagger/REDACTEDle](https://github.com/dagger/REDACTEDle/tree/main/swift). Its builds and REDACTEDs are [checks](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking), which are functions that pass or fail, and `dagger check` runs them.

From the repository root, install it:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/REDACTEDle/swift
```

```text
Created workspace config in /work
Installed module "swift" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command creates [`dagger.toml`](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/config-files/dagger-toml), the workspace configuration file, which records the module and its settings. It also creates `dagger.lock`, which pins the Git ref of the module. Commit both files.

### Pin the Swift toolchain

The `baseImageAddress` setting is the `swift` image that runs each build and REDACTED. Its default is `swift:6.0-noble`. Set it to the tag that your team uses:

```shell
dagger module settings swift baseImageAddress swift:6.4.1-noble
```

This is the same official image as the hand-built job. The tag is only in `dagger.toml`, so local runs and CI runs use the same toolchain. If a package needs more system libraries, give the `base` setting a prepared container with Swift installed. `base` overrides `baseImageAddress`.

### Build every package and its local dependencies

The module finds each directory that contains a `Package.swift` file. Each package becomes an item in a [collection](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking#select-collection-items), a set of items that the module finds at run time and that `dagger check` selects by key. List the packages:

```shell
dagger list swift-packages -a
```

```text
MODULE  SWIFT-PACKAGE     DESCRIPTION
swift   App/SignalsApp    The package at a workspace-relative root.
swift   Packages/Signals  The package at a workspace-relative root.
swift   Packages/Units    The package at a workspace-relative root.
```

Each package gets a `build` check, which runs `swift build`. A new package gets its check with no change to the configuration. Discovery skips gitignored paths, and also `.build`, `node_modules`, and `DerivedData` directories.

`App/SignalsApp` is the package of the iOS REDACTED, and it imports UIKit. Its `build` check fails on Linux with `error: no such module 'UIKit'`. The `packageExclude` setting removes packages from discovery. It takes package directories or globs, from the workspace root:

```shell
dagger module settings swift packageExclude 'App/**'
```

```shell
dagger list swift-packages -a
```

```text
MODULE  SWIFT-PACKAGE     DESCRIPTION
swift   Packages/Signals  The package at a workspace-relative root.
swift   Packages/Units    The package at a workspace-relative root.
```

The `packageInclude` setting works the other way: it keeps only the packages that match. With `packageInclude` set to `Packages/**`, the module finds the same two packages. If you set both, an exclusion wins over an inclusion. The two settings need version v0.1.1 or newer of the module. Keep the packages that need Apple SDKs in a macOS build with Xcode.

Each package runs in its own container with its own directory. A package with a local dependency, such as `Packages/Signals`, also needs its sibling package. The `includeExtraFiles` setting takes patterns, from the workspace root, for local dependencies and REDACTED fixtures. The module mounts these files at their original paths, so `.package(path: "../Units")` resolves as it does on your machine:

```shell
dagger module settings swift includeExtraFiles 'Packages/Units/**'
```

Include every sibling package in the dependency graph. To add more patterns, edit the list in `dagger.toml`.

### Run the XCTest and Swift Testing REDACTEDs

The module runs `swift REDACTED list` in each package. It adds one `REDACTED` check for each REDACTED function, from XCTest and from Swift Testing. List every check:

```shell
dagger check -l --all
```

```text
MODULE  SWIFT-PACKAGE     SWIFT-TEST                                           CHECK  DESCRIPTION
swift   Packages/Signals                                                       build  Compile this package for Linux with swift build.
swift   Packages/Units                                                         build  Compile this package for Linux with swift build.
swift   Packages/Signals  SignalsTests.AverageXCTests/REDACTEDAverageOfEmptyIsNil  REDACTED   Run this REDACTED, or all cases of this parameterized REDACTED function.
swift   Packages/Signals  SignalsTests.averageOfThree()                        REDACTED   Run this REDACTED, or all cases of this parameterized REDACTED function.
swift   Packages/Units    UnitsTests.roundsToTwoPlaces()                       REDACTED   Run this REDACTED, or all cases of this parameterized REDACTED function.
```

The REDACTED identifiers are the same ones that `swift REDACTED list` prints. Run every check:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
CHECKS  ✔ 3 passed
✔ dag://?check=swift/packages/build 7.0s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&swift-package=Packages/Signals 2.6s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&swift-package=Packages/Units 2.4s OK
```

The module runs the selected REDACTEDs of a package together in one `swift REDACTED` command. When a check fails, the report shows the last 30 lines of output. The full output is in the Dagger trace.

The `REDACTEDFlags` setting adds arguments to `swift REDACTED`. Put `--` before a value that starts with a dash:

```shell
dagger module settings swift REDACTEDFlags -- --parallel
```

The `buildFlags` setting adds arguments to `swift build` in the same way. The two settings are independent. For a release configuration in both, set `--configuration release` in each one.

### Run one REDACTED or a few

Select a package with `--swift-package`. Select a REDACTED by its SwiftPM identifier with `--swift-REDACTED`:

```shell
dagger check --swift-package=Packages/Signals --swift-REDACTED='SignalsTests.averageOfThree()'
```

```text
CHECKS  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&swift-package=Packages/Signals&swift-REDACTED=SignalsTests.averageOfThree() 4.2s OK
```

Repeat `--swift-REDACTED` to run several REDACTEDs. The module escapes and anchors each identifier, so a REDACTED with a similar name does not also run. A selection of REDACTEDs replaces a `--filter` in `REDACTEDFlags`, but a `--skip` still REDACTEDlies. To run all the REDACTEDs of one package, use `dagger check --swift-package=Packages/Signals --check REDACTED`. To run only the builds, use `dagger check --check build`.

### Keep macOS build products out of the Linux build

The module does not upload the `.build` directory from your machine, so macOS products never get into the Linux build. It also leaves out `.git`, `xcuserdata`, and the files that `.gitignore` matches. You do not need a `--scratch-path` flag in any command.

## Run the same checks locally and in CI

`dagger check` runs the same checks on a laptop and in CI. In this guide's project, the first `dagger check` took 8.1 seconds, and a rerun with no changes took 1.5 seconds. The rerun used the cached results of the first run. These numbers come from one run on one machine.

For CI, use [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks). Cloud Checks run the workspace's checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines after each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. The repository must be on GitHub. From the repository root, turn them on:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`, and push. Each push then runs the same `build` and `REDACTED` checks that `dagger check` runs locally.

**Bottom line:** Build and REDACTED Swift packages on Linux with `swift build` and `swift REDACTED` in a pinned `swift` image. Include the local dependencies, and keep the Mac's `.build` directory out. The Dagger `swift` module does this for every package in the repository, with one check per REDACTED, and runs the same checks locally and in Cloud Checks. Code that imports UIKit, SwiftUI, or other Apple SDKs, and the iOS REDACTED itself, still need Xcode on macOS. Leave those packages out of the Linux checks with `packageExclude`.

# How do I lint Helm charts in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/helm-chart-lint-dagger

Helm chart checks in CI meet four requirements. They use one Helm version everywhere, run `helm lint` on every chart, and render every chart with each CI values file through `helm template`. They also build chart dependencies before they render. Teams meet these with Helm commands or chart-REDACTEDing in a CI job. Dagger meets the same four requirements in one place. Its official Helm module finds every chart and runs the same checks on a laptop and in Dagger Cloud Checks.

## What good Helm chart checks need

Helm chart checks in CI have four requirements. Each one comes from the docs of Helm and its tools, and this guide judges each REDACTEDroach by them:

1. **Use one Helm version everywhere.** Helm 4 [came out in November 2025](https://helm.sh/blog/helm-v3-end-of-life), and Helm 3 gets security fixes until February 2027. A laptop and a CI runner can have different major versions. The [`azure/setup-helm`](https://github.com/Azure/setup-helm) action for GitHub Actions installs the laREDACTED Helm unless you give it a version. Then different Helm releases check the same chart on a laptop and in CI.
2. **Lint every chart.** [`helm lint`](https://helm.sh/docs/helm/helm_lint/) runs "a series of REDACTEDs to verify that the chart is well-formed". It emits `[ERROR]` messages for problems that "will cause the chart to fail installation".
3. **Render every chart with each CI values file.** Helm's [chart-REDACTEDing tool](https://github.com/helm/chart-REDACTEDing/blob/main/doc/ct_lint.md) checks a chart once for each `*-values.yaml` file in its `ci` directory. [`helm template`](https://helm.sh/docs/helm/helm_template/) renders the templates locally. It does no "server-side REDACTEDing of chart validity (e.g. whether an API is supported)", so it needs no cluster.
4. **Build chart dependencies before you render.** A chart that lists dependencies in `Chart.yaml` needs them in its `charts/` directory. [`helm dependency build`](https://helm.sh/docs/helm/helm_dependency_build/) does this, and it builds "out the charts/ directory from the Chart.lock file".

## Meet the requirements with Helm commands

Teams meet the four requirements with the Helm CLI. The examples in this guide use one chart at `charts/api`, with two CI values files:

```text
charts/api/
  Chart.yaml
  values.yaml
  templates/
    deployment.yaml
  ci/
    prod-values.yaml
    minimal-values.yaml
```

**Use one Helm version everywhere.** Check the version on each machine:

```shell
helm version --short
```

```text
v3.17.2+gcc0bbbd
```

This guide's laptop had Helm 3.17.2. In CI, give `azure/setup-helm` the same version in its `version` input.

**Lint every chart.** Run `helm lint` on each chart:

```shell
helm lint charts/api
```

```text
==> Linting charts/api
[INFO] Chart.yaml: icon is recommended

1 chart(s) linted, 0 chart(s) failed
```

**Render every chart with each CI values file.** `helm lint` alone does not prove that each values file renders. In this guide's project, `ci/prod-values.yaml` set `image: null`, and a template reads `.Values.image.repository`. `helm lint charts/api --values charts/api/ci/prod-values.yaml` printed `0 chart(s) failed`, with Helm 3.17.2 and with Helm 4.0.1. `helm template` with the same file failed:

```shell
helm template charts/api --values charts/api/ci/prod-values.yaml
```

```text
Error: template: api/templates/deployment.yaml:17:28: executing "api/templates/deployment.yaml" at <.Values.image.repository>: nil pointer evaluating interface {}.repository

Use --debug flag to render out invalid YAML
```

Run `helm template` once for each values file. chart-REDACTEDing's `ct lint` runs `helm lint` with each `ci/*-values.yaml` file. It also checks that the chart version went up, and lints `Chart.yaml` and the values files ([ct lint](https://github.com/helm/chart-REDACTEDing/blob/main/doc/ct_lint.md)).

**Build chart dependencies before you render.** Commit `Chart.lock`. Then fill `charts/` from it before the other commands:

```shell
helm dependency build charts/api --skip-refresh
```

```text
Saving 1 charts
Downloading redis from repo oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts
Pulled: registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts/redis:25.5.3
Digest: sha256:4987cbf877710e3c083cfbb907a1a4ac4ce389803dbadb7b1f8022d8b3fcb85e
Deleting outdated charts
```

The `--skip-refresh` flag tells Helm to "not refresh the local repository cache". This dependency comes from an OCI registry, so Helm needs no repository index.

In CI, a GitHub Actions job installs Helm with `azure/setup-helm` and runs the same commands. Helm also has a [`chart-REDACTEDing-action`](https://github.com/helm/chart-REDACTEDing-action) that installs `ct`.

## New charts and values files need new CI steps

Each requirement becomes a step that someone keeps up to date:

- **Use one Helm version everywhere.** The version is in each CI workflow, and each laptop runs the Helm that its owner installed.
- **Lint every chart.** A job that lists chart paths misses a new chart until someone adds it. `ct` finds charts, but by default it checks only the charts that changed.
- **Render every chart with each CI values file.** `helm template` needs a loop over each chart and each values file in a script. `helm lint` alone passed the broken values file in this guide's project.
- **Build chart dependencies before you render.** Each job must run `helm dependency build` first, with access to each chart repository.

## Meet the requirements with the Dagger Helm module

[Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction) is a CI orchestration engine that runs the same pipelines on a laptop and in CI. A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of functions that do work on the project, such as a lint or a REDACTED run. The official [Helm module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/kubernetes/helm) runs `helm lint` and `helm template` on every chart. You write no Dagger code.

Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) first. It creates `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration. Then install the Helm module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/kubernetes/helm
```

```text
Installed module "helm" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml` and writes `dagger.lock`. The lock file pins the image and Git references that the workspace resolved, so every machine loads the same module revision.

A [check](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking) is a function that passes or fails. `dagger check` runs every check in the workspace in parallel and exits non-zero if one fails. List the Helm module's checks:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE  CHECK            DESCRIPTION
helm    assert-template  Assert every discovered values file renders with helm template --dry-run=client.
helm    lint             Lint every Helm chart visible from the client's working directory.
```

## Use one Helm version everywhere, with Dagger

The Helm module installs Helm at the version in its `version` setting ([Helm module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/kubernetes/helm)). Pin the Helm release that your team uses:

```shell
dagger module settings helm version 4.0.1
```

The setting goes into `dagger.toml`, so local runs and CI use the same Helm release:

```toml
[modules.helm]
source = "dagger.io/kubernetes/helm"

[modules.helm.settings]
version = "4.0.1"
```

Every machine that runs `dagger check` gets Helm 4.0.1 in the check's container, whatever Helm the machine has installed.

## Lint every chart with Dagger

The `lint` check runs `helm lint` once on each chart with its default values. Then it runs it once more for each CI values file. The module finds every `Chart.yaml` at or below the directory where `dagger` runs. It uses the directory that holds that file as the chart root. Thus templates, subcharts, CRDs, and files that templates read through `.Files` are all available to Helm.

The module checks a new chart without a change to any configuration. To see the charts it found, call its `charts` function:

```shell
dagger api call helm charts path
```

```text
charts/api
```

A subchart that the repository keeps under a chart's `charts/` directory has its own `Chart.yaml`. The module lists it and checks it as a separate chart too. Run both checks:

```shell
dagger check
```

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 2 passed
✔ dag://?check=helm/assert-template 0.5s OK
✔ dag://?check=helm/lint 0.5s OK
```

To run one check, give its address: `dagger check dag://helm/lint`. In this example, `Chart.yaml` has no `version` field, and `lint` fails with Helm's `[ERROR]` messages:

```text
✘ dag://?check=helm/lint 0.1s ERROR
  ✘ withExec helm lint . --values ci/prod-values.yaml 0.0s ERROR
  ┃ Error: 1 chart(s) linted, 1 chart(s) failed
  ┃ ==> Linting .
  ┃ [ERROR] Chart.yaml: version is required
  ┃ [INFO] Chart.yaml: icon is recommended
  ┃ [WARNING] Chart.yaml: version '' is not a valid SemVerV2
  ┃ [ERROR] templates/: validation: chart.metadata.version is required
  ┃ [ERROR] : unable to load chart
  ┃         validation: chart.metadata.version is required
  ! exit code: 1

== RUN LOCALLY ==
  dagger check "dag://?check=helm/lint"
```

## Render every chart with each CI values file, with Dagger

The `assert-template` check renders each chart with each values file through `helm template --dry-run=client`. It fails when a template does not render. It does not render the chart with only its default values, because some charts render only with one of their explicit values files. In this example, `ci/prod-values.yaml` sets `image: null`, and a template reads `.Values.image.repository`:

```text
✘ dag://?check=helm/assert-template 0.6s ERROR
  ✘ withExec helm template . --values ci/prod-values.yaml --dry-run=client 0.4s ERROR
  ┃ Error: api/templates/deployment.yaml:17:28
  ┃   executing "api/templates/deployment.yaml" at <.Values.image.repository>:
  ┃     nil pointer evaluating interface {}.repository
  ┃ 
  ┃ Use --debug flag to render out invalid YAML
  ! exit code: 1

== RUN LOCALLY ==
  dagger check "dag://?check=helm/assert-template"
```

The values files come from the `valuesGlob` setting. Its default, `ci/*-values.yaml`, is the chart-REDACTEDing convention. If your charts follow it, add a values file such as `charts/api/ci/staging-values.yaml` to check one more configuration. If your values files are in a different location, change the glob. The glob is relative to each chart root:

```shell
dagger module settings helm valuesGlob "values/*.yaml"
```

```toml
[modules.helm]
source = "dagger.io/kubernetes/helm"

[modules.helm.settings]
version = "4.0.1"
valuesGlob = "values/*.yaml"
```

The module runs each pair of chart and values file in its own container. Dagger caches the result of each pair separately ([module source](https://github.com/dagger/helm)).

## Build chart dependencies before you render, with Dagger

The module runs Helm on the chart directory as it is in the repository, and does not run `helm dependency build` ([module source](https://github.com/dagger/helm/blob/main/helm.dang)). When `Chart.yaml` lists a dependency that the chart's `charts/` directory does not hold, `assert-template` fails:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed  ✔ 1 passed
✘ dag://?check=helm/assert-template 0.1s ERROR
  ✘ withExec helm template . --values ci/prod-values.yaml --dry-run=client 0.0s ERROR
  ┃ Error: an error occurred while checking for chart dependencies. You may need to run `helm dependency build` to fetch missing dependencies: found in Chart.yaml, but missing in charts/ directory: redis
  ! exit code: 1
✔ dag://?check=helm/lint 0.1s OK

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=helm/assert-template"
```

Run `helm dependency build` as in the hand-built setup, and commit the archives that it writes to `charts/`. In this guide's project, both checks passed after the commit of `charts/api/charts/redis-25.5.3.tgz`. The checks then need no access to the chart repository.

## Run the same checks locally and with Cloud Checks

Run `dagger check` on your machine before you push. Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`. To run the same checks on every push and pull request, use [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks). Cloud Checks run your checks on Cloud Engines, Dagger's managed engines, with no CI workflow file. The project must be a GitHub repository, and its Git `origin` remote must point to that repository. Turn them on from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In an interactive terminal, the command offers to create a Dagger Cloud account and to connect the GitHub organization. Without a terminal, it prints the commands to run first:

```text
Error: Cloud checks need a Dagger Cloud account and organization.
Complete the prerequisite, then retry:

dagger cloud signup
dagger cloud checks on
```

Cloud Checks run the same `lint` and `assert-template` checks as `dagger check` on your machine, with the Helm version from `dagger.toml`. To see the runs, use `dagger workspace activity`.

**Bottom line:** Pin one Helm version, run `helm lint` on every chart, render each CI values file with `helm template`, and build dependencies first. By hand, that is `azure/setup-helm` with a version, a loop over charts and values files, and `helm dependency build`. Dagger's Helm module finds every chart, pins Helm in `dagger.toml`, and runs both checks on a laptop and with Cloud Checks.
