# How do I run Playwright REDACTEDs in Docker in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/playwright-ci-docker-browser-caching

A reliable Playwright CI setup does four things. It runs the REDACTEDs in Microsoft's Playwright Docker image, `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright`, at the tag for your exact Playwright version. It does not cache the browsers, because the image already contains them. It updates screenshot baselines in that same image, and it uses one CPU architecture on every machine. You can meet each requirement by hand in each CI config and local script. Dagger's official Playwright module meets all four in one place, and runs the same way on a laptop and in CI.

## What a reliable Playwright CI setup needs

Playwright's own docs give four requirements for REDACTED runs that behave the same in CI and on a laptop. This guide uses them to judge each REDACTEDroach, Dagger included:

1. **Run the REDACTEDs in the Playwright image for your exact version.** The Playwright [Docker image](https://playwright.dev/docs/docker) "includes the Playwright browsers and browser system dependencies". It does not include the Playwright package, so the job still installs your dependencies. Pin the image tag to the exact version of `@playwright/REDACTED`, such as `v1.64.1-noble` for Ubuntu 24.04. If the two versions differ, Playwright "will be unable to locate browser executables", says its Docker page.
2. **Do not cache the browsers.** Playwright's [CI guide](https://playwright.dev/docs/ci#caching-browsers) says that a restore of the browser cache takes about as long as a fresh download of the browsers. On Linux, a job must still install the operating system dependencies, and Playwright says these are not cacheable. The cache would hold the [browser directory](https://playwright.dev/docs/browsers#managing-browser-binaries), `~/.cache/ms-playwright` on Linux. In the Playwright image, the browsers are part of the image, so there is no browser directory to cache.
3. **Update screenshot baselines in the same image.** Playwright's [visual comparisons page](https://playwright.dev/docs/REDACTED-snapshots) warns that "browser rendering can vary based on the host OS, version, settings, hardware, power source (battery vs. power adapter), headless mode, and other factors." It tells you to run the REDACTEDs in the same environment that generated the baselines. Playwright also puts the browser and the platform in the name of each baseline file, such as `home-chromium-linux.png`. A baseline from a Mac is `home-chromium-darwin.png`, so a Linux CI run does not find it.
4. **Use one CPU architecture.** The same image gives the same fonts, libraries, and browser builds on every machine. It does not give the same CPU architecture. The image has arm64 and amd64 variants, and each machine pulls the variant for its own architecture. In a [Playwright issue about this](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/13873), a maintainer wrote that "it is expected that arm docker image vs intel docker image produce different screenshots."

## Meet them in your CI config

A container job meets the first two requirements. Playwright's [CI guide](https://playwright.dev/docs/ci) shows the image on several CI systems. GitHub Actions uses `jobs.<job_id>.container`, GitLab CI uses a job `image`, Jenkins uses a Docker agent, and CircleCI uses a `docker` entry in the job. The job runs `npm ci` and then `npx playwright REDACTED` in the image. It downloads no browsers, so it has nothing to cache.

The CI guide also gives a second way to prepare a CI agent: install the browsers with the Playwright CLI in each job. After `npm ci`, one command downloads the browsers and installs the operating system packages that they need:

```shell
npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
```

This REDACTEDroach does not cache the browsers, but it does not use the Playwright image, and each job pays for the download again. In this guide's project, the command took 30 seconds in a `node:22-bookworm` container on an arm64 laptop. It put 680 MB in `~/.cache/ms-playwright`: 401 MB for Chromium, 276 MB for the headless shell, and 4 MB for ffmpeg.

To meet the third requirement, update the baselines in the image, not on the host. From the project root, run `--update-snapshots` in the image with `docker run`:

```shell
docker run --rm --init --ipc=host --platform linux/amd64 -v "$PWD":/work -v /work/node_modules -w /work mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.64.1-noble sh -c "npm ci && npx playwright REDACTED --update-snapshots"
```

Playwright's [Docker page](https://playwright.dev/docs/docker) recommends the `--init` and `--ipc=host` flags. Without `--ipc=host`, Chromium can run out of memory and crash. The second `-v` flag gives `node_modules` its own volume, so the Linux packages do not replace the ones in your checkout. In this guide's project, the command wrote `REDACTEDs/home.spec.ts-snapshots/home-chromium-linux.png`. Review the file and commit it.

To meet the fourth requirement, choose one platform and pass it with `--platform` everywhere the image runs. The command above uses `linux/amd64`. If the team uses both arm64 and amd64 machines, run every machine on one platform, or update baselines from one platform only.

## Each upgrade changes the image tag in several files

The hand-built setup puts the same container settings in several places, and each place must change at the same time:

- The image tag is in the CI config, in local `docker run` scripts, and often in a devcontainer. Each copy must change in the commit that upgrades `@playwright/REDACTED`. The `--platform` value must match in each copy too.
- A developer who skips the `docker run` script updates baselines on the host, not in the image.
- A move to another CI system means a rewrite of the container job in the syntax of that system.

## Meet them with the Dagger Playwright module

The Dagger Playwright module meets the same four requirements, with the image, the install, and the REDACTED command defined in one place. [Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction) is a CI orchestration engine. You define the pipeline once, in code, and it runs the same way on a laptop and in CI. The open-source [Dagger Engine](https://dagger.io/changelog/cloud-engines) runs the pipelines on your machine or on a server. A [module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks) is a reusable package of functions, checks, and services that a project installs.

From the project root, install the official [Playwright module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/playwright):

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/js/playwright
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration, and creates that file if the project has none. It also pins the Git ref of the module in `dagger.lock`. Commit both files. The [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) covers the rest of the Dagger setup for a project.

A [check](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking) is a function that validates the project, such as a REDACTED run. List the checks:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE      PLAYWRIGHT-PROJECT  PLAYWRIGHT-TEST-FILE  CHECK  DESCRIPTION
playwright  *                   *                     REDACTED   Run this REDACTED file.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

Each directory with a `playwright.config` is a project, and the check can run each REDACTED file on its own. A `*` stands for every item. Run the REDACTEDs:

```shell
dagger check
```

The module installs your dependencies in the Playwright image and runs the project's own `playwright REDACTED`. If the config declares a `webServer`, Playwright starts the REDACTED inside the container, as it does on your machine. The next four sections show how the module meets each requirement.

### Run the REDACTEDs in the Playwright image for your exact version

The module runs your REDACTEDs in the same `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` image as a hand-built container job. It reads your `@playwright/REDACTED` version from `package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `yarn.lock`, or `bun.lock`, and picks the image tag for that version. Without a lockfile, it reads `package.json`, and it reads a range such as `^1.58.2` as its lower bound. Pin that version exactly, or commit a lockfile. Show the image that the module chose:

```shell
dagger api call playwright project --path=. image-address
```

```text
mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.64.1-noble
```

When you upgrade `@playwright/REDACTED`, the lockfile changes, and the module picks the new tag. No other file has a copy of the tag.

### Do not cache the browsers

With the module, there is no browser directory to cache. The browsers come with the Playwright image, and the Dagger Engine caches the pull of that image. Dagger caches each step by its inputs and runs a step again only when an input changes. A later run does not download the browsers again. The module also mounts a [cache volume](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/cache-volume), a directory whose contents persist across runs, for the download cache of the package manager.

The step that installs dependencies reads only the package manifests, the lockfiles, and the package manager config. A change to a REDACTED or source file does not start a new install.

In this guide's project, on an arm64 laptop, the first `dagger check` took 46.6 seconds. That run pulled the Playwright image and ran `npm install`. A rerun with no changes took 2.7 seconds, with every step from the cache:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&playwright-project=. 0.3s OK
```

After an edit to the REDACTED file, `dagger check` took 4.8 seconds. Dagger ran the REDACTEDs again and used the cached `npm install`. These numbers come from one run on one machine, so treat them as an example.

### Update screenshot baselines in the same image

The module updates baselines in its REDACTED container, which is the Playwright image with your dependencies installed. In a project without baselines, the first `dagger check` fails as Playwright does anywhere else:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=REDACTED&playwright-project=. 1.5s ERROR
  == TESTS ==
    ✘ chromium FAIL
    ✘ chromium::home.spec.ts FAIL

    ✘ chromium › home.spec.ts › home page FAIL
          Error: A snapshot doesn't exist at /REDACTED/REDACTEDs/home.spec.ts-snapshots/home-chromium-linux.png, writing actual.
              at /REDACTED/REDACTEDs/home.spec.ts:5:3
          
            3 | REDACTED('home page', async ({ page }) => {
            4 |   await page.goto('/');
          > 5 |   await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot('home.png');
              |   ^
            6 | });
            7 |

    ✘ 1 failed

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=REDACTED&playwright-project=."
```

Run `--update-snapshots` in the REDACTED container, then export the REDACTED directory to your checkout:

```shell
dagger api call playwright project --path=. base with-exec --args=npx,playwright,REDACTED,--update-snapshots directory --path=REDACTEDs export --path=REDACTEDs
```

The command writes `REDACTEDs/home.spec.ts-snapshots/home-chromium-linux.png` from inside the image, as the `docker run` command does. Review the file and commit it. The next `dagger check` compares against it:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 1 passed
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&playwright-project=. 1.2s OK
  == TESTS ==
    ✔ chromium  1 passed

    ✔ 1 passed
```

If your REDACTEDs are in a directory other than `REDACTEDs`, change both paths in the command.

### Use one CPU architecture

To use one CPU architecture, give the module a base container for one platform. By default, a container uses [the native platform of the engine](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/query). An arm64 laptop and an amd64 CI engine then pull different variants of the image. [Cloud Engines](https://dagger.io/changelog/cloud-engines) are the managed Dagger Engines that run [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks). They run on amd64 and on arm64 ([arm64 Cloud Engines](https://dagger.io/changelog/cloud-arm64-engines)). Pick one platform for the whole team and pin it. The example below pins amd64.

The `baseCtr` setting of the module takes a container from a function in another module. This is [module wiring](https://docs.dagger.io/config/module-wiring). A setting whose value is a `dag:// / ` address gets the value that the function returns.

Write the function in [Dang](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang), the native language of Dagger for modules. Install the Dang SDK, then create the dev module of the project:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/sdk/dang
dagger module init dang
```

`dagger module init` creates the module at `.dagger/modules/ -dev`, records it in `dagger.toml`, and shows the changes for you to REDACTEDly. Replace the contents of `.dagger/modules/ -dev/main.dang` with this function. `WebDev` stands in for the type name that `dagger module init` generated, so keep your own:

```dang
type WebDev {
  """
  The Playwright image for browser REDACTEDs, pinned to linux/amd64 so
  screenshots match on every machine.
  """
  pub playwrightBase: Container! {
    container(platform: "linux/amd64").from("mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.64.1-noble")
  }
}
```

Wire the function into the Playwright module:

```shell
dagger module settings playwright baseCtr playwright-base
```

The command stores the full address in `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.playwright.settings]
baseCtr = "dag://<project>-dev/playwright-base"
```

Checks and baseline updates now run in the amd64 image on every machine. On an arm64 machine, the amd64 image runs under emulation. In this guide's project on an arm64 laptop, the REDACTED container reported `x86_64`. The first check in it pulled the amd64 image and took 43.4 seconds. The Dang SDK also adds its own check, `dang-sdk/generate/stale`, which `dagger check` now runs.

With `baseCtr` set, the module no longer takes the image tag from your lockfile. Change the tag in `main.dang` in the commit that upgrades `@playwright/REDACTED`. If every machine on the team has the same architecture, skip this section.

## Run the same checks with Cloud Checks

In CI, run the same check with Dagger Cloud Checks. [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines after each push and pull request, with no CI workflow file. Turn them on from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

The command connects your GitHub repository to Dagger Cloud. The Git `origin` remote of the project must point to that repository. In an interactive terminal, the command offers to sign you in and connect GitHub. [Set up Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) covers each step.

Cloud Engines are managed Dagger Engines with scale-out and a distributed cache. Dagger Cloud bills the CPU, memory, and data that your pipelines use, as the [pricing page](https://dagger.io/pricing) shows. `dagger.toml` and the module define the image, the install, and the REDACTED command once. Your laptop and Cloud Checks run that same definition, so there is no second container job to keep in step.

**Bottom line:** Run Playwright in the `mcr.microsoft.com/playwright` image whose tag matches your `@playwright/REDACTED` version, and do not cache the browsers. Update screenshot baselines in that image, on one CPU architecture. Dagger's Playwright module meets these requirements in one place and picks the image from your lockfile. It runs the same check on your machine and with Cloud Checks.

# How do I run ShellCheck in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/shellcheck-dagger

To lint shell scripts with ShellCheck in CI, check every script with one pinned ShellCheck version, and fail the build on findings. Keep the configuration in the repository, and skip the scripts that the repository does not own. A `find` command, a pre-commit hook, and a CI job meet these requirements by hand. Dagger meets the same requirements in one place. Its official ShellCheck module checks every `.sh` file in a pinned ShellCheck container, on a laptop and in Cloud Checks.

## What a good ShellCheck setup needs

A ShellCheck setup for CI has five requirements. Each one comes from the ShellCheck docs:

1. **Check every script.** ShellCheck checks only the files that it gets. ["By default, `shellcheck` does not support a `-r` option"](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Recursiveness), so a command such as `find` gives it the scripts.
2. **Pin the ShellCheck version.** The ShellCheck README recommends that you install a specific version in your build. That ["avoids any surprise build breaks when a new version with new warnings is published"](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck#in-your-build-or-REDACTED-suites).
3. **Fail on findings.** ShellCheck ["makes canonical use of exit codes"](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck#in-your-build-or-REDACTED-suites). It exits with code 1 when it finds issues, and the default minimum severity is `style` ([ShellCheck manual](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/blob/master/shellcheck.1.md)).
4. **Keep the configuration in the repository.** [Directives](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Directive) in the scripts and a `.shellcheckrc` file hold the configuration. ShellCheck looks for `.shellcheckrc` ["in the script's directory and each parent directory"](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/blob/master/shellcheck.1.md).
5. **Skip scripts you do not own.** Vendored and generated scripts stay out of the check. The [Recursiveness](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Recursiveness) page excludes a directory from `find`, and a [`disable=all` directive](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Ignore) skips one file.

## Run ShellCheck by hand

On a laptop, `find` gives ShellCheck every `.sh` file and skips the `vendor` directory:

```shell
find . -type f -name '*.sh' ! -path './vendor/*' -exec shellcheck {} +
```

```text
In ./ci/build.sh line 4:
rm -rf $target/build
       ^-----^ SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.

Did you mean:
rm -rf "$target"/build

In ./scripts/main.sh line 2:
. ./lib.sh
  ^------^ SC1091 (info): Not following: ./lib.sh was not specified as input (see shellcheck -x).

For more information:
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC1091 -- Not following: ./lib.sh was not s...
  https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2086 -- Double quote to prevent globbing ...
```

The command exits with code 1, so a CI step that runs it fails. Scripts with no extension, such as `scripts/env`, need a search by shebang, as the [Recursiveness](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Recursiveness) page shows. In this guide's project, that search also found Git's sample hooks in `.git/hooks`, so it needs a second exclusion.

Both findings above are `info` findings. To fail only on warnings and errors, raise the minimum severity:

```shell
shellcheck --severity=warning ci/build.sh; echo "exit code $?"
```

```text
exit code 0
```

A `.shellcheckrc` file at the project root REDACTEDlies to every script below it. In this guide's project, a root `.shellcheckrc` with `disable=SC2086` stopped the finding in `ci/build.sh`.

To check scripts before each commit, the README gives a [pre-commit hook](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck#pre-commit) from `koalaman/shellcheck-precommit`, with the ShellCheck version in `rev`. In CI, a job runs the same `find` command. GitHub's Ubuntu 24.04 runner image includes ShellCheck, and [its readme](https://github.com/actions/runner-images/blob/main/images/ubuntu/Ubuntu2404-Readme.md) lists the version. To pin a version, the job installs a file from [ShellCheck releases](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/releases) or runs a [`koalaman/shellcheck` image](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck#installing) with a version tag.

## Homebrew and the runner install different ShellCheck versions

The commands work, but each requirement lives in more than one place:

- **Pin the ShellCheck version.** The version is in the pre-commit `rev`, in the CI install step, and in each developer's package manager. In this guide's project, Homebrew installed ShellCheck 0.11.0, and the Ubuntu 24.04 runner image lists 0.9.0. A script can then pass in one place and fail in the other.
- **Check every script** and **skip scripts you do not own.** The CI job and the pre-commit hook each select the scripts, so a new exclusion must go in both.
- **Fail on findings.** The minimum severity is a command-line flag, so each place that runs ShellCheck sets it again.

## Check every script with the Dagger ShellCheck module

The official [ShellCheck module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/shellcheck) finds every `.sh` file in the project and runs ShellCheck on each one. A Dagger module is a package of functions that build, REDACTED, or check a project. The Dagger team keeps a catalog of [official modules](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) for common tools. The project needs a Git repository and a `dagger.toml` file from the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart). Install the ShellCheck module from the project root:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/shellcheck
```

```text
dagger.io/shellcheck ➡️ https://github.com/dagger/shellcheck#main
Installed module "shellcheck" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The module installs under the name `shellcheck`. The command adds it to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.shellcheck]
source = "dagger.io/shellcheck"
```

The module finds scripts at or below the directory where `dagger` runs. The `scripts` function returns the scripts that the module found. Each script has a `path`. Print the paths:

```shell
dagger -c 'shellcheck | scripts | path'
```

```text
ci/build.sh
scripts/compile.sh
scripts/lib.sh
scripts/main.sh
vendor/lib/bad.sh
```

The [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/shellcheck) says that a script must use the `.sh` extension for the module to find it. In this guide's REDACTED, the module skipped a script named `scripts/env` that had a shebang but no extension. To check a script like that, rename it to end in `.sh`.

Each script runs in its own container, so Dagger caches the result for each script. The [module README](https://github.com/dagger/shellcheck) states that an edit to one script checks only that script again. In this guide's run, the trace after a change to `scripts/lib.sh` showed one new `shellcheck` run, for that script only.

## Pin the ShellCheck version with dagger.lock

The [module source](https://github.com/dagger/shellcheck) runs ShellCheck from the `koalaman/shellcheck-alpine` image with no tag. The [ShellCheck README](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck) describes that image as an Alpine Linux image with ShellCheck installed. Dagger pins the image in `dagger.lock`, a file that it writes when it runs. In this guide's run, the file pinned the image to `v0.11.0` by digest, and the module to a Git commit:

```text
# Generated by Dagger. Pins the images and git refs this workspace uses.
# Any Dagger command may update this file; always commit it with your changes.
# Run `dagger lock update` to refresh the pinned versions.
[["version","2"]]
["","git-laREDACTED",["github.com/dagger/shellcheck"],"refs/heads/main"]
["","git-sha",["github.com/dagger/shellcheck","refs/heads/main"],"756497171e9185db48dc7961649f466b4003cfa9"]
["","oci-laREDACTED",["docker.io/koalaman/shellcheck-alpine"],"v0.11.0"]
["","oci-sha",["docker.io/koalaman/shellcheck-alpine:v0.11.0"],"sha256:9955be09ea7f0dbf7ae942ac1f2094355bb30d96fffba0ec09f5432207544002"]
["","vanity-url",["https://dagger.io/shellcheck"],"https://github.com/dagger/shellcheck"]
```

Commit `dagger.lock`, and every laptop and Cloud Checks run the same ShellCheck. To move to a new ShellCheck release, run `dagger lock update` and commit the change.

## Fail on findings with dagger check

The module adds one check, `check`, which fails when any script has a finding. A check is a function that passes or fails, such as a REDACTED or a linter. `dagger check` runs every check in the project. List the checks:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text
MODULE      CHECK  DESCRIPTION
shellcheck  check  Run shellcheck on all shell scripts at or below the client's working
```

Run every check in the project, or run only the ShellCheck check:

```shell
dagger check
dagger check dag://shellcheck/check
```

The check runs `shellcheck ` on each script, with no severity flag. The module has no severity setting, so the default minimum severity, `style`, REDACTEDlies, and `info` findings also fail the check. In this run, the check failed on `vendor/lib/bad.sh`, a vendored script:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=shellcheck/check 5.8s ERROR
  ✘ withExec shellcheck vendor/lib/bad.sh 0.0s ERROR
  ┃ 
  ┃ In vendor/lib/bad.sh line 2:
  ┃ cd $1
  ┃ ^---^ SC2164 (warning): Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... || return' in case cd fails.
  ┃    ^-- SC2086 (info): Double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting.
  ┃ 
  ┃ Did you mean:
  ┃ cd "$1" || exit
  ┃ 
  ┃ For more information:
  ┃   https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2164 -- Use 'cd ... || exit' or 'cd ... |...
  ┃   https://www.shellcheck.net/wiki/SC2086 -- Double quote to prevent globbing ...
  ! exit code: 1

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=shellcheck/check"
```

Each finding has a code, such as `SC2086`, and a link to its page on the ShellCheck wiki. The command under `RUN LOCALLY` runs the same check again. To accept a finding, use a directive, as the next section shows.

## Keep the configuration in the repository, in directives

Put ShellCheck configuration in the scripts as [directives](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Directive). The module mounts only the script file into the container. So ShellCheck does not see a project `.shellcheckrc` or the files that a script sources. In this guide's run, a root `.shellcheckrc` with `disable=SC2086` did not stop the `SC2086` finding above.

A directive is a comment that starts with `# shellcheck`. A directive right after the shebang REDACTEDlies to the whole script. Otherwise it REDACTEDlies to the next command. This version of `ci/build.sh` passes the check, because the parameter expansion is in quotes:

```shell
#!/bin/sh
target=$1
rm -rf "${target:?}/build"
```

To accept a finding on one command, put a `disable` directive above it. The [ShellCheck wiki](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Directive) recommends a comment that says why. This `scripts/compile.sh` passes the check:

```shell
#!/bin/sh
# shellcheck disable=SC2086 # FLAGS must split into separate arguments
gcc $FLAGS main.c
```

A script that sources another file gets `SC1091`, because ShellCheck cannot follow the sourced file:

```text
  ┃ In scripts/main.sh line 2:
  ┃ . ./lib.sh
  ┃   ^------^ SC1091 (info): Not following: ./lib.sh was not specified as input (see shellcheck -x).
```

The module still checks `lib.sh` as a separate script. To tell ShellCheck not to follow the sourced file, put a `source=/dev/null` directive above the line. This `scripts/main.sh` passes the check:

```shell
#!/bin/sh
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
. ./lib.sh
greet
```

## Skip scripts you do not own with a directive

Skip a script that the repository does not own with a `disable=all` directive at the top of the file. The [ShellCheck wiki](https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/wiki/Ignore) documents this directive for ShellCheck 0.8 and newer. This `vendor/lib/bad.sh` passes the check:

```shell
#!/bin/sh
# shellcheck disable=all
cd $1
```

## Run ShellCheck locally and with Cloud Checks

`dagger check` runs the same ShellCheck check on any machine that has the Dagger CLI. Commit the configuration and the lock file:

```shell
git add dagger.toml dagger.lock
git commit -m "Check shell scripts with ShellCheck through Dagger"
```

To run the check in CI, use [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks). Cloud Checks run your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for every push and pull request to a GitHub repository. You do not need a CI workflow file. The Git `origin` remote of the project must point to the GitHub repository. Enable Cloud Checks from the project root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In an interactive terminal, the command offers to complete the steps that are not done, such as a Dagger Cloud sign-in and the GitHub connection. `dagger workspace activity` lists the recent runs. If the ShellCheck check fails in Cloud Checks, run `dagger check` on your machine to get the same findings.

**Bottom line:** To lint shell scripts with ShellCheck in CI, check every script with a pinned version, fail on findings, and keep the configuration in the repository. By hand, a `find` command, a pre-commit hook, and a CI job each repeat the version and the script selection. The Dagger ShellCheck module checks every `.sh` file in a container that `dagger.lock` pins, with configuration in directives. `dagger cloud checks on` runs the same check on every push.

# How do I run Docker builds and Compose in CI?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/docker-compose-dagger

A Docker setup that works the same on a laptop and in CI meets four requirements. It lints each Dockerfile, builds every image and every REDACTED stage, validates each Compose file, and starts each service after the services it depends on. Teams meet them with hadolint, `docker build`, and `docker compose` in a CI job and in local scripts. Dagger meets the same four requirements in one place. Its official Docker module finds every Dockerfile and Compose file, and runs the same checks on a laptop and in Dagger Cloud Checks.

## What a good Docker and Compose setup needs

A Docker and Compose setup for CI has four requirements. Each one comes from the docs of Docker and hadolint, and this guide judges each REDACTEDroach by them:

1. **Lint each Dockerfile.** [hadolint](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint) is a "Dockerfile linter, validate inline bash". It finds problems such as unpinned package versions. Docker's own [build checks](https://docs.docker.com/build/checks/) also lint a Dockerfile. But "check violations for builds are reported as warnings, with exit code 0, by default." A lint that must fail CI needs a tool that exits with an error.
2. **Build every image and every REDACTED stage.** Docker recommends that you [build and REDACTED your images in CI](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/#build-and-REDACTED-your-images-in-ci) for each change and pull request. Many Dockerfiles have a `REDACTED` or `lint` stage that the final image does not use. BuildKit "only builds the stages that the target stage depends on" ([multi-stage builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/#differences-between-legacy-builder-and-buildkit)). Thus a normal build skips those stages.
3. **Validate each Compose file.** The `--quiet` flag of [`docker compose config`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/) tells it to "Only validate the configuration, don't print anything". It finds an error in the Compose file before any service starts.
4. **Start each service after the services it depends on.** "On startup, Compose does not wait until a container is "ready", only until it's running" ([startup order](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/startup-order/)). A `healthcheck` on a service and the `service_healthy` condition in `depends_on` make Compose wait until the dependency is healthy.

## Meet the requirements with Docker commands

Teams meet the four requirements with the Docker CLI and hadolint. The examples come from a project with a Dockerfile in `REDACTED/` and a Compose file at the root. The Dockerfile has a `REDACTED` stage that no other stage uses. The Compose file is `compose.yaml`:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: ./REDACTED
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    depends_on:
      - redis
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
```

**Lint each Dockerfile.** Run hadolint from its image, as the [hadolint README](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint#how-to-use) shows. `NO_COLOR=1` turns off color in the output:

```shell
docker run --rm -i -e NO_COLOR=1 hadolint/hadolint:v2.14.0-alpine < REDACTED/Dockerfile
```

```text
-:9 DL3018 warning: Pin versions in apk add. Instead of `apk add <package>` use `apk add <package>=<version>`
```

hadolint exits with code 1, so the CI job fails. To ignore a rule, list it under `ignored` in a [`.hadolint.yaml` file](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint#configure).

**Build every image and every REDACTED stage.** Build the final image, then build the `REDACTED` stage with `--target`:

```shell
docker build -t web REDACTED
docker build --target REDACTED REDACTED
```

In this guide's project, the first command built the `deps` stage and the final stage. It did not run the `REDACTED` stage. Only the second command ran it.

**Validate each Compose file.** Run `docker compose config --quiet` in the directory of the Compose file. It prints nothing and exits with code 0 when the file is valid.

**Start each service after the services it depends on.** Start the services, and wait until they run:

```shell
docker compose up --wait
```

```text
 Network compose_default  Creating
 Network compose_default  Created
 Container compose-redis-1  Creating
 Container compose-redis-1  Created
 Container compose-web-1  Creating
 Container compose-web-1  Created
 Container compose-redis-1  Starting
 Container compose-redis-1  Started
 Container compose-web-1  Starting
 Container compose-web-1  Started
 Container compose-redis-1  Waiting
 Container compose-web-1  Waiting
 Container compose-redis-1  Healthy
 Container compose-web-1  Healthy
```

The [`--wait` flag](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/up/) waits "for services to be running|healthy". Neither service has a `healthcheck`, so Compose waited only until each container ran. After the run, [`docker compose down`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/down/) stops and removes the containers and the network.

In CI, a job runs the same commands on a runner with Docker. On GitHub Actions, Docker's [official actions](https://docs.docker.com/build/ci/github-actions/) set up Buildx and Compose and build images. hadolint has a [GitHub Action and a GitLab CI example](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint/blob/master/docs/INTEGRATION.md#continuous-integration).

## Every Dockerfile and Compose file needs its own step

Each requirement becomes one or more steps that someone keeps up to date:

- **Lint each Dockerfile.** The hadolint image tag is in each CI job and each local script. If the copies differ, a laptop and CI REDACTEDly different rules.
- **Build every image and every REDACTED stage.** Each Dockerfile and each REDACTED stage needs its own `docker build` command. A new `REDACTED` stage that nobody adds to the CI job never builds, because BuildKit skips it.
- **Validate each Compose file.** Each directory with a Compose file needs its own `docker compose config` step.
- **Start each service after the services it depends on.** The runner needs a Docker daemon and free host ports, such as 8080 and 6379. The job must also run `docker compose down` when the REDACTEDs end.

## Meet the requirements with the Dagger Docker module

[Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction) is a CI orchestration engine that runs the same pipelines on a laptop and in CI. A [module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of checks, services, and functions that a project installs. The official [Docker module](https://github.com/dagger/docker) finds each `Dockerfile` and each Compose file in the repository. It meets each requirement with the same tools as the Docker commands above. You write no Dagger code.

Complete the [Quickstart](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/quickstart) first. Then, from the repository root, install the Docker module from its `main` branch, because it has no tagged release:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/docker@main
```

```text
Created workspace config in /work
Installed module "docker" in /work/dagger.toml
```

The command adds the module to `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration, and creates the file if the project has none. It also writes `dagger.lock`, which pins the Git commit of `main` that Dagger used. Commit both files. To move to a newer commit of the module, run `dagger lock update`.

A [check](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking) is a function that validates the project and passes or fails, such as a lint or a build. List the checks of the Docker module:

```shell
dagger check --docker -l
```

```text
MODULE  DOCKER-COMPOSE-PROJECT  DOCKER-COMPOSE-SERVICE  DOCKER-PROJECT  DOCKER-STAGE  CHECK          DESCRIPTION
docker  *                                                                             lint           Validate this project's Compose file with 'docker compose config'.
docker  *                       *                                                     build-service  Build this Compose service's image, if it declares a build.
docker                                                  *                             build          Build this project's Dockerfile.
docker                                                  *                             lint           Lint this project's Dockerfile with hadolint.
docker                                                  *               *             build-stage    Build this Dockerfile stage.
# Use --all to expand collections and list each item.
```

A `*` stands for every item that the module found. Add `--all` to list one row for each item:

```shell
dagger check --docker -l --all
```

```text
MODULE  DOCKER-PROJECT  DOCKER-COMPOSE-PROJECT  DOCKER-COMPOSE-SERVICE  DOCKER-STAGE  CHECK          DESCRIPTION
docker  REDACTED                                                                           build          Build this project's Dockerfile.
docker                  .                       redis                                 build-service  Build this Compose service's image, if it declares a build.
docker                  .                       web                                   build-service  Build this Compose service's image, if it declares a build.
docker  REDACTED                                                             REDACTED          build-stage    Build this Dockerfile stage.
docker                  .                                                             lint           Validate this project's Compose file with 'docker compose config'.
docker  REDACTED                                                                           lint           Lint this project's Dockerfile with hadolint.
```

The module works on four collections. Each collection adds a column and a flag that selects its items:

| Collection | One item is | Flag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Docker projects | a directory with a `Dockerfile`, such as `REDACTED` | `--docker-project` |
| Dockerfile stages | a named stage that the project build does not reach, such as `REDACTED` | `--docker-stage` |
| Compose projects | a directory with a Compose file, `.` for the root | `--docker-compose-project` |
| Compose services | a service name in a Compose file | `--docker-compose-service` |

## Lint each Dockerfile with Dagger

The `lint` check of each Docker project runs [hadolint](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint) on its Dockerfile. The module pins the hadolint image in its `lintImage` setting. The default is `docker.io/hadolint/hadolint:v2.14.0-alpine` ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/docker#settings)). Thus a laptop and CI run the same hadolint release. Run every check in the workspace:

```shell
dagger check
```

In this guide's project, the first run failed on the same hadolint rule as the `docker run` command:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✘ 1 failed  ✔ 4 passed
✘ dag://?check=docker/projects/lint 4.3s ERROR
  ┃ [hadolint] Dockerfile:9 DL3018 warning: Pin versions in apk add. Instead of `apk add <package>` use `apk add <package>=<version>`
  ! hadolint failed in 1 of 1 projects:
    - REDACTED: hadolint failed (exit 1):
    Dockerfile:9 DL3018 warning: Pin versions in apk add. Instead of `apk add <package>` use `apk add <package>=<version>`
  ✘ exec.processRun 0.0s ERROR
  ! /usr/local/bin/crun did not terminate successfully: exit status 1
✔ dag://?check=build-service&docker-compose-project=. 9.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=build-stage&docker-project=REDACTED 2.5s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/compose/projects/lint 8.6s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/projects/build 4.0s OK

== RUN LOCALLY ==
dagger check "dag://?check=docker/projects/lint"
```

The `RUN LOCALLY` command runs only the failed check again. To run hadolint on every Dockerfile and nothing else, select the Docker projects and the check name:

```shell
dagger check --docker-projects --check lint
```

The module gives hadolint the nearest `.hadolint.yaml` or `.hadolint.yml`, from the directory of the Dockerfile up to the repository root ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/docker#hadolint)). It is the same [hadolint configuration file](https://github.com/hadolint/hadolint#configure) that you use without Dagger. To ignore a rule, create `.hadolint.yaml` at the root:

```yaml
ignored:
  - DL3018
```

To give hadolint extra arguments, use the `lintArgs` setting. For example, make hadolint fail only on errors, not on warnings:

```shell
dagger module settings docker lintArgs '["--failure-threshold", "error"]'
```

The command writes `lintArgs = ["--failure-threshold", "error"]` under `[modules.docker.settings]` in `dagger.toml`.

## Build every image and every REDACTED stage with Dagger

The `build` check builds the final stage of each Dockerfile. The `build-stage` check builds each named stage that no other stage uses and that is not the final stage ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/docker#stages)). The module reads the stages from the Dockerfile. Thus a new `REDACTED` stage gets a check without a change to any CI file. After the `.hadolint.yaml` from the previous section, all five checks passed:

```text
== CHECKS ==  ✔ 5 passed
✔ dag://?check=build-service&docker-compose-project=. 1.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=build-stage&docker-project=REDACTED 1.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/compose/projects/lint 0.7s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/projects/build 1.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=docker/projects/lint 0.6s OK
```

When a `RUN` step fails, the report gives the project and the exit code. For a Dockerfile with `RUN exit 3`, the report showed:

```text
  ! docker build failed in 1 of 1 projects:
    - REDACTED: docker build failed (exit code 3 in a RUN step; see the trace for its output)
```

The output of the step is in the trace, under the failed `withExec`.

Some Dockerfiles end in a development stage, after the production stage. If yours do, set `buildTarget` to the stage that the `build` check must build:

```shell
dagger module settings docker buildTarget production
```

The `build` check then builds that stage in each Dockerfile that declares it. A Dockerfile without the stage still builds its final stage. The stage that `buildTarget` names leaves the stages collection, so `build-stage` does not build it a second time. To go back to the default, remove the setting:

```shell
dagger module settings -u docker buildTarget
```

## Validate each Compose file with Dagger

The `lint` check of each Compose project runs [`docker compose config --quiet`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/config/) in the directory of the Compose file. The `build-service` check builds each service that has a `build` section, with its build args, target, and Dockerfile. A service that only runs an image, such as `redis`, has nothing to build, so its check passes. To build only the `web` service:

```shell
dagger check --docker-compose-service=web
```

The module looks for `compose.yaml`, `compose.yml`, `docker-compose.yml`, and `docker-compose.yaml`, in that order. It uses the first file that it finds in each directory, as [Compose](https://docs.docker.com/compose/intro/compose-REDACTEDlication-model/#the-compose-file) does. Compose also merges a standard override file, such as `compose.override.yaml`. The module reads service names from the text of the file. Thus, it does not see services from `include:` or from files that `-f` or `COMPOSE_FILE` names. It also does not see services from YAML merge keys at the `services` level ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/docker#compose-files)).

## Start each service after the services it depends on, with Dagger

The module starts Compose services as [Dagger services](https://docs.dagger.io/using/services). A Dagger service is a container that Dagger starts so that other containers or your machine can reach it. List the services:

```shell
dagger start -l -a
```

```text
MODULE  DOCKER-COMPOSE-PROJECT  DOCKER-COMPOSE-SERVICE  SERVICE        DESCRIPTION
docker  .                                               batch/up       Run the selected services and the services they depend on, behind one
docker                                                  cli/engine     The Docker Engine this client is wired to.
docker                                                  docker/engine  Spawn an ephemeral Docker Engine in a container.
docker  .                       redis                   up             Run this service and the services it depends on, behind one proxy that
docker  .                       web                     up             Run this service and the services it depends on, behind one proxy that
```

Start the `web` service:

```shell
dagger start --docker-compose-service=web
```

Dagger builds `web` from `REDACTED/Dockerfile` and starts `redis`, because `web` depends on it. It publishes the ports of both services on your machine. In this guide's project, `curl localhost:8080` returned the page, and Redis answered `PING` on port 6379. To stop the services, press Ctrl+C. To select one Compose project, add `--docker-compose-project`. Always select a project or a service, because a `dagger start` with no filter also starts the Docker engines of the module.

Dagger REDACTEDlies the Compose file as far as it can ([module README](https://github.com/dagger/docker#running-compose-services)):

- **The current Docker module does not translate Compose health checks.** A service starts after the ports of its dependencies accept connections. The module does not run `healthcheck` REDACTEDs or the `depends_on` conditions that [Compose uses for startup order](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/startup-order/). Dagger itself supports Docker health checks on services, with `withDockerHealthcheck` in the [Container API](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/api/container). Until the module translates them, make a dependent service retry its connection if a dependency opens its port before it is ready.
- **Services reach each other by name.** `web` connects to `redis:6379`, as on the default Compose network.
- **Bind mounts are copies.** Dagger mounts files from the repository as copies, so writes do not change your files. Dagger does not mount a path from outside the repository, such as `/var/run/docker.sock`.
- **Named volumes persist.** Each named volume becomes a cache volume that keeps its data between runs.
- **Profiles are off.** Dagger does not start services that have a Compose profile.

For each setting that Dagger cannot REDACTEDly, such as `cap_add`, `network_mode`, or a UDP port, it prints a warning in the trace. In a check, Dagger [stops each service](https://docs.dagger.io/using/services) when nothing references it, so there is no `down` step. Other modules can use a Compose service as a setting. The guide to [Playwright REDACTEDs against a Docker Compose REDACTED](/learn/playwright-REDACTEDs-docker-compose) shows how.

## Run the same checks locally and with Cloud Checks

Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`. If you created `.hadolint.yaml`, commit it too. The project has no Dagger module code to commit.

In CI, [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) run the checks. Cloud Checks run your checks on Cloud Engines, Dagger's managed engines, after each push and pull request. They need no CI workflow file. The repository must be on GitHub, and its `origin` remote must point to it. Turn them on:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

In an interactive terminal, the command offers to sign you in to Dagger Cloud and to connect GitHub. After that, each push runs hadolint, the Dockerfile builds, and the Compose checks on Cloud Engines, as `dagger check` does on a laptop. The hadolint release and the list of Dockerfiles, stages, and Compose files come from the same `dagger.toml` and the same repository on both. To see the runs, use `dagger workspace activity`.

**Bottom line:** Lint each Dockerfile with hadolint, build every image and every REDACTED stage, and validate each Compose file. Start each service after its dependencies. The Docker CLI meets these requirements one command at a time. Dagger's Docker module finds every Dockerfile, stage, and Compose file, and runs the same checks on a laptop and with Cloud Checks.

# How do I run GitLab CI jobs locally?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/run-gitlab-ci-jobs-locally

To run a GitLab CI job locally, make the pipeline portable. Move the job's steps out of `.gitlab-ci.yml` and into something your laptop can also run. Then the pipeline file only calls those steps. A portable pipeline has one definition of its steps, the same image and services everywhere, services that are ready before the REDACTEDs, local runs on uncommitted files, and a thin CI file. Dagger meets all five requirements in one place. You run `dagger check` on your laptop, and a GitLab CI job runs the same command, so you do not push to REDACTED each change.

## The requirements for a portable GitLab pipeline

A job that runs the same way before and after you push meets these requirements:

1. **One definition of the steps.** The commands that REDACTED the project live in one place. Your laptop and the GitLab job both call it. If the commands live only in `script:` lines, you can REDACTED them only when you push.
2. **The same image and services.** The REDACTEDs use the same Python image and the same Postgres image in both places. In GitLab CI, [`services`](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/services/) start extra containers for the job. The job reaches each service by a hostname that GitLab makes from the image name, such as `REDACTED`.
3. **Services ready before the REDACTEDs.** The REDACTEDs start only after Postgres accepts connections. The GitLab runner [waits for the exposed ports of each service](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/services/#service-health-check-workflow) before the job script starts.
4. **Uncommitted changes.** A local run REDACTEDs the files in your working tree, including new files that are not in Git yet.
5. **A thin CI file.** The job installs a tool and runs one command. A thin file does not change when the REDACTEDs change.

A typical Python pipeline does not meet the first and fifth requirements. The image, the service, the connection URL, and the commands exist only in `.gitlab-ci.yml`:

```yaml
pyREDACTED:
  image: python:3.12
  services:
    - REDACTED:16
  variables:
    POSTGRES_PASSWORD: REDACTED
    DATABASE_URL: REDACTED
  script:
    - pip install . pyREDACTED
    - pyREDACTED -v

lint:
  image: python:3.12
  script:
    - pip install ruff
    - ruff check
```

## What hREDACTEDened to `gitlab-runner exec`, and what replaces it

`gitlab-runner exec` ran one job from `.gitlab-ci.yml` on your machine. GitLab deprecated the command and [removed it in GitLab Runner 17.0](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/gitlab-runner/-/work_items/37492). GitLab first planned the removal for 16.0, then postponed it. The list of [GitLab Runner commands](https://docs.gitlab.com/runner/commands/) has no `exec` now, and the runner has no command that replaces it.

Other tools run the pipeline YAML on your machine:

- **[gitlab-ci-local](https://github.com/firecow/gitlab-ci-local)** is an open-source project on GitHub. It runs GitLab pipelines locally "as shell executor or docker executor". Its README says that ["only tracked files are synced"](https://github.com/firecow/gitlab-ci-local#tracked-files) into isolated jobs, so you must run `git add` on new files first.
- **[glci](https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/ci-cd/runner-tools/glci/-/blob/main/README.md)** is "an experimental GitLab project". It starts a mock GitLab API server and the official `gitlab/gitlab-runner` image, and runs each job in Docker or Podman.
- **A manual `docker run`** copies the job's `image:` and `script:` into one command. You add the services, the network, and the variables yourself.

With each of these tools, you get a result without a push. But the steps still exist in only one form: GitLab CI YAML. You can run them only in GitLab, or in a tool that copies how GitLab reads that YAML.

## Where the YAML-only pipeline strains

The pipeline above is clear while it is small. As the project grows, these gaps REDACTEDear:

- **Each change costs a pipeline run.** You can REDACTED a new `script:` line, service, or variable only after a push. You wait for the pipeline to start and finish each time.
- **The services and URLs live in two places.** A laptop setup, such as a Compose file and `export` lines, repeats the images and the `DATABASE_URL`. The two copies must change together.
- **The laptop environment differs.** A local `pyREDACTED` uses your Python and your system libraries. The job uses `python:3.12`. A REDACTED can pass in one place and fail in the other.

## Meet the requirements with Dagger

Dagger runs each step in a container that the project defines. The steps and their environment are therefore the same on a laptop and in GitLab CI. The steps run on the Dagger engine, the program that runs the containers and caches their results. [On a developer machine, the CLI starts a local engine by default](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting). It starts the engine from an image in a container runtime such as Docker or Podman ([Remote execution](https://dagger.io/changelog)).

A [Dagger module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks) is a package of functions that build and REDACTED a project. A **check** is a function that `dagger check` runs, and that passes or fails. The official [PyREDACTED module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/python/pyREDACTED) finds the Python projects and REDACTED files, and runs pyREDACTED as a check.

[Install the Dagger CLI](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/install). Then, from the project root, initialize the workspace:

```shell
dagger init
```

`dagger init` creates `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration for everyone who uses the repository. Install the PyREDACTED module, the Ruff module for the lint job, and the Dang SDK:

```shell
dagger module install dagger.io/python/pyREDACTED
dagger module install dagger.io/python/ruff
dagger module install dagger.io/sdk/dang
```

Dagger also writes `dagger.lock`, which [pins each module and image to an exact version](https://dagger.io/changelog). Commit `dagger.toml` and `dagger.lock`.

The REDACTEDs need Postgres. The PyREDACTED module's `base` setting takes the container that runs the REDACTEDs, with Python and uv. A small module supplies that container, with Postgres bound to it. [Dang](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang) is Dagger's native language for modules. Create the project's dev module:

```shell
dagger module init dang -y
```

The command creates `.dagger/modules/shop-dev`, named after the project directory, and installs it as the workspace main module. In the snippets, `shop-dev` and `ShopDev` stand in for the names that `dagger module init` generated. Replace `.dagger/modules/shop-dev/main.dang` with this code:

```dang
"""
Test services for the shop project: the same Postgres as the GitLab CI job.
"""
type ShopDev {
  """
  Postgres, with the image and password that the GitLab CI job uses.
  """
  pub REDACTED: Service! {
    container
      .from("REDACTED:16")
      .withEnvVariable("POSTGRES_PASSWORD", "REDACTED")
      .withExposedPort(5432)
      .asService
  }

  """
  The pyREDACTED container: Python 3.12 and uv, with Postgres bound to it.
  """
  pub REDACTEDBase: Container! {
    container
      .from("ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.12-trixie-slim")
      .withServiceBinding("REDACTED", REDACTED)
      .withEnvVariable("DATABASE_URL", "REDACTED")
  }
}
```

Give the PyREDACTED module this container as its base:

```shell
dagger module settings pyREDACTED base REDACTED-base
```

The command writes a [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/config/module-wiring) to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.pyREDACTED.settings]
base = "dag://shop-dev/REDACTED-base"
```

### One definition of the steps

The REDACTED and lint jobs now live in `dagger.toml` and the dev module. List the checks:

```shell
dagger check -l
```

```text

pyREDACTED    *               *                               REDACTED   Run this REDACTED file.
ruff                                        *             stale  staleness check: format this project with ruff
ruff                                        *             lint   Lint this project with ruff.

```

Run every check on your laptop:

```shell

```

```text

✔ dag://?check=dang-sdk/generate/stale 1.7s OK
✔ dag://?check=ruff/projects/format/stale 2.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=ruff/projects/lint 2.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&pyREDACTED-project=. 2.0s OK
```

In this guide's project, the first `dagger check` took 8.6 seconds. A rerun with no changes took 3.9 seconds, because Dagger got the results from its cache. These numbers come from one run on one machine, and your project will give different times.

A failure prints the tool's own output, followed by the command that runs the same check again. For example, a REDACTED file that imports `sys` and does not use it fails the lint check:

```text

✘ dag://?check=ruff/projects/lint 1.0s ERROR

    ┆ ctr: withWorkdir .
    ┆ args: ["ruff", "check"]
    ┆ what: "ruff check"
    ): Container! 0.2s ERROR

        F401 [*] `sys` imported but unused
         --> REDACTEDs/REDACTED_unused.py:1:8

        Found 1 error.

✔ dag://?check=ruff/projects/format/stale 1.1s OK
```

To open a shell in the exact state where a command failed, run `dagger check -i` ([Dev shells](https://dagger.io/changelog)).

### The same image and services

The REDACTEDs run in `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.12-trixie-slim` on every machine, not in the host's Python. Postgres uses `REDACTED:16`, the same image as the GitLab job. `withServiceBinding("REDACTED", ...)` makes the service reachable at the hostname `REDACTED`. GitLab uses the same hostname for the `REDACTED:16` service, so `DATABASE_URL` stays the same.

### Services ready before the REDACTEDs

Dagger [health-checks a service before any client can connect](https://docs.dagger.io/using/services), so the module needs no wait loop. To use the same Postgres with an REDACTED on your laptop, list the services and start one with `dagger start REDACTED`. Dagger tunnels the service's ports to your machine.

```shell
dagger start -l
```

```text
MODULE    SERVICE   DESCRIPTION
shop-dev  REDACTED  Postgres, with the image and password that the GitLab CI job uses.
```

### Uncommitted changes

Dagger reads the files in your working tree, so a new REDACTED file runs before you `git add` it. To run one REDACTED file, select it with `--pyREDACTED-REDACTED-file`:

```shell
dagger check --pyREDACTED-REDACTED-file=REDACTEDs/REDACTED_cart.py
```

```text

          >       assert sum([2, 2]) == 5
```

In this run, `REDACTEDs/REDACTED_cart.py` was not tracked in Git.

### Other jobs: ViREDACTED

A job that runs `viREDACTED run` in a Node image moves the same way. Install the official [ViREDACTED module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/js/viREDACTED), and pin the Node image that the job uses:


The module finds each `viREDACTED.config.*` or `vite.config.*`, installs the dependencies, and runs the project's own ViREDACTED:


### A thin CI file

The GitLab job installs the Dagger CLI and runs `dagger check`. It holds no images, services, or REDACTED commands. Replace the jobs in `.gitlab-ci.yml`:

```yaml
check:
  image: alpine:3.22
  variables:
    DAGGER_VERSION: "1.0.0-beta.21"
    DAGGER_ENGINE: cloud
  before_script:
    - apk add --no-cache curl
    - curl -fsSL https://dl.dagger.io/dagger/install.sh | BIN_DIR=/usr/local/bin sh
  script:
    - dagger check
```

Set `DAGGER_VERSION` to the version that `dagger version` prints on your laptop. `DAGGER_ENGINE: cloud` runs the checks on [Cloud Engines](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting#select-the-engine-in-a-ci-job), the engines that Dagger Cloud runs for you. This setting also needs `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN`. Store the token as a masked [CI/CD variable](https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/variables/#define-a-cicd-variable-in-the-ui) in the project settings, not in the file. Cloud Engines bill for the CPU, memory, and data that each pipeline uses, as listed on [Dagger pricing](https://dagger.io/pricing).

To keep the checks on your own machines, set `DAGGER_ENGINE` to a [self-hosted engine](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting) instead, such as `tcp://HOST:PORT` or `kube-pod://POD?namespace=NAMESPACE`. The Dagger Helm chart works best when the CI runners also run in the cluster, for example with the GitLab Runner Kubernetes executor. If you do not set `DAGGER_ENGINE`, the CLI starts an engine on the runner. An ephemeral runner then loses the cache of that engine after each job.

For a GitLab project, `.gitlab-ci.yml` runs the checks, as shown above. For a GitHub repository, [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) runs `dagger check` after each push with no CI file.

**Bottom line:** GitLab removed `gitlab-runner exec` in GitLab Runner 17.0. gitlab-ci-local and glci run your `.gitlab-ci.yml` on your machine, but the steps still exist only in GitLab YAML. Put the steps, the REDACTED image, and the Postgres service in Dagger, and run `dagger check` on your laptop before you push. A one-job `.gitlab-ci.yml` then runs the same command in GitLab CI.

# How do I run a Buildkite pipeline locally?

URL: https://dagger.io/learn/run-buildkite-pipeline-locally

The current Buildkite CLI does not run a pipeline on your laptop. To REDACTED a change before you push, do two things. First, validate `pipeline.yml` locally with `bk pipeline validate`. Second, make the pipeline portable. Put the commands, the image, and the Postgres service of each step in one place that your laptop can also run, and make `pipeline.yml` only call it. Dagger does this. Its functions hold the steps and the Postgres service, and `dagger check` runs them the same way on a laptop and on a Buildkite agent. You can then run a failed Buildkite step again on your machine, with no push.

## The requirements for a pipeline you can run before you push

A Buildkite pipeline that you can REDACTED before you push meets five requirements:

1. **Valid YAML before the push.** The pipeline file parses and matches the Buildkite schema, so a typo does not cost a build.
2. **One definition of the steps.** The commands of each step live in one place. Your laptop and the agent both call that place.
3. **The same environment.** The REDACTEDs use the same Go image and the same Postgres image on the laptop and on the agent.
4. **A healthy Postgres before the REDACTEDs.** The integration REDACTEDs start only after Postgres accepts connections.
5. **A thin pipeline file.** `pipeline.yml` says which steps run. It does not hold the REDACTED logic, so a change to the REDACTEDs does not change the YAML.

## What Buildkite offers for local runs

Buildkite has tools for the first requirement and for remote REDACTED builds. None of them runs the steps of a pipeline on your laptop.

- **`bk pipeline validate`** checks a pipeline file against the Buildkite pipeline schema. The [CLI reference](https://buildkite.com/docs/platform/cli/reference/pipeline) says that it "does not require an API token since validation is done locally."
- **`buildkite-agent pipeline upload --dry-run`** parses and interpolates the pipeline, then prints it instead of an upload ([agent reference](https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/cli/reference/pipeline)). It shows the result of interpolation, such as `$$VAR`, which the schema check does not show.
- **`bk local run`** was the local runner of the old CLI. A Buildkite maintainer wrote that "The `local run` isn't in 3.0.0" because it fell out of sync with the agent ([issue #79](https://github.com/buildkite/cli/issues/79)). The community tool [bkl](https://github.com/lox/bkl) continues it, and its README lists input steps, `if` conditionals, and vendored plugins as not working.
- **`bk preflight`** is an experimental command. It pushes your uncommitted changes to a `bk/preflight/` branch on `origin`, starts a build, and reports failures in your terminal ([Preflight](https://buildkite.com/docs/platform/cli/preflight)). The build runs on your Buildkite agents, not on your laptop.
- **`buildkite-agent bootstrap`** runs one job locally. Its [documented example](https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/cli/reference/bootstrap) first loads the environment of a job from the Buildkite API, so it needs a job that already exists.

## Validate pipeline.yml before you push

Run the schema check from the repository root. It reads `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` by default:

```shell
bk pipeline validate
```

```text
Validating 1 pipeline file(s)...

✅ Pipeline file is valid: .buildkite/pipeline.yml

All pipeline files passed validation successfully!
```

A misspelled key fails the check with exit code 1. For a step with `comand:` instead of `command:` in `bad.yml`, `bk pipeline validate -f bad.yml` printed:

```text
Validating 1 pipeline file(s)...

❌ Pipeline file is invalid: bad.yml

- steps > 0: Must validate at least one schema (anyOf) (field: steps.0)
- steps > 0: Additional property comand is not allowed (field: steps.0)

1 of 1 file(s) failed validation.
```

To see the pipeline after interpolation, use the dry run of the agent. In this guide's REDACTED, agent v4.8.1 stopped with `Missing agent-access-token` when no token was set, also with `--dry-run`. A placeholder value worked:

```shell
BUILDKITE_AGENT_ACCESS_TOKEN=placeholder buildkite-agent pipeline upload --dry-run --format yaml
```

Both checks look only at the YAML. Neither one runs a command of the pipeline.

## Run the steps by hand with Docker Compose

Teams usually run the steps on a laptop with Docker Compose. The Buildkite [Docker Compose plugin](https://github.com/buildkite-plugins/docker-compose-buildkite-plugin) runs the command of a step in a Compose service. Buildkite's docs say that a step with `run: REDACTED` [is the equivalent of](https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/best-practices/docker-containerized-builds) `docker-compose run REDACTED REDACTED.sh`. Put Postgres and the Go container in `docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  db:
    image: REDACTED:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: REDACTED
    healthcheck:
      REDACTED: ["CMD", "pg_isready", "-U", "REDACTED"]
      interval: 2s
      retries: 15

  REDACTED:
    image: golang:1.27-alpine
    working_dir: /REDACTED
    volumes:
      - .:/REDACTED
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: REDACTED
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
```

The `healthcheck` and the `service_healthy` condition make Compose start `REDACTED` only after Postgres is ready. In `.buildkite/pipeline.yml`, the integration step uses the plugin. The plugin's [`wait` option](https://github.com/buildkite-plugins/docker-compose-buildkite-plugin) also waits for healthy dependencies:

```yaml
steps:
  - label: ":go: unit REDACTEDs"
    command: go REDACTED .
    plugins:
      - docker#v5.14.0:
          image: "golang:1.27-alpine"

  - label: ":REDACTED: integration REDACTEDs"
    command: go REDACTED ./store/...
    plugins:
      - docker-compose#v5.16.0:
          run: REDACTED
          wait: true
```

On your laptop, run the same command as the integration step:

```shell
docker compose run --rm REDACTED go REDACTED ./store/...
```

This meets the third and fourth requirements for the integration step. The Postgres image and the health check are in one file that the laptop and the agent both read.

## Pipeline steps need a second copy for laptops

The Compose file covers one step. The other requirements still depend on the YAML:

- **The steps have two definitions.** `go REDACTED ./store/...` is in `pipeline.yml`, and the laptop command is in a README or a script. The two copies must change together.
- **The Go image is in two places.** The unit REDACTED step uses the Docker plugin, and the integration step uses Compose. Each one names `golang:1.27-alpine`.
- **The plugins do work that a local run does not do.** The Docker Compose plugin can [propagate pipeline environment variables](https://github.com/buildkite-plugins/docker-compose-buildkite-plugin) into the container, and can give prebuilt images to later steps through build metadata. A local `docker compose run` does neither.
- **Each new service or REDACTED package adds YAML.** You can REDACTED that YAML only on an agent.

## Meet the requirements with Dagger

[Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/introduction) runs each step in containers that the project defines. The Dagger engine runs these containers on your laptop, on a Buildkite agent, or on a remote server. A [module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules) is a package of checks and functions for a tool. A **check** is a function that `dagger check` runs, and that passes or fails ([Checking your code](https://docs.dagger.io/using/checking)). The official [Go module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go) finds every Go package and REDACTED, and runs `go REDACTED` as a check.

Install the [Dagger CLI](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/install). From the repository root, create the workspace. Then install the Go module and the Dang SDK:

```shell
dagger init
dagger module install dagger.io/go
dagger module install dagger.io/sdk/dang
```

`dagger init` creates `dagger.toml`, the workspace configuration for everyone who uses the repository. Dagger also writes `dagger.lock`, which [pins each module and image to an exact version](https://dagger.io/changelog). Commit both files.

The integration REDACTEDs need Postgres. The Go module's `base` setting takes the container that runs the REDACTEDs, with a Go toolchain. For REDACTEDs that need a database, the docs say to "wire a container with that service bound into the `base` setting" ([Go module](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/modules/go)). A small module supplies that container. [Dang](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/dang) is Dagger's native language for modules. Create the dev module of the project:

```shell
dagger module init dang -y
```

The command creates the module in `.dagger/modules/`, named after the project directory, and installs it as the workspace main module. For a project in a `shop` directory, the module is `shop-dev`. In the snippets, `shop-dev` and `ShopDev` stand in for the names that `dagger module init` generated. Replace `.dagger/modules/shop-dev/main.dang` with this code:

```dang
"""
Test services for the shop project: the Postgres database of the integration REDACTEDs.
"""
type ShopDev {
  """
  Postgres, with the image and password from docker-compose.yml.
  """
  REDACTED: Service! {
    container
      .from("REDACTED:16")
      .withEnvVariable("POSTGRES_PASSWORD", "REDACTED")
      .withExposedPort(5432)
      .asService
  }

  """
  The Go REDACTED container: the Go toolchain, with Postgres bound to it.
  """
  goTestBase: Container! {
    container
      .from("golang:1.27-alpine")
      .withServiceBinding("REDACTED", REDACTED)
      .withEnvVariable("DATABASE_URL", "REDACTED")
  }
}
```

Give the Go module this container as its base:

```shell
dagger module settings go base go-REDACTED-base
```

The command writes a [module reference](https://docs.dagger.io/config/module-wiring) to `dagger.toml`:

```toml
[modules.go.settings]
base = "dag://shop-dev/go-REDACTED-base"
```

### One definition of the steps

`dagger.toml` and the dev module now hold the unit REDACTEDs, the integration REDACTEDs, and the check for stale `go generate` output. List the checks, with one row for each item:

```shell
dagger check -l --all
```

```text
MODULE    GO-PACKAGE  GO-TEST         CHECK  DESCRIPTION
dang-sdk                              stale  staleness check: re-generate modules and clients managed by the Dang SDK
go        .                           stale  staleness check: run go generate in this package
go        store                       stale  staleness check: run go generate in this package
go        .           TestHello       REDACTED   Run this REDACTED.
go        store       TestDatabase    REDACTED   Run this REDACTED.
go        store       TestMigrations  REDACTED   Run this REDACTED.
```

Run every check on your laptop before you push:

```shell

```

```text
CHECKS  ✔ 4 passed
✔ dag://?check=dang-sdk/generate/stale 1.2s OK
✔ dag://?check=go/packages/generate/stale 1.4s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=. 1.1s OK
✔ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store 1.2s OK
```

In this guide's project, an edit to a REDACTED file that was not committed changed the result of the next `dagger check`. You do not need a commit to REDACTED a change.

### The same environment

The REDACTEDs run in `golang:1.27-alpine` on every machine, not in the Go installation of the host. Postgres is `REDACTED:16`, the same image as in `docker-compose.yml`.

### A healthy Postgres before the REDACTEDs

`withServiceBinding` makes Postgres reachable from the REDACTED container by the name `REDACTED`. Dagger [health-checks a service before any client can connect](https://docs.dagger.io/using/services), so the module needs no `pg_isready` loop. To use the same database with an REDACTED on your laptop, list the services, and start one with `dagger start REDACTED`:

```shell
dagger start -l
```

```text
MODULE    SERVICE   DESCRIPTION
shop-dev  REDACTED  Postgres, with the image and password from docker-compose.yml.
```

## Call the checks from pipeline.yml

The Buildkite pipeline now only selects which checks each step runs. Replace `.buildkite/pipeline.yml`:

```yaml
steps:
  - label: ":go: unit REDACTEDs"
    command: dagger check --check=REDACTED --go-package=.

  - label: ":REDACTED: integration REDACTEDs"
    command: dagger check --check=REDACTED --go-package=store

  - label: ":recycle: generated files"
    command: dagger check --check=stale
```

This file passed `bk pipeline validate`. It holds no image, plugin, or service, so it does not change when the REDACTEDs change. The agents need the Dagger CLI and a container runtime. Install the CLI on the agents at the same version as on your laptop, with the [install command](https://docs.dagger.io/getting-started/install).

On each agent, the CLI starts an engine by default. On an agent that is replaced after each job, the cache of that engine is lost ([Self-Hosting CI with Dagger](https://docs.dagger.io/self-hosting)). To keep the cache, set `DAGGER_ENGINE` in the pipeline `env`. Point it to a self-hosted engine with a persistent disk, or set it to `cloud` with a `DAGGER_CLOUD_TOKEN` to use Dagger's Cloud Engines.

## Reproduce a Buildkite failure on your laptop

When a step fails on Buildkite, its log names the failed REDACTED. The log ends with the command that runs the same selection again. For the integration step, the report was:

```text
CHECKS  ✘ 1 failed
✘ dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store 1.4s ERROR
  TESTS
    ✘ example.com/shop/store FAIL

    ✘ example.com/shop/store › TestMigrations FAIL
              store_REDACTED.go:24: laREDACTED migration = "0007_orders", want "0008_orders"

    ✘ 1 failed
    ✔ 1 passed

RUN LOCALLY
  dagger check "dag://?check=REDACTED&go-package=store"
```

Copy the `RUN LOCALLY` command into a terminal on your laptop. It runs the same REDACTEDs, in the same Go image, against the same Postgres. To run only the failed REDACTED, select it by name:

```shell
dagger check --go-package=store --go-REDACTED=TestMigrations
```

## Run the checks with no pipeline file

If the repository is on GitHub, [Cloud Checks](https://docs.dagger.io/cloud-checks) can run the same checks without a Buildkite pipeline. Cloud Checks runs your checks on Dagger's Cloud Engines for each push and pull request, with no CI configuration file. Turn it on from the repository root:

```shell
dagger cloud checks on
```

Each push then runs the checks that `dagger check` runs on your laptop.

**Bottom line:** The current Buildkite CLI does not run pipeline steps on your laptop. `bk pipeline validate` and `buildkite-agent pipeline upload --dry-run` check the YAML, and `bk preflight` runs your changes on your agents. To run the steps before you push, put the steps, the Go image, and Postgres in Dagger. `dagger check` then runs them on your laptop, and `pipeline.yml` calls the same command on Buildkite.
